pv: Re8 Rxe8+
e: The rook on the seventh is White's whole advantage, so offer to trade it: Re8 forces Rxe8+ and after you recapture, the pressure on f7/g7 disappears and your knight and rook get to breathe. Trading one pair of rooks is the standard way to defuse a bind like this.
ep: Rh6 leaves the rook offside and does nothing about e7. Nf5 comes with tempo against the rook and the g7 pawn, and after Rg6 g4 White simply keeps everything and adds threats, as the game showed.

pv: Ne4 Rxf7+ Kg8 fxe4 Rxd6 Re7 dxe4 R1xe4 Kf8 R7e6 Rd2 Re2 Rxe2 Rxe2 Rd8 Kf2
e: Ne4! is the practical way out: it offers the knight to eliminate the octopus on d6. After fxe4 Rxd6 the annoying knight is gone, and even a pawn down your rooks get active squares along the d-file instead of sitting and waiting to be squeezed.
ep: h5 does nothing about the two rooks and the Nd6, and Rxf7+ is simply available: Kg8 Rb7 and the second rook joins with Nf5. In the game the f7 pawn fell at once and the rooks doubled on the seventh.

pv: O-O Bd2 d6 b4 Nbc6 b5 Nd4 O-O h6 a4 Qc7 a5 bxa5 Ra3 a6 Nxd4
e: Castle first: O-O. The f5/e4 tension is yours to keep — White cannot resolve it favorably — and the plan flows naturally: d6, Nbc6 and then Nd4!, planting a knight in the hole in front of the d3-pawn (b4 Nbc6 b5 Nd4 in the line). King safety plus the better structure gives Black a stable pull (+0.9).
ep: fxe4 resolves the tension into White's hands: dxe4! recaptures toward the center, leaves your e6-pawn as the lasting weakness, and gifts White a free attacking plan with h4–h5 (Be3, O-O, h4 and h5 in the line). A structural concession (-0.4) the game never repaired.

pv: Nbc6 Be3
e: Finish development: Nbc6. The knight covers e5 and d4 and keeps the structure elastic — the d5 break stays in reserve for a moment when it doesn't leave e6 hanging behind it. After Be3 the position is roughly balanced with all your pieces working (-0.5).
ep: d5? leaves e6 without a single defender: Ng5! and it cannot be covered — dxe4 Nxe6 forks queen, rook and bishop, and Qc8 Nxg7 Kxg7 wins pawn and dark-squared bishop for the knight. In the game White missed it for a move (Qc2), but the same Ng5 motif landed shortly after anyway.

pv: d4 Nd1 Qd6 Ra2 Nd7 b3 h6 Re1 Qc6 Nb2 Qxe4 Bd3
e: d4! closes the position on your terms: the c3-knight is hit and must go backwards (Nd1), and — crucially — you keep the g7-bishop, guardian of your king's dark squares. The line runs Qd6, Nd7, h6 and later Qc6xe4, winning the e-pawn while White's pieces stand tangled (+1.3).
ep: Bxc3? sells your best defender for White's worst piece: after the recapture, dxe4 is met by Ng5!, and White regains e4 (Re1, Nxe4) with every dark square around your king sore. The game showed the price at once — Bh6, Ng5 and Nxf7! won the exchange.

pv: Nf5 Bxf8 exf3 Bxf3 Nc6 Bxc5 bxc5 Bxc6 Bxc6 Qe5 Qe7 b4 Rf8 Rad1 Nh4 f3
e: Nf5! answers the threat with a threat: the knight hits the h6-bishop, and if Bxf8 you have the zwischenzug exf3!, winning the f3-knight (Bxf3 follows). The f8-bishop eventually slips out via Bxc5, but material stays roughly level (+0.3) — a world away from losing the exchange.
ep: Rf7?? puts the rook on a forking square: Ng5! attacks f7, e6 and e4 all at once — Qe8 Nxf7 Qxf7 and the exchange is gone, with f3 undermining your e4-pawn next (-3.5). The game went exactly Ng5 Qe8 Nxf7.

pv: Nd4 Qg3 Nd7 Rad1 Re8 Rd2 Bc6 Bh6 e5 b4 Qxc4 Bxd7 Bxd7 bxc5 bxc5
e: Nd4! plants the knight where no pawn can ever touch it and threatens Ne2+, forking king and the c3-queen. White must give ground (Qg3), and only then come Nd7, Re8 and Bc6 — later even Qxc4 in the line, regaining a pawn. Activity first, then development (-1.8, but fighting).
ep: Nd7 lets White remove your one active piece: Bxf5! exf5 Rad1 and the d-file invasion is unstoppable — Rd6 hits b6 and g6, the rooks double, Rd8 lands. The game followed the script (Rad1, Bxf5, Bg5, Rd6) and the position slowly caved in (-3.3).

pv: Nd4 Be3 e5 Rd2 Nf6 Bd1 Qe6 Bh6 Re8 Re1 Bc6 b4 Nh5 Bg4
e: Nd4! was still there: it threatens Ne2+ forking king and queen, and after Be3 you finally get e5! — cementing the knight, hitting the f4-bishop and freeing your game, with Qe6, Re8 and Bc6 to follow. Worse but very holdable (-1.6).
ep: Nf6 attacks the g4-bishop but invites exactly the trade White wants: Bxf5! gxf5 Rd6! and the rook lands on the sixth rank with your dark squares leaking. The game went Bxf5 exf5 Bg5 Nd7 Rd6 — the same invasion the d4-knight would have prevented.

pv: Qf8 Qc6 Nxb4 Qc7 Nd3 Ra1 a6 Qxb6 Qc5 Rb1 Qxb6 Rxb6 Kf7 Rc6 Bd7 Rxa6
e: Qf8! is the only defense: White threatens Bh6 followed by Qg7#, and only the queen can physically hold g7. There is life afterwards — Qc6 Nxb4! grabs a pawn and the knight keeps kicking (Qc7 Nd3) — a bad position (-4.2), but a position, not a mating net.
ep: Ba6 ignores the mating net: Bh6! threatens Qg7#, and Qe7 only delays it — Qxe7 (nothing can recapture) and Qg7# next: mate in three. White's b5? in the game handed you one more chance to play Qf8; it had to be taken immediately.

pv: Qf8 Qxf8+ Kxf8 bxa6 Nc5 Be3 Ke7 f4 Na4 Rc1 Kf7 Rb1
e: Qf8 is still forced — it alone covers g7 against Bh6 and Qg7#. The price is real: Qxf8+ Kxf8 bxa6 wins the stranded bishop, though Nc5 goes hunting the a6-pawn while your king walks over. A grim ending (-5.4), but mate in three is grimmer.
ep: Bc8 rescues the bishop while the king burns: Bh6! came instantly in the game, and Qg7# cannot be parried — Qe7 Qxe7 Kh8 Qg7#. When mate is threatened, material stops mattering; only Qf8 kept the game alive.

pv: O-O Nxc6 bxc6 Qb4 Nxc4 e4 Bg4 Qc3 h6 Bf4 a5 a4 Bh5 h4
e: Castle first — the c4-pawn can't run. After O-O Nxc6 bxc6 the b5-queen is hit and must step to b4, and then ...Nxc4 wins the pawn anyway, now protected by d5, with your king safe and both rooks in the game.
ep: Grabbing at once lets White liquidate favourably: Nxc4 dxc4 pulls your d-pawn out of the centre, and e4! hits the f5-bishop with Qxb7 hanging over you — all with your king still on e8. In the game White regained the pawn with Qxc4 and stood better.

pv: O-O Bb2 Qg5 h4 Qg4 Qxg4 Bxg4 f3 Bf5 Rfc1 Rcd8 Bxc6 bxc6 g4 Be6 Bc3
e: Everything hinges on f7 — castle and it's covered: after O-O the f8-rook defends f7, all the Bxf7+ tricks vanish, and ...Qg5–g4 forces the queens off into a safe position.
ep: Ne7 drops f7: Bxf7+! is immune (Qc4 backs the bishop, so Kxf7 is illegal), and after ...Kf8 Qf4 protects it while preparing Bb3+, a discovered check from the f4-queen that forces ...Qxf4 Bxf4 — White emerges a clean pawn up with your king stranded, exactly the game.

pv: Kd8 e3 Rf8 h4 Bd7 Bc2 g6 Be4 b5 Kf1 Rf6 Ke2 Ke7
e: c7 is the only entry square for White's rook — Kd8 covers it and shuts the rook out completely. Down a pawn, that's the priority: after e3 Rf8 h4 Bd7 you finish development, the h8-rook joins on f8, and White's activity comes to nothing.
ep: Rd8 leaves c7 open: Rc7+!, and after Kd6 Rxg7 the rook eats the kingside — Rg8 then forces a trade into a two-pawns-down ending. In the game the checks (Rc7+ Kf6 Rf7+ Kg6 Re7) chased your king while the rook camped on the seventh.

pv: h6 Rdc1 Rc6 g3 Rfc8 Rxc6 Rxc6 Rd1 Qc7 Rb1 a5 Qe4 Rc5 Kg2 Rc4 Qe5
e: h6! is the move of a player in control: it gives the king air, forbids Ng5, and changes nothing about your grip — the d5-knight blockades everything, and the c-file comes next with Rc6 and Rfc8 doubling in the line. With no targets and no tricks, White can only sit and wait (+1.5).
ep: Rc3?? trusts the d5-knight to cover c3, but the knight is overloaded: Qxc3! — and if Nxc3, the knight abandons the d-file, so Rxd6 wins your queen, exactly as the game went (Rxd6, then Rxa6). Net result: you are a full rook down.

pv: Bd6 Qd8 Be5 Kg8 c4 Nh5 Qh3 Nf6 a4 Nd7 Qg3 Nxe5 Qxe5 f6 Qg3 a5
e: The c7-bishop is attacked, and Bd6! saves it with tempo on the e7-queen; after Qd8 Be5 it lands on the dream square, teaming with Qg3 against f6 and g7, and c4 fixes a lasting bind (+2.1).
ep: On a5 the bishop hits nothing, and Be4! offers to swap off your dangerous d3-bishop — after Bxd3 cxd3 the kingside pressure evaporates. In the game Nd5 saw the bishop scurry straight back to d2, a wasted trip.

pv: c4 Ne7 Qxc7 Rxc7 Rab1 b6 f3 Kg8 Kf2 g5 Bb4 Rd8 Be2 Ng6 Be1 f6
e: c4! kicks the d5-knight while your queen x-rays c7 along the g3–c7 diagonal: after Ne7 Qxc7 Rxc7 you trade into a clearly better endgame — two bishops, queenside space, and the offside a4-bishop to chase (+2.7).
ep: Qh3 goes the wrong way: Nc3! forces Bxc3 Qxc3, swapping off your dark-squared bishop and activating Black's queen, and with your own queen offside you had to offer Qf3 to trade back in a much worse version.

pv: d5 Nd7 Re1 Qd6 Rac1 Nc5 Bf1 Qg6 Qe3 Kh7 Bb4 b6 h3 Bd7 Kh2 f5
e: d5! locks the center a clean pawn up: the f6-knight loses its targets and must reroute via d7 to c5, met calmly by Re1 and Bf1. The h6-pawn is a tempting hook, but the position wants patience, not a sacrifice (+1.9).
ep: Bxh6? gxh6 Qxh6+ is refuted by Nh7! — the knight seals the h-file and you have no second attacker, leaving you a bishop for two pawns down. In the game exd4 soon followed and Black took over.

pv: Rab1 Rg8 Qe3 f6 dxe5 fxe5 Qxa7 Bc6 Rb3 Rg7 Re1 Ng5
e: Rab1 puts your idle rook to work against b7: after Rg8 Qe3 f6 dxe5 fxe5 Qxa7 you win a pawn back, and active heavy pieces are the only real chance while material is against you (-1.0).

pv: Rab1 Re6 Qd2 Rxe4 Bf3 Qf4 Qb4 Bc6 Rd1 a5 Qc4 Rg8 Bxe4 Qxe4 Qxd4+ Qxd4
e: Rab1 finally generates counterplay against b7: if Re6 then Qd2 hits the d4-passer, and when Rxe4 comes, Bf3! strikes the rook with b7 behind it, winning back time. It keeps you fighting at -2.5.
ep: Bh5 eyes f7, but Rxe4! calls the bluff: after Bf3 Qf4! the queens come off, and Bxb7 Rxc2 leaves Black's d4-passer and active pieces decisive. In the game Qc6 defended f7 first — and the e4-pawn fell anyway.

pv: Qxc6 Bxc6 Bxf7 Rxe4 f3 Re2 Bc4 Rd2 Bb3 Re8 Rd1 Ree2 Rxd2 Rxd2 Re1 Kg7
e: Qxc6! is the resource: after Bxc6, Bxf7! grabs a pawn while hitting the e8-rook, so material comes back, and with queens off Black's initiative fades — after Rxe4 f3 Re2 Bc4 the bishop slips out. Still worse (-2.3), but your king is finally safe.
ep: Qf4 drops e4 with tempo: Rxe4! attacks the queen, and after Qxf7 Rf8 Qg6 Re5 the h5-bishop is caught in the crossfire — the queen trade comes anyway in a far worse version. The game's Qxg6 Bxg6 Ng5 let Black consolidate the extra piece.

pv: Rd2 Nb5 h4 a5 f3 Rc8 Ra2 Nc3 Ra1
e: Your d1-rook is attacked by the c3-knight, and Rd2 solves everything: it steps out of the attack, keeps hitting d4, and still meets Bxc2 with Rxd4 tricks. After Nb5 h4 a5 f3 the game is dead level (0.0).

pv: Rxb7 Rxa4 h5 Nd4 Rd7 Ne2+ Kf2 Nf4 Rf7 a5 Ra7 Ra3 Kg3 Ne2+ Kh4 Rxf3
e: The rooks stare at each other on the d-file, but his d4-rook is defended by the c6-knight and your d7-rook is not — so it must earn its keep with Rxb7!. After Rxa4 h5 your active rook and kingside pawns hold the balance (+0.1).
ep: h5 overlooks that your d7-rook stood attacked and undefended: Rxd7 won it on the spot (Rxd4 was never available, since Nxd4 recaptures). The game record stops right there.

pv: Bxf3 Qxf3 Qb6 b3 Nd7 Qg3 Ne7 Bd3 h5 O-O h4 Qf4 Qc7 Re1 g6 Bb2
e: Bxf3 is the right answer to h3: after Qxf3 you hit b2 with ...Qb6, forcing b3, and develop calmly with ...Nd7 and ...Ne7 against the overextended e5-pawn. Giving up the bishop pair costs little here — White's remaining bishop stays passive behind its own pawns, and you keep the healthier structure (+0.8).

pv: O-O f4 c5 Nf3 Nbc6 Rg1 Qa5 Kb1 Nd4 Qe1 Nxf3 gxf3 b5 Rxg7+ Kxg7 Qh4
e: Castle first — every attacking idea works better with the king safe. After O-O f4 c5 the d4-knight is pushed back, ...Nbc6 and ...Qa5 follow, and ...Nd4 invades White's camp; even the desperado Rxg7+ Kxg7 doesn't bail White out (+2.1). The queen sortie can wait one move.

pv: b6 Na4 Qxe5 d4 Qc7 h4 Nd7 h5 a5 a3 b5 Nac5 a4 Nxd7 axb3 Nc5
e: b6! evicts the c5-knight, and after Na4 you collect the e5-pawn with Qxe5 — it is undefended and your c7-queen sees it down the c7–e5 diagonal. White's most active piece ends up on the rim, you win a center pawn, and your queenside structure stays untouched (+2.0).
ep: Na6 invites Nxa6 bxa6, wrecking your queenside into doubled isolated a-pawns; after d4 the freeing ...c5 break just drops a pawn to Nxc5 (-2.0). You offered to trade White's strong knight when one pawn move would have driven it away at a profit.

pv: e6 Qe2 Be7 Rd1 O-O a3 b6 Nc3 Bb7 b4 Rc8 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 Bxd5
e: e6 is the solid move: it shuts the c4 bishop's diagonal, unblocks ...Be7 and ...O-O, and only then do you worry about the pin. After Qe2 Be7 Rd1 O-O a3 b6 Black finishes development, gets the bishop to b7 and the extra tempo White has from the gambit fizzles out.

pv: Qd5 Qe2 e6 Nc3 Qd7 Bf4 Be7 Rfd1 Qc8 Ne4 O-O Nxf6+ Bxf6 Rac1 a6 Ba4
e: Qd5 centralises and offers the trade: from d5 the queen defends c6, controls the light squares and stops White's pieces from coming with tempo. After Qe2 e6 Nc3 Qd7 you get ...Be7 and ...O-O in and the extra pawn is neutralised by simply finishing development.

pv: Qc7 Bf4 Qb6 Rac1 Bxa3 Bxc6+ bxc6 Rxc6 Qd4 Rxe6+ fxe6 Qxa8+ Qd8 Qxd8+ Kxd8 bxa3
e: Qc7 steps out of the tactic before developing. From c7 the queen no longer stands on the b6 square where a deflection works, and ...Bxa3 followed by ...Bd6 comes next. The line Bf4 Qb6 Rac1 Bxa3 shows the point: once the knight on a3 is traded, White's pressure down the c-file is manageable.

pv: Qd5 Rxc6 Qxf3 Rc5+ Qc6 Bxc6+ bxc6 Rfc1 Ke7 Rxc6 Rhb8 b3 Nd5 Nc4 Rb5 Rd1
e: Qd5 does two jobs: it leaves the c-file pin and attacks the white queen on f3. That is the whole difference, because Rxc6 can then be answered by Qxf3! taking the queen first, and after Rc5+ Qc6 Bxc6+ bxc6 the material comes out level and Black is fine.
ep: Qb6 keeps the knight pinned against nothing and removes the ...Qxf3 resource, so Rxc6! simply wins: bxc6 Bxc6+ Ke7 Bxa8 and a whole rook is gone. The game followed the same idea with Bxc6+ first.

pv: Qd8 Rd1 Nd5 Nc4 O-O Ne3 Rb8 Nxd5 exd5 Qc3 Re8 Rc5 Qf6 Qxf6 gxf6 Rc2
e: Qd8 gets the queen off the a8-h1 diagonal, where the queen on f3 is lurking behind the rook on c6, and covers d-file entry squares. After Rd1 Nd5 Nc4 O-O Black finally castles, the knight sits beautifully on d5, and White's advanced rook has to retreat.

pv: Rc1+ Rxc1 Qxc1+ Kh2 Qb2 Kg1 h6 g3 a5 g4 a4 Kg2 g6
e: Your queen on b2 is attacked by the rook — Rc1+! answers by force: Rxc1 Qxc1+ Kh2 and now Qb2! returns to the same great square with the rooks traded, hitting a3 and f2. A pawn up with the far queenside majority (...a5–a4 in the line) and zero counterplay for White (+3.2).
ep: Qc3 offers exactly the trade White dreams of: Qxc3 Rxc3 and Rxb7! — the rook grabs a pawn and turns active, with Ng5xf7 tricks in the air. From +3.2 the game fell to +0.4; Rxb7 duly arrived, and the ending was eventually lost.

pv: Nc6 Ng5 h6 Nxf7 Rxa3 Nd8 Nxd4 Rb4 Ra1+ Kh2 Rd1 h4 a5 Ra4 Nb3 Nxe6
e: The b7-rook attacks your e7-knight along the seventh rank, and nothing defends it. Nc6! saves the piece and counterattacks both d4 and e5; after Ng5 h6 Nxf7 Rxa3 the pawn grabs cancel out and the game is level (+0.1) — the line even ends with ...Nxd4 and ...Nb3 hitting back.

pv: Bxf3 Rxf3 e5 Rff1 Qf7 dxe5 Qe7 b4 fxe5 Rxf8+ Rxf8 Rd1 Qf7 Qb3 Ne7 Nd7
e: The c5-knight eyes e6, so resolve the tension now: Bxf3! removes the f3-knight while the h5-bishop still can, and after Rxf3 e5! the e6-pawn steps out of Nc5's attack and strikes at d4; Qf7 then covers everything (+0.9).
ep: Rc7 leaves e6 hanging: Nxe6! forks the c7- and f8-rooks and hits g7. After Qh6 Nxc7 white wins the exchange plus a pawn (-2.7). In the game Nxe6 Re7 Nxf8 Kxf8 cost you the same material.

pv: Re2 Ne1
e: Re2! plants the rook on the second rank, hitting a2 with g2 next in its sights — white's best is the sad retreat Ne1 just to hold everything. Down the exchange, that active rook is exactly your compensation (-0.9).
ep: Qe4 steps onto the open e-file in front of its own rook: Rce1! attacks the queen, and the try Bxf3 loses to Rxe4 Bxe4 — queen for rook and knight. In the game the queen fled with Qf5, but Rxe7 Nxe7 Qxb7 followed and white consolidated (-4.1).

pv: Qe2 Rf3 Be8 Kh2 h5 Qb6 Ng6 Rxf6+ gxf6 Qxf6+ Kg8 Qe6+ Kh7 Nxg6 Qe4 Qxe4
e: Qe2! hits the f1-rook with the queen and — the real point — keeps the h5-bishop guarding e8. That defuses the back rank: Qb8+ Nc8 Qxc8+ can always be met by Be8 blocking the check. After Rf3 Be8 you are still down material (-4.6) but very much alive.

pv: h5 Qc7 h4 Nb6 Kg6 Qd7 Nf5 Nxd5 Ng3+ Kh2 Qd2 Qe8+ Kf5 Qf7 Qg5 Qd7+
e: You are worse but not without play: h5! starts the plan h5-h4, fixing white's g2 and h3, after which the e7-knight jumps to f5 and into g3+ — the engine line ends with your knight landing on g3 with check against the cornered king (-3.2).
ep: Kg6 strengthens the clearance sac Ne5+!: fxe5 vacates d7 with check, so Qxe7 regains the piece, and now Qe6+ and Qxe5+ force the queens off into a lost ending with your king stranded (-5.2). The game went exactly Ne5+ fxe5 Qxe7.

pv: Kh6 Qe5 Qd2 Qxe4 g5 Qe6+ Kg7 d5 g4 d6 h5 Qe5+ Kh6 Qf6+ Kh7
e: The king must step back: Kh6 stays out of the queen's reach, and after Qe5 you have Qd2, keeping your queen and e2-bishop active while the g- and h-pawns start running — still losing on material (-5.8), but there is fight left.

pv: hxg5 cxd5 Qd3 Qb6 O-O-O Qe6 Nb5 Bxb5 Qxb5+ Qd7 Qb3 e6
e: hxg5 is the recapture that keeps everything good about your position: the f4-bishop stays on the board raking the b8-h2 diagonal, the h-file opens against the weak h5-pawn, and black's knight on h7 remains entombed. After cxd5 Qd3 Qb6 O-O-O you castle into the attack with Nb5 ideas (+3.6).

pv: Qd3 Qc7 O-O-O e6 Nge2 Qd6 Qe3 Be7 f4 a6 Bh3 Nc6 Na4 Na5 Nc5 Nc4
e: Qd3 is the developing move that keeps the bind. It eyes the queenside and prepares O-O-O, after which Nge2 heads for f4 to hit e6 and h5 while the g5-pawn keeps black's kingside frozen. Black stays cramped and has to find squares for the b8-knight and f8-bishop first.

pv: Qd2 Nc6 O-O-O O-O-O Bh3 Qf6 Qe3 Rdf8 Nxe6 Qxf3 Qc3 Qxc3 Nxc3 Bxe6 Bxe6+ Kb8
e: Qd2 gets the queen off the back rank, connects the rooks for O-O-O and, crucially, takes the sting out of black's dark-square checks. The f4-knight then stays where it belongs, eyeing e6: in the line Bh3 Qf6 Qe3 Rdf8 Nxe6 White breaks through on the e-file at just the right moment.

pv: Rab1 Qd4+ Kc1 Rc8 Rd1 Qf6 Qxf6+ gxf6 Rxb7 Rc7 Rb5 e5 Nh4 Nd4 Rd5
e: The black queen on b2 is loose, and Rab1 attacks it immediately. After Qd4+ Kc1 Rc8 Rd1 Qf6 you force the queen trade on your terms (Qxf6+ gxf6) and the rook lands on b7, so instead of being overrun you reach an endgame where your rooks are the active pieces.

pv: e5 dxe5 Bb4+ Kd1 Qa6 Nf3 Nc5 Nbd4 Bd3 Bd2 Bxf1 Bxb4 Qd3+ Ke1 Bxg2 Bxc5
e: Strike back with e5!: after dxe5, Bb4+ forces Kd1 (no more castling), and Qa6! piles on the b5-knight, which only the white queen defends. White's tangled pieces can't hold everything — in the line Nf3 Nc5 Nbd4 Bd3! even wins the f1-bishop, and the c7-pawn falls before it does any damage (-0.1).

pv: Qf8 Rc1 Bg6 Bb5 a6 Be2 e5 c8=Q Rxc8 Nxc8 exd4 Nxe7+ Qxe7 Nf3 Qb4+ Kf1
e: The d6-knight attacks your queen while guarding the pawn's queening square on c8 — Qf8! is the one square that keeps the queen safe and useful. Bg6 next rescues the f5-bishop, and when White finally cashes c8=Q you answer Rxc8 Nxc8 exd4, giving material back but staying afloat at -3.7.
ep: With the knight now on d6, the f1–a6 diagonal is wide open: Qa6 simply hangs the queen to Bxa6 — nothing can recapture on a6 (and note Nb6 blocks any attack on the c6-queen). White chose c8=Q+ in the game instead, also crushing.

pv: Nd6 Bxd7 Nf5+ Kh3 Rxd7 f3 Bd3 Rd1 Bb5 g4 Ne3 Rc1 e5 dxe5 d4 Rc5
e: Bb5 attacks the d7-knight, but instead of defending it, counterattack: Nd6! hits the bishop, and after Bxd7 the zwischenzug Nf5+ forces Kh3 before Rxd7 regains the piece. The trade comes on your terms — the knight lands actively on f5 with Ne3 and Bd3-b5 ideas to follow (-1.2).
ep: Nf8 defends d7 but ties both knights to passive squares: Ba6! keeps probing (it eyes c8), and after Nd6 f3 Bg6 Ne2 White calmly untangles, keeps the extra exchange, and your pieces stay on the back foot (-2.5).

pv: h5 f3 g5 g4 hxg4+ Kxg4 Bd3 h4 gxh4 Rxh4 Rg7+ Kh3 Nxh4 Kxh4 Bf5 Be8
e: White's king is stranded on h3 — go after it with h5!: the plan is g5 and hxg4+ to rip open its shelter. After f3 g5 g4 hxg4+ Kxg4 the quiet Bd3! swings the bishop toward the king hunt, and gxh4/Rxh4 wins material while every black piece takes aim (+1.9).
ep: Ng6 gives White the tempo for Ne2!: after Bd3 g4 Bxe2 gxf5 the attackers get traded off and Nf4+/Nh5+ is only a repetition (+0.0). In the game White played f3?? instead and got mated anyway: Nf4+ Kg4 h5+ Kxf4 g5#.

pv: g6
e: g6 keeps the c8-h3 diagonal clear behind your g4-bishop, and that detail is everything: White's big trick is Qa4+, forking king and bishop along the fourth rank, and with the diagonal open you simply block with ...Bd7!, keeping the piece. Then ...Bg7 and ...O-O follow with a comfortable game (+0.5).
ep: e6?? blocks your bishop's own escape route: after Qa4+! the ...Bd7 block is impossible (your e6-pawn sits on the g4-d7 diagonal), so the fork wins the g4-bishop - ...Nc6 Qxg4, exactly as in the game, and the ...O-O-O counterplay never made up for the piece (-4.2).

pv: Qc5 O-O Qxc4 Ng3 cxd5 Nh5 O-O Rb1 f6 Bc1 Nc6 Ba3 Rd8 h3 Re8
e: Qc5 is a double attack in disguise: from c5 the queen hits the loose bishop on c4 down the file and also eyes f2 along the a7-g1 diagonal, so White never gets a free tempo to rescue it. After O-O Qxc4 you simply pocket the piece, and the knight on e4 still sits on a superb post hitting d2 and c3.
ep: cxd5 attacks the bishop too, but only with a pawn, so White gets the tempo to step aside with Bb3 - exactly what happened in the game. The queen on a5 was doing nothing; from c5 it would have hit c4 with a piece that cannot be shooed away.

pv: Qd7 Qb4 Rab8 a4 h6 a5 Rdc8 Kg1 Rc7 f4 Rd8 fxe5 fxe5 Rf1
e: Your knight on f5 is doing double duty: it blocks the g4-e6 diagonal, and the bishop on e6 has no other defender. Qd7 supplies that second defender, keeps the knight on its strong post and connects the rooks. White then has no entry square at all, and you are two pawns up with a big centre.
ep: Nh6 unblocks the g4-e6 diagonal and the bishop just falls: Qxe6+ Kh8 Qh3 and White is back in the game with your king airy. In the game he missed it with Qg3 and you got away with it.

pv: h3 Re8 Bd3 Nb4 Nf3 Bd7 e5 Nxd3+ Qxd3 Ng8 Ne4 Bc6 Rhe1 Bxe4
e: h3! takes g4 away from the f6-knight before committing the center. Then e5 becomes a real threat played on your terms — in the line White finishes development with Bd3 and Nf3 and only then pushes e5, when the pawn cannot be harassed. A small move that turns a space edge into a lasting one (+1.9).
ep: e5? releases the tension while g4 is still open: dxe5 Qxd8 Nxd8 fxe5 and Ng4! wins the e5-pawn — the g1-knight must grovel with Nh3, and after Nxe5 Black is simply a pawn up. The game followed the same path: fxe5 Ng4 and the pawn fell.

pv: b3 Rd8 Be4 h5 Rf1 Rd4 Re1 Kf6 c3 Rd7 Re2 h4 c4 Rd4 Kc2 a5
e: Quiet consolidation with b3! You are a clean pawn up, and the one thing to avoid is contact on the e-file, where Nd3+ tricks lurk. b3 takes c4 from the knight and prepares Kc2; note the line only plays Re1 after Black's rook has left e8 — it is the e8-rook's cover of e1 that makes the fork work (+1.9).
ep: Re1?? steps onto the fork square: Nd3+! hits c1 and e1 — cxd3 Rxe1+ loses rook for knight, and king moves allow Nxe1, when the knight is protected by the e8-rook. Black missed it once (Kf6), but your c4 next move allowed it again and Nd3+ landed.

pv: Rf1+ Kg5 g3 Rd8 Bb7 Rd4 Re1 Kf6 b3 h5 h4 Nf7 Re4 Rd7 Rf4+ Ke5
e: Rf1+! rescues the rook with check — Black must answer the check, so Nd3+ never gets in. After Kg5 g3 boxes the king, b3 secures the queenside, and White keeps the extra pawn; the rook can even return to e1 later once the e8-rook has moved, because the fork only works while Black's rook covers e1 (+1.8).
ep: c4?? allows the fork after all: Nd3+! Kd2 Nxe1 — and Kxe1 is illegal since the e8-rook guards the knight, so the rook is lost outright (the knight later bails out with Nxg2). The game ended just so: c4 Nd3+, rook for knight, endgame gone.

pv: Nd3 exd4 exd4 Rh6 Qf5 g6 Qg5 Rh7 Re1 Re7 Ne2 Nh7 Qh6+ Ke8 Nef4 Kd8
e: The h5 pawn is defended by the rook on h8, so there is nothing to grab. Nd3 keeps the knight covering the centre and supports the queen's outpost: after exd4 exd4 Rh6 Qf5 g6 Qg5 the queen keeps her grip on the dark squares while Re1 and Ne2-f4 pile in.
ep: Nxh5 overlooks the h8 rook guarding down the file — Rxh5 wins a piece on the spot, and in the game dxe5 Qxe5 f4 Qxe3+ let the black queen into your king's position as well.

pv: Re1 Re5 Rxe4 dxe4 Rf1+ Ke8 Kc1 e3 Re1 e2 Qh2 Kd8 Rxe2 Rge8
e: Re1! hits the queen on e4 down the file and she has no square that keeps everything defended. After Re5 Rxe4 dxe4 Rf1+ Ke8 Kc1 you have swapped a rook for the queen, and the runaway e-pawn is stopped in time by Re1 and Qh2.
ep: Rf1+ is a check that helps black: Nf6 blocks with tempo and, from f6, the knight covers e4 for good. Once the queen is protected, the Re1 idea is gone and it was your pieces that ended up loose.

pv: Re1
e: Re1 is still the move — challenging the queen on e4 is worth more than any check, because she is the piece holding black's whole position together. Forcing her to declare herself buys the time you need to consolidate the king and bring the second rook in.
ep: Qd6+ pushes the black king exactly where it wants to go: Qe7! offers the trade, and after Qg3 Kf7 Rhg1 g6 the black rooks come to e8 and h5 with all the play while your queen has to trek back.

pv: Kb1 g5 b3 Rf4 Qxc6+ Rf6 Qc8 Rf4 Qh8+ Kg6 Qg8+ Ng7 Qxd5 g4 a4 g3
e: King first, then the pawns, then the queen. Kb1 steps off the exposed a-file so that b3 can follow with the shelter intact, and only then does the queen go hunting: Qxc6+ and the checks on the h-file collect the loose pawns while the knight on h5 never gets a check of its own.
ep: Qb3 uses the queen for a job the b-pawn should do; after g5 she has to come back to e3 anyway, and with the queenside not yet solid ...Rxc2+ ideas keep hanging over you — the same rook infiltration showed up in the game.

pv: Kb3 c5 a4 Rb4+ Ka3 Re4 Qxc5 g4 Qf2 Kg5 a5 d4 Qg1 Re6 Ka4 Ne2
e: Kb3! walks straight at the rook on c4 and it has to be answered. After c5 a4 Rb4+ Ka3 Re4 the rook has been pushed around and Qxc5 collects the pawn, while your own pawns on a4/b2 shield the king from the checks.
ep: Kb1 retreats and lets black organise instead: ...Re4 comes with tempo on the queen and ...g4 gets the pawns rolling, and in the game you were reduced to Qxc6+ and Qxd5+ Nxd5, giving the queen up for the knight.

pv: Qc3 Kh4 Qh8+ Kg3 b4 Kf3 Qh1+ Kf2 Qh2+ Ng2 Qh6 Nf4
e: The d5 pawn is guarded by the knight on f4, so it is not on offer. Qc3 keeps the queen on the long diagonal where she stops the g-pawn and holds b2 — from there Qh8+ and Qh1+ give an endless supply of checks and the position is a draw.
ep: Qxd5+ runs into Nxd5, because the f4 knight covers d5 — and with the queen gone there is nothing left to stop the g-pawn: c3 g3 Kc2 g2 and it promotes with mate to follow.

pv: Bd6 Qe3 Bxh2+ Kh1 Bd6 Qd3 Rc8 Rab1 Qc6 Kg1 O-O Bg5
e: Bd6 develops with tempo, hitting the queen on e5, and after Qe3 there is the extra point Bxh2+, winning a pawn: Kh1 lets the bishop step back to d6 safely. So the same move develops, gains time and picks up material, while the rook on h8 gets ready to come to the c-file.
ep: Nd7 also hits the queen, but it blocks your own bishop and gives up the ...Bxh2+ resource, so after Qe3 (Qg5 in the game) White keeps everything defended and later crashed through with Rxe6+.

pv: Qxd4 Rad1 Bd6 Be3 Qe5 Qh4 Qf5 Rfe1 Nf6 Bd4 O-O Bxf6 Qxf6 Qxf6 gxf6 Ne4
e: Qxd4 just takes the free centre pawn while your d5-pawn is still protected by the g7-pawn's cover of f6. After Rad1 Bd6 blocks the file, Be3 Qe5 offers the trade and Qh4 Qf5 keeps your queen active - you finish development a pawn up (+1.7).
ep: g6 quietly removes the g7-pawn's guard of f6, and that is the whole game: Nxd5 hits your queen, and after Qc6 Nf6+ Nxf6 Qxf6 White wins material with the knight fork you had just enabled.

pv: Qc6 Qxd5 Bg7 Qxc6 bxc6 Be3 Nb6 Ne4 O-O c3 a5 Kf1 a4 Nc5 Rfe8 Nd3
e: Qc6 defends d5 a second time and offers the trade of queens - after Qxd5 Bg7 Qxc6 bxc6 the queens come off and your king finds a home by castling, with the doubled c-pawns a small price for surviving the attack. Keeping the d5-pawn guarded is what stops all the Nxd5 tricks.
ep: Qxd4 grabs the pawn but leaves d5 hanging with the rook now on e1: Nxd5 hits your queen, and after Qc4 Rad1 Bd6 Nf6+ the knight fork wins the piece back with a crushing attack on the stranded king.

pv: Bg7 Nd5 Qe5 Re1 Qxg5 Bxg5 Rhe8 Rd1 Rac8 c3 Re2 Bd2 Rd8 Kf1 Re5 c4
e: Bg7 solves two problems at once: it blocks the a1-h8 diagonal, which is where all of White's tricks live, and it attacks the knight on f6. After Nd5 Qe5 Re1 Qxg5 Bxg5 you trade into a comfortable endgame with your rooks coming to e8 and c8 (+0.8).
ep: Qxf6 walks into the fork: Qxf6+ Kxf6 and now Bc3+ skewers king and rook, so after Kf7 Bxh8 White wins the exchange. The dark-squared bishop was aimed at h8 the whole time - as the game confirmed.

pv: h3 g3 h5 Kh2 h4 Rg1 Re8 Kxh3 hxg3 fxg3 Bxc3 Rf1+ Kg6 Bc1 Bf6 Rf2
e: h3 is the move that fixes White's kingside: after g3 your pawn on h3 is a permanent thorn that ties the white king down, and h5-h4 follows to open lines. The line h3 g3 h5 Kh2 h4 Rg1 Re8 shows the plan - the rook belongs on e8 behind the passed pawn, not on the long diagonal.
ep: Rg7 puts the rook on the b2-h8 diagonal, and the rook on d1 exploits it: Rd5 pins your bishop against the king on f5, and after h3 Rxe5+ Kxe5 Bd4+ forks king and rook. In the game Bd4 came at once.

pv: Bd6
e: Bd6 develops with tempo on the e5 knight and, more importantly, clears the back rank so the king can get off e8 — your c6 knight is pinned down the a4-e8 diagonal by the bishop on b5, so the king sitting in the middle is the real problem.
ep: Ne7 blocks the f8 bishop in and leaves the queenside undefended: Qxa7 f6 Nxg6 hxg6 Qxb7 hits the pinned knight, and Bxc6 Rxc6 Qb5 leaves white two pawns up. In the game Bg5 f6 Nxc6 and Bxc6+ exploited the same pin.

pv: bxc6 Ba6 fxg5 Bxc8 Nxc8 Qxc6+ Qd7 Qxd7+ Kxd7 Nd2 Bd6 Ke2 Ne7 h4 gxh4 Rxh4
e: bxc6 is the right recapture because the pawn attacks the bishop on b5 — white has to spend a move on it, and that tempo lets you take the loose bishop on g5 with fxg5. After Ba6 fxg5 Bxc8 Nxc8 Qxc6+ Qd7 Qxd7+ Kxd7 you reach an ending a clear piece for a pawn ahead.
ep: Nxc6 doesn't touch the b5 bishop, so white gets the free tempo Bf4 to rescue the bishop that was hanging to your f6 pawn — after a6 Be2 Bd6 Bxd6 the whole point of the position has evaporated.

pv: Rfc8 Rf3 Rb6 b3 Rbc6 Qb4 Qxb4 cxb4 Rc2 Rf2 h6 Re1 Rf8 Nf3 Rc3 Ne5
e: It matters which rook goes to c8: Rfc8 keeps the c6 rook glued to the backward c3 pawn and brings the second one to help. The plan Rb6, Rbc6 doubles on the file, and after Qb4 Qxb4 cxb4 the rook drops into c2 and the endgame runs itself.
ep: Rcc8 gives up the pressure on c3 and invites Rxf8+, trading a pair of rooks off; with fewer heavy pieces there is nothing left to attack and the edge shrinks to nothing.

pv: Rxf1
e: Rxf1 is the accurate way to trade: you decide when the exchange happens, white has to recapture, and your remaining rook is the one that owns the open f-file afterwards. Keeping the initiative on that file, with the bishop on g6 eyeing the light squares, is the whole of your advantage.
ep: Rf4 puts the rook where Rxf4 wins the tempo instead — after Qe2 Rcf8 Rxf4 Rxf4 Rf1 in the game it was white's rook that took over the f-file, and Be4+ Nxe4 finished the liquidation.

pv: Qe7 Qg3 Qe8 Re1 Rxe1 Qxe1 Qg6 Qe3 h6 Kg3 b5 h4 h5 g5 Kf8 Qf4+
e: Qe7 covers f7 and f8 — the two squares white's queen and rook need for an invasion — and prepares Qe8 to offer the trade. After Qg3 Qe8 Re1 Rxe1 Qxe1 the heavy pieces come off, your king is safe and there is nothing left to attack.
ep: h6 creates the hook white's attack needs: Qf7+ Kh7 g5! rips the shelter open, and after hxg5 Qh5+ Kg8 Qe8+ Kh7 Rf8 you are being mated. White missed it in the game with Rf2.

pv: Ng6 Bxf8 Nxf8 Rac1 Ng6 c4 dxc4 bxc4 O-O cxb5 Nf4 Qf3 Rxc1 Rxc1 Qxd4 Ne4
e: The bishop on a3 is what stops you castling, so give the f8 bishop a replacement: Ng6. If Bxf8 Nxf8 and the knight comes back to g6, while otherwise the knight heads for f4 hitting the queen's post — either way the king finally gets out of the centre.
ep: Qb6 leaves the f8 bishop tied down and lets white plant the bishop on c5, gaining a tempo on your queen; b4 and a4 then take over the queenside and the c4 break comes with everything ready, as in the game.

pv: Kxf8 Ne5 Nxe5 dxe5 Kg8 Qe3 h6 Rac1 Rxc1 Rxc1 Qb7 h4 g6 h5 gxh5 Rc4
e: Kxf8 is the right recapture — castling was never going to happen anyway, and it keeps the knight on g6, your most useful defender. After Ne5 Nxe5 dxe5 Kg8 you walk the king to safety by hand and the rook on c6 stays active on the open file.
ep: Nxf8 buries the knight on the back rank and gives white the e5 square for nothing: Ne5 hits c6 and f7 at once, and while you are tangled up Qxa6 collects the pawn and the a-file — which is what the game showed.

pv: Nxe5 dxe5 Rc4 Qa3 Qc5 Qa8+ Qc8 Qxc8+ Rxc8 a4 Rc7 a5 O-O Rfc1 Ra7 Rcb1
e: Trade the dominating knight while you can: Nxe5 dxe5 fixes white's pawn on a dark square and hands your rook the c-file. Rc4 then hits the pawns, and after Qa3 Qc5 Qa8+ Qc8 Qxc8+ Rxc8 the queens come off and you can finally castle.
ep: Rb7 leaves the knight on e5 in charge and your king stuck in the middle; Qa3 stops you castling and you are forced into Nxe5 dxe5 anyway a tempo down, with the rook now misplaced on b7.

pv: Qb8 Qxb8+ Nxb8 Rfc1 O-O a4 Ra7 a5 f6 Nd3 Kf7 Nb4 Rd8 Rc4 Rd6 Rc8
e: White's queen on d6 is the whole problem, so force her off: Qb8! After Qxb8+ Nxb8 you reach an ending only a pawn down where the knight comes back via d7 or c6 and the king walks to f7 — a far better version than being squeezed with queens on.
ep: Rb6 does nothing about the queen on d6 or the knight on e5: Rac1 takes the open file and Nc6 breaks in. In the game Qxd7+ Qxd7 Nxd7 Kxd7 dropped you into a much worse ending with the king stranded.

pv: d5
e: d5! takes the centre with tempo, hitting the e6 pawn and shutting the b7 bishop's diagonal before black can free himself. The pawn on d5 cramps him badly and, with the bishop already on f4 and his king still on e8, you keep a lasting initiative.
ep: Qd2 leaves d4 to be swapped off: cxd4 Qxd4 and the centralised queen becomes a target for ...b5, ...Qa5 and ...Nc6 with tempo, so black solves his opening problems for free - just as in the game.

pv: Bd3
e: The knight on c3 is pinned against your queen on d2 by the bishop on b4, so it cannot really defend e4. Bd3 is the move that fixes that: it adds the second defender to e4 while developing, and only then can you castle and think about untangling with a3 or Qc1.
ep: Nge2 does not defend e4, so Nxe4! is simply on: after Qe3 d5 O-O-O Bc5 Qxe4 dxe4 the pin on c3 means black comes out a clean pawn up with the better structure.

pv: Rd1 Be7
e: Rd1 completes development, takes the open file and supports the queen on d2 - which matters because the knight on c3 is pinned against that queen by the bishop on b4. Once the rook is in, black has to spend a move on ...Be7 and you can start untangling with a well-defended centre.
ep: Nd4 walks into the sequence Nxd4 Qxd4 Bxc3+! Qxc3 Qxc3+ bxc3: with queens off and your pawns shattered, black then just takes the loose pawn on e4. The game followed almost exactly that path.

pv: e5 Kh1 e4 Ng1 f5 Ne5 Bxe5 dxe5 Rd7 g4 Qe6 Rbd1 Nc6 gxf5 Qxf5 Ne2
e: e5! gets the central pawn mass rolling with tempo: e4 next shoves the f3-knight back to g1, and f5 hits the g4-knight — White's pieces are driven backwards while your pawns and the g7-bishop take over the board (+1.3).
ep: Re7 is a waiting move that concedes the initiative: White simply plays Kh2 and reorganizes. Nothing is lost concretely (+0.2), but the moment for e5–e4–f5, pushing both knights back, never returned — the game drifted into h4–h5 instead.

pv: Kh7 Nf3 Bh6 Qd1 Qd6 Nxe5 fxe5 Ne4 Qc6 Ng5+ Bxg5 hxg5 Qd6 Rf1 e4 Qd4
e: Kh7 keeps your superb e5-knight on its post and steps off the check: after Nf3, Bh6! comes with tempo on the d2-queen, and even Nxe5 fxe5 leaves you a strong pawn duo and the freer game (+0.7). The knight was the whole position.
ep: Ng4+ swaps your best piece for the passive f2-knight: Nxg4, and suddenly the e7-rook is a problem — the game's Qxg4?? dropped it to Rxe7, and even the correct hxg4 leaves White on top after Rxe7 Qxe7 Re1 with Ne6 coming.

pv: hxg4 Rxe7 Qxe7 Re1 Qd7 Ne6 Kf7 Qd3 f5 Qe3 Kg8 Qg5 Re8 Qxg6 Qf7 Qxf7+
e: hxg4 is the only recapture: the queen stays on d7 guarding the e7-rook, so Rxe7 Qxe7 is a simple trade. You are worse (-1.8) because of the kingside holes and the strong d4-knight, but material stays level.
ep: Qxg4 abandons the e7-rook — the queen was its only defender — and Rxe7 took it clean; Bf8 chased the rook but Re3 kept everything, leaving you a full rook down.

pv: Nge7 dxc5 Nf5 Bg5 Qb8 O-O Bxc5 Na4 Be7 Bxe7 Nfxe7 c4 dxc4 Nc5 Qc7 Rc1
e: Keep the tension and develop: Nge7 heads for f5. After dxc5 Nf5 hits the e3-bishop, and ...Bxc5 regains the pawn with every piece pointing at d4 — White's central pawn is the permanent sore spot, so the last thing to do is release the pressure on it.
ep: c4 releases the central tension: d4 is no longer attackable, so White's centre stands rock-solid and he castles and expands at leisure — and your g4-bishop became the target instead, pushed around by h3 and Nh4 in the game.

pv: Nb6 Ra7 Rg3 Kc7 Nc4 d5 Rg7 dxc4 Rxh7 Nd7 e5 c5 Bxc4 Ra8 Rxf7 Rh8
e: Nb6 hits the a8-rook and takes d7 and c8 away from Black's pieces at the same time. After Ra7 the rook is buried, and only then does the rook swing over: Rg3, Nc4, Rg7 attacking f7 and the h7-knight that is the h6-pawn's only jailer. The h6-pawn is your winning asset — everything aims at the pieces holding it back. Rxh7 in the line is the payoff, and it stays around +4.6.
ep: Bh5 chases the f7-pawn and forgets the a8-rook, which lets Black activate: Nd7! and after Bxf7 Kc7 Bg6 Rh8 the rook sits behind the h-pawn, ...Nhf8 frees the h7-knight, and the pawn is blockaded on dark and light squares alike. +4.6 down to +1.6, and the game was drawn. Winning a pawn on f7 is worth far less than stopping ...Rh8 and ...Nf8; in this ending the passer is the only thing that wins.

pv: b3 Kg5 Nc6 Ne3 Nd4 Kf4 Ne2+ Ke5 Nxc3 Kd4 Nb5+ Kc5 Na3 Kc6
e: b3! declines the trade and keeps both pawns, and the c3-pawn is going nowhere — the engine simply walks the knight over to collect it: Nc6-d4-e2xc3, while a2 and b3 sit untouched and mutually shielded from the black knight. Knight plus two connected pawns against a bare knight is a genuine winning attempt, roughly +3.5. The rule in knight endings a pawn up is do not trade pawns — the extra pawn is the entire advantage.
ep: bxc3 hands the game away: Nxc3 recaptures with tempo on a2, and the a-pawn cannot be saved — a3 Nb5 Kc2 Nxa3+ and it is knight versus knight, dead drawn. +3.5 collapses to +0.2, and the game duly ended in a draw. Capturing towards the enemy knight gave it the perfect square on c3, from which it forked the pawn and the queenside at once.

pv: Nc6 Nxd7 Qxd7 Nxb5 Nf6 Bxc4 e6 Nc3 a5 d4 Bb4 Qe2 O-O O-O Rab8 Rd1
e: Nc6 develops and deals with the real danger: Qf3!, double-attacking f7 and the a8-rook, must not be allowed. After Nxd7 Qxd7 Nxb5 Nf6 Bxc4 White picks up pawns, but your pieces are finally out and the king castles - worse, yet defensible rather than lost.
ep: Qb6 permits Qf3!, hitting f7 and the a8-rook at once - nothing covers both, and even the best Qf6 loses the exchange after Qxa8 Qxe5 Rxa7. In the game Nc6 came a move too late: Qxf7+ Kd8 Qxf8+ and the attack decided immediately.

pv: Nxf7 Kxf7 a5 Ke6 a6 Kd7 b4 Kc8 Kd2 Bg4 Nd5 Kb8 Nf6 Be6 Ke3 Bc4
e: The knight on d8 is attacked by the king and has no safe retreat, so cash it in for the pawn it can reach: Nxf7! Kxf7 and now the queenside runners decide. a5, a6 and b4 send the pawns up while Black's bishop and knight are stuck on the wrong wing, and his king can't be in two places at once — he cannot both stop the a-pawn and hold e5/h4.
ep: Nc6+ drops the knight for free — the bishop on f3 takes it along the f3-c6 diagonal with Bxc6. Your opponent replied Ke6 and let you keep the piece.

pv: Nc7 Kb8 Kb6 Kc8 a7 Kd7 a8=Q Ng7 Qc6+ Kd8 Kb7 Ne6 Qe8#
e: Nc7! builds the mating net instead of chasing the king with the king. The knight covers a8 and the escape squares while the a-pawn is now free to run: Kb8 Kb6 Kc8 a7 Kd7 a8=Q and the new queen finishes it with Qc6+ Kd8 Kb7 Ne6 Qe8#. That is mate in 7 — the knight's job here is squares, not checks.
ep: Kc6 forgets that Black's knight has a check of its own: Nd4+ forks your king and the b5 pawn, and after Kc5 Ne6+ the knight keeps harassing until b6+ Kxa6 collects your a-pawn. You still win, but the forced mate is gone.

pv: Rc2 Bxe4 Rxc4 Bxb1 Kxb1 Rb8+ Kc2 Kf8 Re4 h5 Kc3 a5 g4 h4 Re5 Re8
e: Rc2! answers the bishop stand-off with a counterattack on the c4-rook, so Black must resolve the tension on your terms. After Bxe4 Rxc4 Bxb1 Kxb1 the trades leave your rook on c4 defending c5, the d6-passer untouched, and Black without counterplay - close to winning at +4.3.
ep: Bxd5? cxd5 repairs Black's pawns and leaves c5 loose to the c4-rook: Rxc5 follows, and in the game Rc1+ Kb2 Rxc5 won it exactly that way. You stayed on top thanks to the d6-pawn, but gave back a large chunk of the advantage.

pv: Reb2 Rxc5 Rb8 Rcc8 Rxc8 Rxc8 Rb5 Kf8 Rxd5 Rb8 a4 f6 Rc5 Rd8
e: Reb2 doubles rooks on the open b-file with the threat of Rb8, forcing trades that clear the d-pawn's path. Even after Rxc5 you have Rb8 Rcc8 Rxc8 Rxc8 and then Rb5!, hitting d5 and regaining the pawn with the d6-passer still alive and your rook active.
ep: Rb7 lets Black grab c5 with tempo: Rc1+ drives your king to b2 and Rxc5 scoops the pawn, after which the black king gets back to f8 in time to hold up d7. The game went exactly Rc1+ Kb2 Rxc5 - only your opponent's later errors saved the point.

pv: Qd6 Qxd6 Nxd6+ Kc7 Nf7 Rhf8 Nxd8 Kxd8 b3 Kc8 Rh2 Nc5 Rh3 Nd7
e: Trade queens so the recapture comes with check: Qd6! Qxd6 Nxd6+ and Black has zero time; now Nf7! forks the d8- and h8-rooks and Nxd8 wins the exchange (+3.9). The tempo gained by Nxd6 being check is the entire trick.
ep: Nd6+ first runs into Kc7!, hitting the knight: after Nb5+ Kb8 Qd6+ Qxd6 Nxd6 the recapture comes without check, Black slips in Rhf8, and the Nf7 fork never happens (+1.4). In the game Kb8 let you keep more, but the clean exchange-win was gone.

pv: Rh2 Nb6 Qc5 Rhe8 Rhd2 Nc8 a3 Rd7 Ne4 Rxd2 Rxd2 Qxc5 Nxc5 N8e7
e: Bring the last piece: Rh2! prepares Rhd2, doubling behind the strong d6-knight, and keeps Qc5 in reserve against Nb6 (line: Rh2 Nb6 Qc5 Rhe8 Rhd2 Nc8). With every piece working, White's bind is worth +1.5.
ep: Qb5 achieves little: b7 is covered by the king, and Nb6 shores up c8 while preparing Nc4. In the game your follow-up Nc4?! then traded off the prize d6-knight via Rxd1+ and Nxc4, and the advantage evaporated (+0.3).

pv: Qc5 Qe6
e: Qc5! guards the d6-knight - the piece your whole grip leans on. With it defended, Rxd1+ Kxd1 achieves nothing, and after Qe6 the game stays balanced (+0.2). Not glamorous, but every alternative lets the d-file tactics work for Black.
ep: Nc4? drops coordination at the worst moment: Rxd1+ Kxd1 Nxc4 Qxc4 Qd6+! and Black takes the d-file with check - Qe6 and Rd8+ follow, harassing your king while a2 hangs (-1.5). The game's Rxd1+ Kxd1 e4 was the same story.

pv: Qb2 Qa5+ c3 Nxc3 Qd2 Nc6 Rc1 Na4 Nf3 dxc4 Bxc4 Qxd2+ Nxd2 cxd4 Bb5 Nc3
e: Qb2 prepares the only good answer to Qa5+, which is c3 — and now the queen on b2 defends it. After Qa5+ c3 Nxc3 Qd2 Nc6 Rc1 Na4 Nf3 White untangles and is only a shade worse (-0.5). The b1-queen was the problem piece; solve that before touching anything else.
ep: f3 kicks the e4-knight but ignores the a5-e1 diagonal, and Qa5+! wins the queen by force. Both blocks fail: Qb4 cxb4, and c3 Nxc3 forking the queen on b1. After Qb4 cxb4 fxe4 the b-pawn even goes b3+ as a discovered check from a5, and b2 queens. -5.7, and the game was over two moves later.

pv: e5 Ng8 Kb1 b5 Nf3 h6 Bd3 Nb6 h4 Qd7
e: e5! punishes Black's setup at the right moment: the f6-knight has no decent square — the main line's retreat is Ng8, all the way home. After e5 Ng8 White enjoys a huge space edge and a free hand: Kb1, Nf3, Bd3 and h4 build the attack while Black spends moves untangling.
ep: Be2 lets Black's counterplay begin: b5! arrives, and in the game b5 f3 Nb6 g4 Nc4 forced Bxc4 bxc4 — your freshly developed bishop traded itself off and the b-file opened toward your king. The e5 push was free just one move earlier.

pv: e5
e: e5! is still the right push: it kicks the f6-knight backwards and seizes space before Black's queenside storm lands. Delay it once more and the knight gets d5 instead of retreating — one tempo decides which attack arrives first.
ep: f3 is a slow move your king can't afford: b4! drives the c3-knight to b1, then c5! hits the centre — and when e5 finally comes, Nd5! plants the knight instead of retreating it. After cxd4 the lines open against your king; the race is lost by exactly one move.

pv: Bh6 Bxh6 Qxh6 c6 Nh3 Bxh3 Qxh3 Qc7 Qh6 b4 Nb1 c5 dxc5 Qxc5 Nd2 Rc8
e: Bh6! trades off the g7-bishop — Black's best defender and the engine of his coming b4/c5 play. After Bxh6 Qxh6 c6 Nh3 the exchanges leave White comfortable, the queen active on the kingside dark squares, and the pawn storm loses most of its teeth without that bishop.
ep: g4 ignores the queenside race: b4! kicks the c3-knight at once, and in the game Nc4 Bxc4 bxc4 traded your light-squared bishop and half-opened the b-file at your king — Black's attack ran well ahead of your g4/h4 storm.

pv: Na5 Qa4+ Bd7 Bb5 a6 Bxd7+ Nxd7 Nf3 b5 Qd1 g6 O-O Bg7 Qc2
e: Na5! puts the question to the queen instead of grabbing: after Qa4+ Bd7 Bb5 a6 Bxd7+ Nxd7 the checks are spent, White's queen goes home (Qd1), and you complete development with b5, g6 and Bg7. The d4-pawn was poisoned all along — White's d5-pawn blocks your queen's defense of d4.
ep: Nxd4?? drops a piece to Qa4+!: the knight on d4 has no defender (your queen is blocked by White's d5-pawn), so the check collects it — b5 Qxd4, and Bd7 allows Qxd4 just the same. You are left a piece for a pawn down (-4.2); the game's Qa4+ was instant.

pv: hxg5 Kg1 Qc7 g3 Rh7 c4 Qxe5 Qe3 f5 Rac1 Kb8 Nc6+ bxc6 Qb6+ Kc8 cxd5
e: hxg5! Recapture with the pawn and the h-file opens straight at the white king on h1 — Rh7 and Rdh8 follow, and White has to burn moves on Kg1 and g3. Meanwhile the knight on e4 stays where it is, which is worth more than any g-pawn. Kg1 Qc7 g3 Rh7 c4 Qxe5, +2.2.
ep: Nxg5 trades off Black's monster on e4 for a pawn and leaves h6 on the board, so the h-file stays shut and the attack never starts. White takes over on the other wing: b4 Qc7 a5 Ne4 b5 Qc4 Qxc4+ dxc4 bxa6 and it is his king that is safe and Black's on c8 that is opening up. +2.2 to -1.9.

pv: Ng3+ Kh2 Nxe2 Nxe2 Rdf8 Raf1 Rxf7 Rxf7 Qxb2 Nf4 Rg8 Re7 Kb8 a5 Qxc3 Ng6
e: Ng3+! is a family fork — the knight checks the king on h1 and hits the queen on e2 in the same move. Kh2 Nxe2 Nxe2 Rdf8 and Black is a clean piece up while the f7-rook is rounded up next (+5.9). One knight jump, whole game.
ep: Rd7 defends the rook but throws away the fork. Qf3! and now White's queen both defends and attacks — after Qxb2 Re1 Rxf7 Qxf7 Qf2 Qxf2 Nxf2+ the queens come off and everything is level. +5.9 to 0.00. The knight was one square from the enemy queen; look for checks before defending.

pv: Qa5+ c3 Qxf5 f4 e6 Nf3 Bd6 Ne5 Qe4+ Kf2 Nbd7 Bd3 Qd5 Rf1 Bc7 Kg1
e: Qa5+ is a check that also hits the loose knight on f5 - nothing defends it. After c3 blocks, Qxf5 simply picks the piece up, and the follow-up f4 e6 Nf3 Bd6 lets black finish development and meet Ne5 with ...Qe4+ trading into a good position. Always look for the check that comes with a second threat.
ep: e6 is a normal developing move but it gives the knight time to save itself with Ne3, and after Qc7 c3 Bd6 white is simply better developed with the extra centre pawn. The free piece was there for one move only.

pv: Bxd4 Rhf1 Bxc3 Rd3 Qe4 Bf3 Bxb2 Bxe4 fxe4 Rd2 Rxc2 Rxc2 Bh8 Ne2 Nb6 f5
e: Bxd4 removes white's strongly centralised knight and clears the way for the follow-up ...Bxc3, tearing into the shelter around the king on b1. After Rhf1 Bxc3 Rd3 Qe4 the bishop and queen dominate, and ...Rxc2 ideas on the c-file are always in the air with the knight on a4 helping.
ep: Qc5 steps off the defence of b5: Nxb5 wins the pawn at once, and after ...Nxb2 Qxb2 Rab8 Ncb3 white is simply better with a safe king. In the game Nxb5 followed immediately and the knight then landed on d6.

pv: Rxc3 bxc3 Nxc3+ Qxc3 Bxc3 Rd3 Bf6 Nc4 Qf2 Rd2 a5 Rf1 Qa7 Kc2 a4 Nc1
e: Rxc3! blows the king open: bxc3 Nxc3+ Qxc3 Bxc3 leaves black with two pawns and a bishop planted on c3 for the exchange, and the king on b1 has no shelter left. The pattern to spot is that the rook on c8, the knight on a4 and the queen on b6 were all already aimed at b2/c3 - that is what makes the sacrifice work.
ep: Rc6 keeps material even but lets white untangle with Nc4 and Ne5, hitting your rook and queen and driving the pieces back. The sacrifice on c3 only existed while all three attackers pointed at the king.

pv: Rxb2+ Qxb2 Nxb2 Kxb2 Bxe5 fxe5 Qxc5 Rd4 Qxe5 Bc4 h5 a4 Qc5 Bb3 Kf8 Rc1
e: Rxb2+! is the way out: Qxb2 Nxb2 Kxb2 strips the king of its cover, and then Bxe5 fxe5 Qxc5 collects the second knight, leaving you with queen and pawns for the rook and bishop and real counterplay against the exposed king. Both white knights were loose once the queens came off - that is the resource.
ep: Nxc5 grabs the knight but leaves the rook on b8 and queen on c7 doing nothing; Ka1 tucks the king away and b4 gains time, and white simply consolidates with the extra material and a safe king.

pv: dxc5 Nxc5
e: dxc5 opens the game while Black's pieces are still awkward: after Nxc5 the d-file is yours for the rook on d1 and the knight on c5 can be hit by b4 or Be3. Just as important, releasing the centre denies Black the closed structure his ...b5-b4 storm against your king on c1 needs.
ep: d5 shuts the centre and effectively invites the attack: Qa5, Rb8 and b5-b4 all come with tempo at your king while your own kingside play is a move slower - the game's Qa5 and later b5 show exactly that.

pv: Kb1 Rb8 Nb5 Qxd2 Rxd2 a6 Na7 Nb6 Nxc8 Rfxc8 g3 Na4 Bh3 Rc7 Ne2 b5
e: Kb1 is the standard prophylaxis in opposite-castling races: the king steps off the c1-h6 diagonal and off the a5-e1 line, so ...c4 and Qa5 tricks lose their sting. Concretely, with the c3 knight no longer pinned to the king, Nb5! becomes possible - Qxd2 Rxd2 a6 Na7 and the knight lands on c8.
ep: Be2 spends a tempo on nothing while the storm is already rolling: b5! and after Bxb5 Rb8 the b-file opens straight at your king, with sacrifices on b5 giving Black a serious attack.

pv: g4 Bxg4 fxg4 hxg4 h5 b5 hxg6 fxg6 a3 b4 Nb1 Rh8 axb4 cxb4 Rxh8 Rxh8
e: This is a race, so open lines rather than shore things up: g4! immediately. After Bxg4 fxg4 hxg4, h4-h5 rolls and hxg6 rips the shelter off the king - all while Black's b5-b4 is still a move away from arriving.
ep: a3 is a defensive tempo that Black simply attacks: b5 and b4 come with gain of time against that very pawn (a3 b5 Nb1 b4 in the game), the knight is shoved back to b1, and your own attack never gets going.

pv: Qd4 cxb3 axb4 Qxb4 Qxb4 Rxb4 cxb3 e6 Nc3 Rxb3 Kc2 Rb6 dxe6 Bxe6 Ra1 Nc4
e: Your knight on f2 is already in the queen's sights along the a7-g1 diagonal and nothing defends it. Qd4! plants the queen right in the middle of that diagonal: it blocks the attack and offers a trade that defuses the whole b4/c4 pawn storm - cxb3 axb4 Qxb4 Qxb4 Rxb4 cxb3 and you are back in the game.
ep: a4 leaves the diagonal open and Qxf2 simply picks the knight up; Bxc4 does not win it back after Qc5 holds everything. The game showed it - cxb3 cxb3 Qxf2 and the piece was gone.

pv: Bf7 f4 Ng6 Nxg6 Bxg6 a4 Qe8 f5 Bh5 g4 Bf7 a5 Rb8 Ba3 d4 Ne4
e: The h4-knight is attacking your g6-bishop — Bf7! tucks it away, and after f4 Ng6! you trade knights on your terms (Nxg6 Bxg6), blunting the kingside push. The bishop later shuttles via h5 and f7, holding the light squares while Qe8 and Rb8 cover both wings.
ep: a5? opens lines at the wrong moment: b5! and after cxb5 Nxg6 hxg6 Nxb5 the knight lands on b5 hitting the c7-bishop, with the protected c5-passer and the a5/d5 pawns as lasting targets. In the game Nxg6 hxg6 Qg4 also left you defending g6 and trading queens into the worse ending.

pv: Bxb2 Nxb2 Kf7 Nd1 Ke6 Nc3 Ke5 Ne2 Nb5 Nc3 Nc7 Ne2 Ne6 Kc3 f4 h3
e: Bxb2! trades on your terms: after Nxb2 the knight is far from the action and your king marches first — Kf7-e6-e5 with f4 in hand; the line Kf7 Nd1 Ke6 Nc3 Ke5 shows the king arriving in time and the position holding comfortably.
ep: Bf6? lets White choose the trade: Bxf6! gxf6 shatters your kingside into doubled f-pawns with e4 fixed as a target. The knight then probes at leisure (Nc3 with Ne2 in the line, the game's Nb6 hitting d5) while your a7-knight watches from the corner — the static weaknesses decide.

pv: Ke5 Na4 f4 h3 Nf5 Ke1 Ne3 b5 cxb5 c6 Nxg2+ Ke2 f3+ Kf2 Kd6 c7
e: Ke5! keeps every pawn defended and centralizes: e4 stays covered by f5, the king shoulders White's pieces, and f4 comes next under escort — after Na4 f4 h3 the knight swings Nf5-e3, hitting g2, and with c6 and Nxg2+ the pawns break through on both wings.
ep: f4? abandons the e4-pawn — f5 was its only defender — and Nxe4! takes it while also hitting g5. The extra pawn and the bind vanish in one move: the game's Kf5 Nd6+ and Nf7+ kept harassing, and a +2.9 endgame collapsed to nothing.

pv: g4 Kd3 Nf5 g3 fxg3 Nxg3 Ne7 Nf1 Nd5 Kc4 Ke5 Nd2 Ne3+ Kc3 Kd5 Kd3
e: g4! fixes the kingside and keeps the f4/g4 duo intact: after Kd3 Nf5! the knight covers everything — g3 fxg3 Nxg3 Ne7! and the knight reroutes to d5, setting a blockade White cannot crack. A clean hold.
ep: Kf5? attacks the e4-knight but walks into Kd3! — suddenly your own d4-knight is the piece attacked, and after Ne6, Nd6+ turns the tables with tempo. h3 and g3 then dissolve your pawns; the game's Nd6+ Ke5 Kd3 came to the same thing.

pv: f3
e: f3! was the saving resource: the pawn trades itself favourably — gxf3 Nxf3 and your knight hits h2, regaining the pawn with a level knight ending. With White's knight this active, every pawn has to stay tactically accounted for, and f3 is the only move that does it.
ep: g4?? hangs the pawn to a merry-go-round of forks: Nc4+! Kd5 Nb6+ Ke5 Nd7+ Kd5 Nf6+ — every check herds your king — and Nxg4+ finally scoops the pawn with yet another fork. Nothing could be done in between; the game's Nf7+ and Ng5 won it only slightly more slowly.

pv: Nf5 h3 Ne3 Ne4 Ke5 hxg4 Nxg4 Nd6 Kd5 Nc8 Ne5+ Kc3 Ng6 Kb3 Kd4 Na7
e: Nf5! keeps the knight in the defensive zone: it heads for e3 hitting g2, and after h3 Ne3 Ne4 Ke5 hxg4 Nxg4! the f4-pawn stays escorted while the kingside liquidates — a comfortable hold.
ep: Nb3? sends the knight to the wrong wing: h4! and the h-pawn simply runs — even gxh3 gxh3 only replaces it, and the knight is far too slow to come back. The game showed exactly that: after the Nc1/Nb3 shuffle, h4 decided.

pv: Na2+ Kb3 Nc1+ Ka4 f3 gxf3 Kc4 Ka5 Nb3+ Kb6 Kxb4 Kxc6 Nxc5 Kd5 Nd3 Nf4
e: Na2+! checks from the safe side: Kb3 Nc1+ Ka4 and now f3! gxf3 Kc4! — your king attacks b4, and after Ka5 Nb3+! Kb6 Kxb4 the pawns come off in pairs (Kxc6, Nxc5) with a dead draw.
ep: Ne2+? checks into the king's reach: Kd2! attacks the knight, and after f3 gxf3 Nd4 White saves everything with Nf4+! followed by Ng6+ and Nh4, guarding f3 with tempo — two clean pawns up. The game's repetition of Nc1+ and Ne2 only postponed the same fate.

pv: Na2 Nxf4+ Kc4 Kd2 Nxb4 Ne6 Kd5 Nd8 Na6 Ke3 Nxc5 Nxc6 Ke6 Kf4 Nd3+ Kg5
e: Na2! hits the b4-pawn and forces the liquidation you need: Nxf4+ Kc4! Kd2 Nxb4 and the pawns disappear in pairs — Ne6 Kd5 and later Nxc5 against Nxc6 leave nothing on the board: a book draw.
ep: Ne2? keeps the knight where the king hounds it: Kd2! and after f3 gxf3 Nd4 White holds the f3-pawn with checks — Nf4+ Ke5 Ng6+ Kf6 Nh4 — and stays two pawns up. The knight had to go for b4 via a2, not shuffle in the corner.

pv: Na2+ Kb3 Nc1+ Kc2 Na2 Nxf4+ Kc4 b5 Nb4+ Kd2 cxb5 Nd3 Nxd3 c6 Nc5 c7
e: Na2+! again: Kb3 Nc1+ Kc2 Na2 and the knight clings to the b4-counterplay from the safe corner — after Nxf4+ Kc4! b5 Nb4+! Kd2 cxb5 the queenside liquidates and the ending is holdable.
ep: Ne2+? loses to the familiar mechanism: Kd2! hits the knight, f3 gxf3 Nd4 Nf4+! and Ng6-h4 secures f3 with tempo — White keeps b4, c5 and f3 against your lone c6-pawn. In the game Kb3 let you continue, but the position kept sliding the same direction.

pv: Kd4 Nf3+ Kd5 Ka4 Nc1 Ka5 Nd3 Nh4 Ne5 Nf5 Ke6 Nd4+ Kd5 Nc2 f3 gxf3
e: Kd4! keeps the king on the squares that matter: it stays in touch with c5 and shepherds the knight home — Nf3+ Kd5 Ka4 Nc1! and Nd3 hits both b4 and c5, tying White's king and knight down while f3 stays in reserve. That is a hold.
ep: Ke3? drifts away from the queenside: Nf3! builds a barrier over d4 and e5, and your checks only lose time — Nc1+ Kb2 Nd3+ Kc3 and the knight must run again, after which b5! breaks through on the queenside while your king is stranded on e3.

pv: Nd4
e: Nd4! is the only square that holds: from d4 the knight covers both b5 and c6 in one move, freezing the b4-b5 break for good — and with the break stopped, White's king has no way through while f3 waits in reserve. One square, two duties.
ep: Ng3? steps away from the queenside duties: b5! breaks at once — after cxb5+ Kxb5 the c5-pawn runs with the king escorting it and your pieces a world away. The game made the point brutally: Ne4 Nxe4 Kxe4 c6 and the pawn promotes.

pv: Nf5 Nh3 Ke4 c6 Ne7 c7 Kf5 Nf2 Ke5 Kc5 Nc8 Kc6 Kf5 Kb7 Nd6+ Kb8
e: Nf5 keeps your knight alive for the one job that matters: stopping the c-pawn. It reroutes via e7 to c8 (Nf5, then Ne7 and Nc8 in the line), the only blockading square, while your king and f-pawn stay active on the other wing. You are worse either way, but with the knight camped on c8/d6 White's king can't just escort the pawn home.
ep: Ne4 offers exactly the trade White wants: Nxe4 removes the only black piece that can catch the c-pawn. In the game Kxe4 c6 followed, and with the b5-king escorting from the side, your king can never reach the pawn - it queens by force.

pv: Nf3 cxd4 Nxd4 a6 Be3 Ngf6 f3 h5 Be2 Qc7 a4 Ne5 Nd5 Nxd5 exd5 O-O
e: Nf3 develops and adds the needed defender to d4 — the one pawn under real pressure from ...cxd4 and the g7-bishop's long diagonal. After ...cxd4 Nxd4 everything is covered, and Be3, f3 and a4 give a comfortable, normal middlegame (+0.5).
ep: Bb5? drops the center: ...cxd4! and the pawn can't be regained — Qxd4 runs into ...Bxc3+! bxc3, the g7-bishop striking through with check and wrecking your queenside — so even best play (Nd5) grovels a pawn down. The game's Nce2 conceded it too, and ...e5 seized the initiative (-2.3).

pv: f3 d5 c3 dxe4 cxd4 exd4 Bd6 d3 Rc1 Qb6 Bc7 Qa7 Bd6 Bf8 Bxf8 Rxf8
e: f3 holds things together: it defends e4 and prepares c3 to dissolve the cramping d4-pawn — after ...d5 c3 dxe4 cxd4 the center liquidates, every white piece stays defended, and the dark-squared bishop finds work via Bd6. You're still worse after the shaky opening (-2.8), but there are no tactics against you.
ep: Qb4? goes pawn-hunting while behind in development: ...a5! hits the queen, and after Qxd6 Ra6! it must scurry to a3, when ...Nxe4 wins the central pawn with every black piece joining the attack (-4.8). In the game ...Nxe4 landed a few moves later with the same effect.

pv: Qxd4+ Qxd4 Nxd4 a5 a3 a4 Ba2 Nc4 Bxc4 bxc4 Nge2 Bg4 O-O Bxe2 Nxe2 Rab8
e: Qxd4+! does three jobs at once: it removes the dangerous passed d-pawn, gives check on the long diagonal, and attacks the e4-knight — so Black has nothing better than trading queens, and after ...Qxd4 Nxd4 you reach a slightly worse but very holdable ending (-0.8). With your king stuck in the center, the queen trade was the resource to grab.
ep: Nh3? hangs the knight: ...Bxh3 gxh3 Qh4+! forces the block Ng3, and ...Nxg3 hxg3 Qxg3+ strips your king bare — the game continued exactly this way, the h1-rook and exposed king collapsing together (-4.2).

pv: Qe3 Qb6 O-O-O Bf5 Bd3 Bxd3 Rxd3 Na5 b3 Nc6 Bd6 Rc8 Nf3 Nb4 Bxb4 Qxb4
e: Qe3 first, castling second: on f3 the queen invites ...Bg4, and the difference is whether your rook is already on d1 when that hit lands. After Qe3 Qb6 O-O-O Bf5 Bd3 you finish development, trade the light-squared bishops and stand normally (-0.7).
ep: O-O-O walks into ...Bg4!: the queen must step away (Qe3), and ...Bxd1 wins rook for bishop — the rook you just castled onto d1. The game saw exactly ...Bg4 (Qg3 Bxd1 Nxd1) and the exchange was gone (-2.5).

pv: Kd2
e: Kd2 handles the stray a2-knight the safe way: it keeps c3 solidly covered and — the real point — makes sure any ...Nxc3 comes without check, so the knight stays a bystander. The king also heads for the centre, keeping the game balanced (-0.4).
ep: Kb1 attacks the knight but stands on the one square where ...Nxc3+! works: the check forces bxc3, and after ...Rxc3 Black has two pawns and total command of the c-file for the knight — your queenside is wrecked and the rooks invade (-3.4), as the game showed.

pv: Na2 Ne4 Qg2 Qh4 Ng3 Nd6 f3 O-O Kb1 Rfd8 Rg1 c5 dxc5 Nxc5 Rd4 g6
e: Na2 steps aside before ...b4 hits the c3-knight, and keeps the game closed while your attack isn't ready. The regrouping Qg2 and Ng3 follows, covering e4 and h5, and after Nd6 f3 O-O Kb1 White's setup holds together at +0.5.
ep: g5 simply drops a pawn: hxg5, and there is no good recapture - Qxg5 invites b4! axb4 Bc4, when the a6-bishop forces its way to f1 and Black's play arrives first. In the game Nh5! hit your queen before recapturing, and the kingside fell apart anyway.

pv: Ng3 Nxg3 Qxg3 b4 gxh6 g6 Nb1 Bxf1 Rdxf1 bxa3 Nxa3 Rab8 h4 Kh8 h5 g5
e: Ng3 deals with the real nuisance - the h5-knight - and gives your stranded queen a road home: after Nxg3 Qxg3 she returns from c7 in one move. Then b4 gxh6 g6 Nb1 keeps things messy at only -0.9. The c6-pawn was never worth touching.
ep: Qxc6? walks into Rfc8!, hitting the queen with tempo. The desperado Nxd5 exd5 Qxd5 keeps material level, but Black's b4, Rab8 and Qxb4-Qa2 arrive with a decisive attack on your c1-king (-3.9) - in the game the b-file pressure duly won.

pv: e4 Rh2+ Ke3 Re1+ Kd3 Nh5 g4 Nf4+ Kc4 Rc1 Kb5 Rcxc2 Rxc2 Rxc2 Ra3 g5
e: e4 gets the central pawns moving and shelters your king: after Rh2+ Ke3 Re1+ Kd3 the checks dry up, the king slips toward c4 and b5, and the d4/e4 duo plus the active a4-rook give real saving chances (-1.8).
ep: Rb3 offers a trade Black has no reason to take: Rh2+!, then Rf1-f2 doubles on your second rank and f3 falls (Rxf3), while your rooks end up bunched passively on a3/b3. The game went the same way - Rg1, Rh2+, and the f- and g-pawns dropped.

pv: d5 Nf5 Re4 Rg2+ Kd3 Rh1 Rbb4 Rd1+ Kc4 Rc2+ Kb3 Rcc1 Kb2 Ra1 Rbc4
e: d5! keeps the connected passers together and clears the fourth rank: after Nf5 (hitting e3) Re4! both defends e3 and confronts the g4-rook. With c6 and d5 ready to roll and both rooks active (Rbb4), White is worse but very much alive (-2.1).
ep: c7 pushes the pawn onto a dead square: the d6-knight controls c8, so it can never queen. Black simply ignores it - Rg2+ Kd3 Rhh2 doubles on your second rank with Rd2+/Rc2+ chasing your king, and in the game Rxf4 collected another pawn while c7 stood useless.

pv: Nf3 b5 a3 Ng4 Ng5 Ndf6 Bxg4 Bxg4 f3 h6 Nh3 Bxh3 Rxh3 h5 Be5 a5
e: Nf3! develops while guarding e5 - the exact square Black's g7-bishop, f6-knight and d7-knight are all pointed at - and keeps your king flexible. After b5 a3 Ng4 Ng5 you meet the wing demonstration calmly and stand clearly better.
ep: O-O-O? castles into the storm and gives up e5 in the same breath: e5! dxe5 Nxe5 frees Black's whole game, and a5/b5 arrives quickly against the c1-king. In the game e5-e4 gained space at once, Bxg7 was forced, and your attack never started.

pv: Nf2 Nd5 Nd1 h6 a3 a5 c4 Nb6 Nf2 Ba6 b3 a4 Kc2 axb3+ Kxb3 Rb8
e: Nf2! keeps the knight in touch with g4 - the tactical weak point - and reroutes toward d1, where it holds e3 and keeps the e8-rook out. After Nd5 Nd1 h6 the position stays level; every White piece just has to keep one eye on that g4-pawn.
ep: Ng5? abandons g4: h6! forces Nh3, and then Nxg4! wins the pawn, because Bxg4 Bxg4 renews the attack against the h3-knight - it can never be kept. The game went exactly h6, Nh3, Nxg4, and after the trades Black had the pawn and the initiative.
