pv: Re1+ Kf5 Re5+ Kg6 f5+ Kh6 Ne3 g6 Rxc5 Re8 Rd5 Bb6 Ng2 Bc7 Nhf4 b6
e: Re1+! starts a king hunt: Kf5 Re5+ Kg6 f5+! Kh6 boxes the stray king in on h6. Then Ne3 consolidates and Rxc5! simply collects the loose knight — the checks did double duty, caging the king and leaving c5 undefended. White stays completely winning.
ep: Ng5+? lets Black trade off the attacker: Bxg5!, and after Re1+ Kf3 fxg5 Be6 the king slips out via f3 while the bishop challenges your c4/d5 battery — still better for White, but the mating net and the win of the c5-knight are gone. In the game Bxg5 fxg5 Bg4+! activated Black further.

pv: dxe4 Rd7 Rc1 Qf1 Qc3 Rxc1 Qxc1 Rd8+ Kh7 Rxc8 Qxc8 Qa1 f5 a4 Qc4 Qb2
e: Take first: dxe4! wins the e4-pawn — nothing defends it — and the c-file grip does not run away: after Rd7 you still play Rc1, and Qf1 Qc3 leaves your heavy pieces dominating both open files a clean pawn up (+3.2). White's rooks are stuck defending each other on d1/d2 and the a6-queen is completely out of the defense.
ep: Rc1 lets White resolve the centre his way: exd5! and after exd5 Rxd5 the pawn fell with tempo — in the game Qc6 Qxa7 Qxd5 Rxc1 fizzled into simplification and near-equality (+0.3). The central tension favoured you; the move order handed the capture to the wrong side.

pv: Qd5 g4 Rh1+ Kg3 Rg1+ Kf4 g5+ Ke3 Re1#
e: Qd5! spins the mating net: the queen seizes the long diagonal and covers h1, so Rh1# is the immediate threat — the king cannot touch the rook. After g4, Rh1+ Kg3 Rg1+ Kf4 g5+! Ke3 Re1# — mate in 5, your g-pawn delivering the check that drives the king onto the e-file where the rook waits.
ep: Qd1 lets White's queen start checking: Qa8+ Kh7 Qe4+! forces f5, and the pawn drops with more checks to follow — still winning (+5.2), but mate-in-5 became a defensive task. In the game White instead collapsed with Qxf7+?? and Kxf7 ended it at once.

pv: c4 Qd2 dxc3 Bxc3 cxd3+ Kb2 Nxg3 h5 Nxh1 hxg6 hxg6 a4 Qxc3+ Qxc3 Rxc3 Kxc3
e: c4! blasts open the queenside where the white king sits on c2. After Qd2 you continue dxc3 Bxc3 cxd3+, winning the d3-pawn with check and stripping the king; then Kb2 Nxg3 lets the h5-knight collect g3 and even the h1-rook (Nxh1). And if white grabs with dxc4, Qxc4 crashes in with checks against the bare king (+6.7).
ep: Red8 gives white time to play c4 himself — exactly what happened in the game. The queenside closes, your c5-pawn is fixed, and the attack on the c2-king loses its battering ram. You stayed clearly better (+3.9), but the forced win of material was gone.

pv: exd5 bxc3 Nxc3 Bb4 dxe6 fxe6 Rhe1 O-O Rxe6 Kh7 Qe3 Qa5 Qe4 Qf5 Nd5 a5
e: Ignore the hit on the knight — exd5! strikes the center first: after ...bxc3 Nxc3 the piece comes back with the position opening, and dxe6 fxe6 followed by Rhe1 and Rxe6 tears open the e-file against a king stranded on e8. White emerges a pawn up with a raging initiative (+2.5).
ep: Na4 parks the knight on the rim, where it attacks nothing and becomes the target — in the game ...Qa5 hit it at once and ...c3 followed. Meanwhile the central moment passed: after ...Be7 and ...exd5 exd5 Black consolidates and the game is dead level (-0.2).

pv: d6 Bd8 Qf3 Nb6 Be3 N8d7 Bxb6 Nxb6 d7+ Nxd7 Rhf1 Rh7 a3 bxa3 Nexc3 Nb6
e: d6! rams the e7-bishop: it must retreat to d8, buried alive, and Black never coordinates again. Qf3 and Be3 then win the minor-piece battle — Bxb6 removes a defender, and the pawn gives itself at the perfect moment with d7+ to keep Black's knights tangled (+2.5). The e7-bishop was Black's glue; hit it while you can.
ep: Be3 lets the bishop breathe — ...Bd6 in the game — and allows ...Qb5, offering the queen trade that kills your initiative: after the game's ...Qxd3 cxd3 the attack was gone while Black's b4- and c3-pawns remained a long-term asset (+0.9).

pv: Rf6 Nxf6 Rxf6 exd4 Nxd4 Rfd8 Nb5 Bc5 Nxc5 Nxc5 Nd6 Rxd6 Rxd6 Nxe4 Ra6 Nc5
e: Rf6! forces matters: the rook attacks both the d6-bishop and g6, so Black more or less must take, and after ...Nxf6 Rxf6 the second rook renews both threats. Then ...exd4 Nxd4 Rfd8 Nb5! and the knights land on b5, c5 and d6 — full positional compensation for the exchange, keeping the balance (+0.1) in a position where quiet moves drift into trouble.
ep: Bf2 drifts: ...Rce8 reroutes the a6-knight via c7 toward b5 while your a4-knight sits offside, and Black slowly takes over the open lines (-1.4). In the game ...exd4 Nxd4 Ne5 planted a dominant central knight immediately — the very piece Rf6 would have removed.

pv: Nb5 Nd3+ Kc2 Nxf2 R1xf2 Bg3 Rg2 Nc7 Nxc7 Bxc7 Nb6 Be5 Rc6 Rd6 Rxd6 Bxd6
e: Nb5! keeps the knight attacking — it hits the d6-bishop, and the tactics hold: ...Nd3+ Kc2 Nxf2 R1xf2 Bg3 is met by Rg2, and later Nxc7 plus Nb6 (the a4-knight) collects Black's queenside. The d4-knight was your proudest piece — reroute it to where it bites, don't swap it off (+1.2).
ep: Nc6 offers a trade Black loves: ...Nxc6 dxc6 repairs his structure, and ...Be5! then hits your f6-rook while ...Rd2 invades — in the game the rook had to crawl back to f2 and was exchanged, and Black's rooks took over the second rank (-1.5).

pv: Nd1 f6 Nf2 Rh7 Nxc6+ bxc6 Rxg3 c5 g5 c4 gxf6+ Kxf6 Ng4+ Bxg4
e: Nd1! re-routes to f2, where the knight attacks the rook on h3 and covers h1 against back-rank checks. After f6 Nf2 Rh7 the knight on g3 has run out of defenders, so Nxc6+ bxc6 Rxg3 nets a clean piece.
ep: b3 ignores the pieces swarming around f3 and h3: Rh1+ Kb2 Nf1 hits the d2 rook and pulls your rooks apart, and Rd1 Nh2 Rxh1 Nxf3 in the game handed the exchange straight back.

pv: Na5 Rc8 Rf1 Ke5 Nc3 b4 Nb1 Kxe4 Nc4 Rh8 Nbd2+ Kd5 Re1 Rh7 Nf3 Rh5
e: You are a piece up, so the job is simply to keep the knights safe. Na5 does it — the knight cannot be attacked there, it covers c4 and b7, and after Rc8 Rf1 you improve the rook and the king while black has no counterplay whatsoever.
ep: Na7 walks into the corner where Ra8 traps it: c8 is covered by the rook, c6 by the king, and b5 is a pawn — so you have to bail out with Nxb5+ axb5, giving the extra piece back for a single pawn.

pv: Nf4 Kb6 Nxe6 fxe6 Rf7 b4 a4 bxa3+ Kxa3 Ra8 b4 cxb4+ Kxb4 Rxa7 Rxa7 Kxa7
e: Don't cash in the trapped knight yet — Nf4! activates the other one with tempo on the e6 bishop. After Kb6 Nxe6 fxe6 Rf7 you win the bishop and the seventh rank, and even when the a7 knight finally goes (Rxa7 Rxa7 Kxa7) you are the side with the material.
ep: Nxb5+ axb5 swaps your extra piece for one pawn and opens the a-file for black's rook; the e2 knight had the far better resource of hitting the e6 bishop first.

pv: Nf6 Rc8 Rd2+ Ke5 Nxd7+ Kxe4 Re2+ Kf4 Nf6 c4 Nd5+ Kf3 Re5 f5 bxc4 bxc4
e: Nf6! forks the bishop on d7 and the rook on g8 — black cannot save both. After Rc8 Rd2+ Ke5 Nxd7+ the bishop is gone with check, and Re2+ keeps gaining time while the e-pawn and the extra piece decide the game.
ep: Rxf7 wins a pawn but hands over the initiative: Be6 hits the rook and the d5 knight at once, and after Rf3 Bxd5 exd5 Kxd5 black liquidates into a holdable position — the game followed exactly that.

pv: Rf3 Bxd5 Rd3 Rg4 exd5 Rb4 a3 Rh4 a4 bxa4 c4 Kc7 Rg3 Kb6 Rg8 Rh3
e: Rf3 steps out of the bishop's attack and sets up the real idea: if Bxd5, then Rd3! pins the bishop against the king on d6 and it is lost, so exd5 leaves you a clean piece ahead with the rook already active on the third rank.
ep: Rf6 defends nothing and lets the king march in: Ke5 forces Rh6, and Bxd5 exd5 Kxd5 wins back the last pawn with the knight gone for free. That is how the game slipped to a draw.

pv: e6 g4 Bg6 Ne5 Nxe5 dxe5 a6 f4 Bb4 Qd4 Bxc3+ bxc3 Be4 Rg1 Ne7 Bd3
e: e6! readies the counters before White's pawns roll: when g4 Bg6 Ne5 comes, you trade (Nxe5 dxe5) and strike back with Bb4 and Be4! - the light-squared bishop lands on a dream central post (line ends Bxc3+ bxc3 Be4). +0.5 with a healthy game.
ep: Nf6 develops straight into the storm: g4! Bg6 Ne5 comes with a big gain of space, and h4-h5 keeps harassing the g6-bishop while the e5-knight dominates (punish: Qb6 Bb5 e6 h4 Bd6 h5 Be4). Near equal still (-0.6), but White attacks for free.

pv: Qf6 Ne5 Bxh1 O-O-O Be4 g5 Qf5 h4 Nxe5 dxe5 O-O h5 Qxe5 h6 Qa1+ Kd2
e: The f3-knight is all that blocks your e4-bishop's path to the h1-rook, and it is already attacked once. Qf6! attacks it a second time, threatening Bxf3 to win a piece - and if it moves, Ne5, then Bxh1 grabs the rook (line: Qf6 Ne5 Bxh1 O-O-O Be4). +4.1.
ep: h5 lets White sidestep with g5!: the pawn slides by, no lines open, and though Bxf3 and Nxd4 tricks still leave you on top (+1.9), the forcing win of the h1-rook is gone. In the game White defended with Rg1 and you kept strong pressure.

pv: g5 b4 gxh4 Bf2 Bg6 Bxg6 Nxg6 Rxe6 Bf4 Rd1 Kf7 Ree1 a5 bxa5 Bxd2 Rxd2
e: g5! traps the knight on h4. It has no squares at all: Ng6 runs into hxg6, Nf5 into exf5, and f3 and g2 are blocked by White's own pawns. He can only ignore it with b4, when gxh4 leaves you a clean piece up with a solid centre.
ep: Ng6 rescues White's worst piece for free - after Nxg6 Bxg6 the knight that had no square is off the board, and the game's Bxg6 hxg6 left a completely ordinary position.

pv: Ba5 dxe5 bxc3 bxc3 Bxc3 exf6 Bxe1 Rxe1 Rc2 Nd7 d4 fxg7 Raa2 Nf6+ Kxg7 Ne4
e: Don't release the tension yet - Ba5! first, adding the bishop to the pressure on b4/c3 and lining it up against the rook on e1. After dxe5 bxc3 bxc3 the point appears: Bxc3! attacks the rook, and exf6 Bxe1 Rxe1 Rc2 wins the exchange with total control of the second rank.
ep: bxc3 resolves things a move early: after bxc3 the pawn is solidly held, rooks come off with Rxe2 Rxe2, and the bishop never gets to a5 with tempo against e1.

pv: Bb6 Nd7 Ba7 Bxe5 fxe5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 Ra3 Rxd5 Rxc3 Rd7 Ra3 g3 Kh7 f4
e: Bb6 puts the bishop on the a7-g1 diagonal, where it attacks the knight on c5 and the d4 pawn at the same time and ties White to their defence; Nd7 is answered by Ba7, keeping the bind. Squeezing is worth more here than any immediate capture.
ep: Ba5 is the wrong diagonal - the bishop attacks nothing and Nb3! hits it at once: Ra3 Nxa5 Rxa5 dxe5 frees White completely and leaves your rook offside.

pv: Bb6 Rb2 Bxc5+ Ke2 fxe5 Rb5 Ra5 Rxa5 Nxa5 Bxe5 Nc4 Bd4 Bd6 Be3 Nxe3 Kxe3
e: Bb6 again, and here it is decisive: the knight on c5 is attacked and undefended, and White's king on f2 stands on that same a7-g1 diagonal, so the capture will come with check. Rb2 Bxc5+ Ke2 fxe5 and you emerge a piece to the good.
ep: Nxe5 grabs a pawn and lets everything off the hook: Bxe5 fxe5 activates White's pieces and the knight on c5 - the piece that was in real trouble - escapes. The game's Bxe5 fxe5 Rxe5 Bxc3 Rxd5 levelled the material out.

pv: Bb5 O-O Bxc6 bxc6 Be5 Qa5 Qd4 Ne8 Bxg7 Nxg7 h5 Rb8 hxg6 fxg6 O-O-O Rb4
e: Bb5 targets the c6-knight, the piece pressing on your extra c5-pawn: after O-O Bxc6 bxc6 black's queenside is wrecked, and Be5! then offers the strong g7-bishop a trade it can hardly refuse. White keeps the pawn with the sounder structure (+0.2).
ep: Nb5's threat of Nc7+ is easily met — simply castling defuses it, or Qa5+! as in the game, when after c3 the knight had no follow-up and e5 grabbed the center with tempo on your f4-bishop. The knight ends up biting air with a6 always looming (-1.1).

pv: b4 Nxb4 Bxe5 Nc6 Nc7+ Kf8 Bd6+ Kg8 Ne2 Ne8 Nxa8 Bxc3+ Nxc3 Qxc3+ Ke2 Nxd6
e: b4! hits the a5-queen and wins material by force: after Nxb4 Bxe5 white grabs a central pawn and renews Nc7+ — Kf8 Bd6+ Kg8 and Nxa8 picks up the rook in the corner, the fork landing before black's pieces can help (+1.7).
ep: Bg5 lets black castle out of every Nc7+ trick, and the tempo on the queen is spent: after O-O b4 Qd8 the attack must start from scratch (+0.4). In the game Ne4! hit the bishop at once and things unravelled from there.

pv: Qxd5 Nxg5 hxg5 Be6 Qe4 O-O a4 Bb3 Nf3 Rfd8 Be2 Rd7 Nd2 Rxd2 Kxd2 a6
e: Qxd5! does two jobs at once: it wins the d5-pawn and attacks the e4-knight. After Nxg5 hxg5 you are two pawns up with a dominant centralized queen and Nc7+ ideas still in the air (+2.5).
ep: Nd6+ trades off black's e4-knight but loses a piece: after Nxd6 cxd6, f6! traps the g5-bishop — e5 covers f4, your own e3-pawn blocks the way home, and h4 is occupied. The game's h6 and Be7 Nxe7 won it the same way (-2.0).

pv: gxf3
e: Recapture with the pawn: gxf3 keeps the e2-bishop guarding the queenside, and the doubled f-pawns are a small price — e4 can then simply be met by fxe4, and the half-open g-file even gives your rook work. You stay in the fight (-0.7).
ep: Bxf3 runs into e4!: the bishop must go to g4, where f5 snares it. The game's retreat Be2 was worse still — Bxc3+! forked king and rook, and after Kf1 Bxa1 black had won a whole rook (-3.9).

pv: h4 Bxf4 exf4 h5 g5 Ng4 Nh3 Qd6 f5 exf5 Rhe1+ Kd8
e: With opposite-side castling it is a race, and h4! starts yours. ...Bxf4 exf4 does not slow it: g5 comes with tempo on the f6-knight, h5 and Nh3 keep the pawns rolling, and the line ends with f5! ripping open the center while Black's king still sits on e8 (+1.3).
ep: a3? gives the storming pawns a hook: ...b4! now opens lines by force, and after Nb1 Ba6! the key light-square defender gets traded (...Bxd3 cxd3) - Black's attack plays itself (-1.1). In the game ...b4, ...bxa3 and ...Bxa3 shredded your king's cover.

pv: Bxb8 Nxb8 h4 Ba6 Kd2 c5 g5 Nfd7 Bxa6 Nxa6 Ke1 cxd4 exd4 hxg5 hxg5 Rxh1+
e: Bxb8! simply wins the exchange: the f4-b8 diagonal is wide open and the rook is defended only by the d7-knight, so after ...Nxb8 you have rook for bishop. With h4 and g5 to follow you keep the initiative on top of the material (+2.4).
ep: Kd2? gives Black one tempo to fix it: ...e5! attacks the bishop and closes the diagonal for good (dxe5 leaves your own pawn sitting on e5) - the exchange is gone (+0.2). In the game ...Rb2! simply activated the rook and it was never caught.

pv: Nc3 Rxb1 Rxb1 Qa7 Qg3 Kd8 Qh4 Rg8 Bd6 Ba6 g5 hxg5 Qxg5 Kc8 h4 Qa8
e: Everything hangs on b1: your c2-pawn blocks the bishop's defense of that square, so after ...Rxb1 Rxb1 the rook would stand there unprotected. Nc3! supplies the missing defender - then ...Rxb1 Rxb1 Qa7 and Black's raid has achieved nothing while your play continues (+2.5).
ep: h4?? ignores the loose back rank: ...Rxb1 Rxb1 Qxb1! wins a whole rook, since nothing can recapture on b1 and the late Nc3 is met by ...Qg1, slipping out. The game went exactly this way (-3.2).

pv: Nc3 Qg1 Qf4 Qxg4 Qh2 Nfd7 h5 Qf3 Kc1 Qf6 f4 Rg8 a4 g5 hxg6 Rxg6
e: Nc3! finally evicts the queen that has been living on b1: it must go to g1, and after Qf4 Qxg4 Qh2! you offer the queen trade that would kill the attack. You are still much worse (-3.1), but coordinated - every other move loses faster.
ep: g5? attacks the f6-knight, but it leaps in with Ne4+!: check plus a fork on the d6-bishop, so Qxe4 dxe4 - queen for knight - is already the best on offer; then ...exd3 and ...Nc4+ strip the rest (-7.1). In the game ...Nc4+ and ...Ne4+ came in the other order, with the same collapse.

pv: Bd6 Nf3 Nf6 Qe2+ Qe7 Qxe7+ Bxe7 O-O O-O Nc3 Bd6 Bg5 Nbd7 Rfe1 Nb6 Bb3
e: Bd6 is simple and best: develop the bishop to its most active diagonal, castle next, and let the symmetric structure work for you. After Nf3 Nf6 Qe2+ Qe7 the queens come off and Black is close to fully equal — White's c4/d4 duo gives nothing once your pieces are out.
ep: c5 loosens your grip on d5: White answered d5! in the game, a clamp that shut your c8-bishop out of play (Nf6 Bg5 Nbd7 Nc3 followed). It also leaves f7 tender — the punish line's Nf3 Nf6 Ng5 aims straight at it — all while your king still sits in the centre.

pv: Bd6 Nf3 O-O O-O h6 Bh4 Re8 Qb3 a6 a4 Rb8 Rfe1 Qa5 Bg3 Rxe1+ Rxe1
e: Bd6 gets your king castled next move — the one thing this position demands. After Nf3 O-O h6 Bh4 Re8 you are fully mobilized, the Bg5 pin is neutralized, and White's d5-pawn becomes a target rather than a strength.
ep: a6 spends a tempo on the wing while your king sits in the centre: d6! throws the wedge forward, and after Ne5 Qe2 Bxd6 Bxf6 gxf6 your kingside is wrecked before you have castled. The game's a4 Nb6 Ba2 left you untangling for several more moves instead.

pv: Na5 O-O
e: The c4-knight is attacked by the b3-pawn and Na5! is the only good square: it stays active, counterattacks b3, and keeps c4 and c6 available for the return trip. White has nothing better than castling, and the position remains roughly level.
ep: Nb2 hops into a cage: Rd2! attacks the knight and its lone escape is poisoned — Nxa4 Nxa4 and the piece is gone for a pawn, because White's c3-knight covered a4 all along. The game went exactly Rd2 Nxa4 Nxa4, and Nxc5 soon followed.

pv: Nf6 Bg5 h6 Bxf6 Qxf6 e3 Bb4 Bxc4 Bxc3+ bxc3 Nd7 Qf3 Qxf3 gxf3 Ke7 Nf5+
e: Nf6 is the healthy developing move and prepares to hand the gambit pawn back on good terms: after Bg5 h6 Bxf6 Qxf6 e3 Bb4 Bxc4 you have traded a pair of pieces, kept a solid structure and can finish with ...Nd7 and ...O-O. In the Queen's Gambit Accepted the c4 pawn is never meant to be defended by force.
ep: c5 pushes past the knight and hands White Ndb5, when the threat of Nc7+ forking king and rook on a8 forces you into awkward contortions — in the game you had to trade queens and stick a knight on the edge at a6.

pv: Nb4 Na3 Nd3+ Bxd3 cxd3 b3 Ne7 Bb2 Nc6 Ncb5 h5 Bc3 Rh6 O-O-O Be7 Rhg1
e: Nb4 activates your worst piece. From b4 the knight heads for d3: Na3 Nd3+! and after Bxd3 cxd3 you have traded your offside knight for White's light-squared bishop and left a protected passed pawn wedged on d3 that blocks the whole kingside development. Then ...Ne7-c6 and ...Rh6 give you a comfortable extra pawn.
ep: Nc7 sends the knight backwards to a passive square and gives up on holding c4: Na3 followed by Bxc4 simply collects the pawn, and White completes development for free.

pv: Rxd1 Rxd1 b5 Rxd8+ Bxd8 f4 f5 e4 Kb7 exf5 Bxf5 a4 b4 Nd1 Bf6 Bxc4
e: Rxd1 is the simple technical route: trading one pair of rooks kills the pressure against d7, and after Rxd1 b5! the extra pawn on c4 gets a permanent defender. Then ...Kb7 and the b/c pawn duo start rolling, with the bishops covering the entry squares.
ep: Nd5 leaves the c4 pawn loose and allows Bxc4!, which works because Nxc3 is met by Rxd7 first; after Rxd7 Bxe6 White untangles with Ne2+ and recovers everything. The extra pawn simply disappears.

pv: Ra8 a3 b4 axb4 Ra1+ Kd2 cxb4 Rc1 c3+ bxc3 Ra2+ Kd3 b3 g4
e: Ra8 puts the rook where it belongs: on the open file, hitting a2 and behind the coming pawn storm. After a3 b4! axb4 Ra1+ Kd2 cxb4 the rook is behind White's lines and the connected passers roll with c3+ and b3. Rooks support passed pawns from behind; blockading them from in front does nothing.
ep: Rd5 leaves the rook staring at its own pawns, and after Rc2 White seizes the only open file and offers the trade. In the game the rooks came off with Rd2 Rxd2 Kxd2 and without them the queenside pawns could not advance a single square.

pv: b4+ Kc2 Ka4 Kb1 f6 Bd3 h6 Bg6 Ka5 a3 c4 Kc2 Bd7 axb4+ Kxb4 Be4
e: b4+! is the move: it gains space with check, drives the king to c2 and clears the way for ...Ka4, where your king supports the pawns from the side. Follow with ...f6 and ...h6 to keep White's bishop out, and the passed b- and c-pawns plus an active king give real counterplay.
ep: Bxa2 wins a pawn and loses the bishop: b3! takes b3 away, leaving only b1, and Kb2 traps it in the corner. The same trap arrived a move later in the game.

pv: b4+ Kc2 Bd5 Bxh7 f6 Bd3 c4 Be2 f5 h3 Kb6 g4 fxg4 hxg4 Kc5 f4
e: b4+ has to come first, with check: the king is forced to c2 and only then does Bd5 escape the net before b2-b3 seals the bishop in. Giving up h7 to Bxh7 is a fair price — you keep the piece and the c- and b-pawns, supported by the king, become genuinely dangerous.
ep: h6 is a free tempo for White, and b3 immediately entombs the bishop on a2 — it has no route out and can only be handed back for pawns, which is how the game went after ...c4 bxc4.

pv: f4 b6 Be2 e6 O-O-O Ba6 Bxh5 gxh5 h3 Nc6 g4 Kh8 Kb1 Ne7 Nf3 Bh6
e: f2-f4 nails down the e5 pawn and takes the g5 and e5 squares away for good, which is the whole point of this structure. It also pre-empts Black's own ...f4 hitting your bishop on e3. After b6 Be2 e6 O-O-O the knight on h5 is stranded on the rim and Bxh5 gxh5 later leaves Black with a ruined kingside.
ep: Be2 gives Black the tempo he needs: ...f4! comes with an attack on the e3 bishop, and suddenly you are the one reacting. In the game that pawn push forced Bxh5 and then fxe3, handing over the bishop pair and the initiative.

pv: g4 fxe3 fxe3 Nf6 exf6 exf6 O-O-O Re8 Nh3 c6 Nf4 f5 Rdg1 Qe7 gxf5 Bxf5
e: g4! traps the knight on h5 rather than trading for it. Its squares are gone: f4 is a pawn, g7 a bishop, and Ng3 drops to hxg3, so after fxe3 fxe3 Nf6 exf6 exf6 you win the piece straight back and stand with a healthy extra centre. Take the material off the board on your terms instead of letting Black dictate.
ep: Bxh5 forgets that Black doesn't have to recapture: fxe3! comes first, and after Qxe3 gxh5 he has taken two bishops for a knight and a pawn. That in-between capture is exactly what happened in the game.

pv: O-O-O c5 f4 Nc6 dxc5 b6 g3 Ba6 cxb6 Qxb6 Qxb6 axb6 Nd4 Nxd4 Rxd4 b5
e: A piece down, the king on e1 is the urgent problem, not the queen. O-O-O gets it out of the centre, connects the rooks and lets f2-f4 back up the e5 pawn. After c5 f4 Nc6 dxc5 b6 the position stays messy, the e5 wedge cramps Black, and you still have practical chances.
ep: Qf4 puts the queen on a square the rook on f8 already sees down the open f-file: Rxf4 simply takes it, and Nxf4 gets back only a rook. The game ended right there with Rxf4.

pv: g4 b5
e: g4! is the right kind of move here: black's king is still on e8, so open the position where you are stronger. The pawn takes g4/h5 away, prepares g5 to chase the knight on f6 - the only real defender of d5 - and gets your kingside majority rolling before he can castle out of the way.
ep: Nb1 undevelops your best-placed piece and loses two tempi. Black gets ...Bd7, ...Qa4 and ...Rc8 with a free attack on your king on c1, and after ...Bxa3+ the pawn shelter goes; in the game he simply grabbed d4 a few moves later.

pv: Bd3 Nc6 f4 e5 fxe5 Ng4 Nc3 Nxh6 Nxd5 Qa5 Nxe7 Nxe7 Nf3 Be6 Qg5 Ng4
e: Bd3 develops the last minor piece and prepares the f4 break: Nc6 f4 e5 fxe5 Ng4 Nc3 and the knight on c3 hits d5 while the bishop on h6 remains a thorn. It also gets the bishop off f1 so the rooks connect - with a shaky queenside king you need pieces out, not more pawn moves.
ep: Nf3 leaves the queen on g3 exposed to ...Nf5, hitting the queen and the bishop on h6 at once: Qh3 Nxh6 Qxh6 Ng4 forks f2 and after Qf4 Nxf2 Rd2 Nxh1 black wins the exchange. In the game black just traded on f3.

pv: Qe3 Qxe3+ fxe3 Nf2 Be2 Kc7 Rhf1 Nxd1 Kxd1 f5 g4 Kd6 Nd2 Rg8 Re1
e: You are a rook up, so simplify: Qe3 offers the queen trade and defends f2 at the same time. After Qxe3+ fxe3 the pawn covers f2, the knight on e4 has no targets, and Be2 with Rhf1 rounds it up - Nf2 Be2 Kc7 Rhf1 Nxd1 Kxd1 and the game is over. Trading queens when material up is the whole technique.
ep: Nc3 leaves f2 undefended, and Nxf2 forks the rooks on d1 and h1. That is exactly what happened: after Bd3 Nxh1 black won the exchange back and the win became much harder.

pv: Qg3 Qd4 Qd6 Qh4 Re2 Qg5+ Kb1 Qd8 Qg3 Bc6 Na2 Qc7 Re5 d4 Nb4
e: Qg3 keeps the queen on the active b8-h2 diagonal, hitting toward c7 and d6 and pinning black down: Qd4 Qd6 Qh4 Re2 holds everything while your extra piece counts. The knight on c3 stays put blockading d5, and black is never allowed the freeing ...e5.
ep: Nd1 retreats the piece that held d5 and e4, and black immediately frees himself with ...e5 and ...d4, gaining space and activity for the pawns he is down. In the game that break came at once and the position got much harder to hold.

pv: Qxd4 Qc7 g3 g5 Qf6 h6 Nc3 f4 Bh5 Re6 Qh8+ Bc8 Rxe4 fxg3 hxg3 Qxg3
e: The d4 pawn is simply hanging: nothing on c5 or e5 guards it and the c6 queen doesn't cover d4 either, so Qxd4 wins it and kills Black's connected central duo in one go. After Qc7 g3 the queen swings to f6, Nc3 hits e4 and Bh5 pressures the e8 rook, and once Qh8+ drives the bishop back Rxe4 mops up the second pawn. The point is not the pawn alone but that the d4-e4 pair was Black's only counterplay.
ep: Bc4 leaves the pawn duo intact and hands Black free tempi: a5 hits the queen, Qb3 a4 gains another, and the pawns start rolling. In the game b5 and d3 arrived and the pawn even reached c2 with check.

pv: Nc3 dxc2 Kxc2 f4 Kb1 g5 Bf7 Re5 Qf8+ Kc7
e: Nc3 brings the last piece into play and immediately hits e4 and b5, and it invites dxc2 Kxc2 when your king safely eats the intruder that was cramping the back rank. After f4 Kb1 g5 the bishop lands on f7 hitting the e8 rook and Qf8+ picks up more. The knight on d1 was doing nothing but babysitting c3 squares.
ep: Kb1 is a wait move that leaves the d3 pawn alive and the d1 knight buried; Black gets Be6 to trade off your excellent light-squared bishop, which is the piece doing all the work against f7 and the black king.

pv: Qe5+ Kc8 Qxb5 Rd7 Rc1 Rc7 Qa6+ Kb8 Qd6 f4 Qd8+ Bc8 Qxc7+ Kxc7 Bb1+
e: Qe5+ is a fork: from e5 the queen checks the b8 king down the diagonal and simultaneously eyes b5, a pawn no black piece defends. After Kc8 Qxb5 you are two pawns up with the queen dominating, and the follow-up Rc1, Qa6+ and Qd6 ties Black's rook to the seventh before Qxc7+ liquidates into a won ending.
ep: Nd1 walks into Qc4+, forcing the queen trade, and after Qxc4 Bxc4+ the king is deflected so the knight on d1 falls. That's exactly the game: Bc4+ Kf2 Rxd1 and most of the advantage was gone.

pv: e6 O-O Nf6 Nc3 Qa5 h3 Bxf3 Bxf3 Bb4 Be3 Rd8 Rc1 O-O Bxc6 bxc6 a3
e: Finish development first with e6: it opens the Bf8, secures d5 and keeps the bishop pair. The trade on f3 is still there later on your terms — in the main line Nf6, Qa5 and only after h3 do you play Bxf3 Bxf3 Bb4, when your queen is not the thing being hit.
ep: Bxf3 gives up the bishop pair and, worse, does it with tempo against yourself: after Bxf3 the bishop attacks your queen on d5, so Qd7 is forced and White gets d5! kicking the knight and seizing the centre for free.

pv: Qd8 d5 Ne5 Bf4 Nxf3+ Qxf3 g6 d6 Bg7 Qxb7 exd6 Bxd6 Qc8 Qe4+ Qe6 Qxe6+
e: The queen has been chased and must retreat: Qd8 keeps everything defended. After d5 Ne5! the knight is well placed and Nxf3+ trades off White's strong bishop, so you emerge with a pawn deficit at most instead of a disaster.
ep: Qxd4 hangs the queen to a check: Bxc6+ takes the knight and after bxc6 Qxd4 the queen is gone. That is precisely how the game ended.

pv: b5 b3 bxc4 bxc4 Rd3+ Kc2 Bb4 Kd1 Rhd8 Ke2 Bc3 g4 Bg6 Rb1 R3d7 Rb5
e: White's king is stuck on c3 with all your pieces pointing at it, so open lines fast: b5! hits the bishop on c4 and after b3 bxc4 bxc4 Rd3+ Kc2 Bb4 the rook and bishop swarm the exposed king while you keep the extra material. Slow moves let him consolidate; a lead in development plus an exposed king means you must strike now.
ep: Rd7 gives white the tempo he needs to free himself with e4!, hitting the bishop on f5 and undermining e5 - after Bxe4 Re1 he wins the pawn back and the attack on the c3 king is gone. In the game Nxe5 just took the pawn.

pv: Nd5+ Kd4 Bc5+ Kxd5 Rd8+ Nd7 Rdxd7+ Ke5 Bg6 Kf4 Bd6+ Kf3 Nxc4 Nxc4 Rxc4 Rd1
e: Nd5+ drags the king into the open: Kd4 Bc5+! and if Kxd5 Rd8+ Nd7 Rdxd7+ the white king is stranded in the middle of the board with checks from every direction. The point is that every black piece already bears down on the c3 king, so the check on d5 costs nothing and gains everything.
ep: a6 is a wasted move that hands white the time for b3 and Kb2 - and once the king can hide, ...Nd5+ no longer bites: b3 Nd5+ Kb2 and after Bb4 e4 white even wins the exchange back on a1.

pv: Nd5+ Kd4 Bc5+ Kxd5 Rd8+ Nd7 f6 Bb5 axb5 Ne4 Rdxd7+ Nd6+ Rxd6#
e: Nd5+ forces mate: Kd4 Bc5+ Kxd5 Rd8+ Nd7 and now f6! shuts the escape route, Bb5 axb5 Rdxd7+ Nd6+ Rxd6#. Mate in 7. The check on d5 is what pulls the king off c3 into the net your rooks and bishop have already built.
ep: Re8 lets the king slip away - b3 gives it b2 and the whole mating net dissolves. You are still winning, but a forced mate turned into a long technical grind.

pv: Bc2 Qd2 Bxb3 Rfc1 Rxc1+ Qxc1 Bc4 Rb1 O-O Kh2 Nf5 Bd2
e: Bc2! forks queen and knight: the d1-queen is the b3-knight's only defender, so after Qd2 comes Bxb3 and the knight is simply lost. The cleanup is easy — Rfc1 Rxc1+ Qxc1 Bc4 tucks the bishop away and you castle next, a full piece to the good (+4.0).
ep: b6? passes on a free piece. After Rc1 White contests the c-file and consolidates; you kept your extra pawn (+2.3) and went on to win anyway, but Bc2, available for exactly one move, would have decided the game on the spot.

pv: Qg3+ Kf1 bxc4 f5 Bxf5 gxf5 cxb3 Rxc8+ Kh7 Bxh6 b2 Rb8 b1=R+ Rxb1 Qd3+ Kg2
e: Insert the check first: Qg3+! Kf1, and only now bxc4 — the pawn takes the knight and hits the b3-queen in the same breath, keeping d5 intact. White's counter f5 fails spectacularly: Bxf5 gxf5 cxb3! wins the queen outright, and after Rxc8+ Kh7 Bxh6 b2 the passed pawn decides (+6.8).
ep: dxc4 wins the same knight but skips the check, and the difference is Bf2!: your queen is hit first, and after Qd8 Qf3 the b3-queen slips away — you stay clearly better (+2.8) but the forced win is gone. In the game Qc3? let you throw in Qg3+ after all, and the attack crashed through.

pv: Nh3 f4
e: Nh3 gets the last piece out and keeps g4 as a genuine threat instead of a pawn offer: the knight eyes f4 and g5, and after O-O White's extra space and grip on e5 are a lasting plus.
ep: The immediate g4 is simply a pawn: fxg4, and after Bd3 Black has Nb4!, swapping off your attacking bishop - Qxg4 Nxd3+ cxd3 and Black keeps the pawn with the better structure. In the game f4 declined it, locking the kingside, and g5 soon buried your knight on h3.

pv: Nf3 d6 Qd2 Bd7 exd6 Bxd6 O-O-O O-O-O Ne4 Kb8 Rhe1 Rhf8 Bc4 Bc8 Nxd6 Rxd6
e: Nf3 puts the knight on a working square: it guards d4, supports the e5-wedge and keeps g5 and h4 available. After d6 exd6 Bxd6 you castle long with every piece placed, and Ne4 next probes the loose f4-pawn and the dark squares.
ep: Nh3 walks into g5!: with pawns fixed on f4 and g5 the knight has literally no move and stays entombed in the corner - precisely what the game showed, while Black expanded with Bb4 and took over the initiative.

pv: Ne4 d5 Nf6+ Ke7 Nf2 c5 h4 Qg6 Qd2 Bd7 dxc5 Bxc5 c4 Rab8
e: Ne4 - the c3-knight - heads for the hole on f6: after d5 Nf6+ the king must move (Ke7), forfeiting castling for good, and only then does Nf2 bring the corner knight back. All of Black's dark squares around the king are soft; f6 is the entry point.
ep: Nf2 recycles the wrong knight first: without Nf6+ inserted, Black keeps castling rights and simply develops the c8-bishop (Ba6 in the game). The chance to fix the king in the center - the main prize here - quietly disappears.

pv: Nce4 Qe7 c3 c5 a4 cxd4 a5 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 cxb4 Qxb4+ Qd2 Qb5 Rc1 Qxe5
e: Nce4 occupies the central hole where the knight watches both d6 and f6: Black's bishops on a6 and b6 hit only granite, and after Qe7 c3 you build up slowly - the g5/f4 pawns and the dark squares around Black's king remain chronic problems.
ep: Qd2 gives Black time for O-O-O!: the rooks connect, and the freeing d6-break (after Na4, d6! exd6 e5) turns the passive bishops loose with a rolling center and near-equality. In the game Rb8 and Qe7 were slower and your grip held.

pv: h4 Kf7 hxg5 hxg5 Nce4 d6 Rh5 dxe5 Nxg5+ Kg8 Rxh8+ Kxh8 Nfe4 Bxd4 Qh2+ Kg8
e: h4! opens the file you already own: hxg5 hxg5, then Nce4 and the lift Rh5! - the g5-pawn falls with Nxg5+, and after Rxh8+ Kxh8 Nfe4 and Qh2+ the attack pours down the h-file with decisive force (+2.5). Everything was in place; only the file needed opening.
ep: Nb1 retreats at the critical moment and invites c5!: cxd4 and the pawn storms on with d3, heading for c2 with your army stuck on the back ranks. In the game Black chose the slower Bc4 plan and the moment passed unpunished.

pv: h4 gxh4 Ne4 Rf8 Qf2 d5 Nc5 h5 Rxh4 hxg4 Rxg4 Bxc5 dxc5 Rb5 Rh1 Qxc5
e: h4 still works: gxh4 Ne4! brings the knight in with Nc5 ideas, and Rxh4 regains the pawn while the h- and g-files open against Black's still-uncastled king - Rxg4 and Rh1 follow with the initiative all yours.
ep: b3 chases the c4-bishop exactly where it belongs: Bd5 anchors on the long diagonal and c5 pries at your center next. In the game the position closed up (c5, c4, Ba8, d5) and Black castled in comfort - the h-file attack never happened.

pv: Kb2 gxh4
e: Kb2 meets the threat you cannot otherwise parry: Rxb3! - the b3-pawn has no defender and no pawn can ever recapture there, since the a-pawn only captures toward b4. With the king covering b3 the sac is off, and gxh4 can be answered in your own time.
ep: hxg5 lets the shot land: Rxb3! is untouchable and strips your king - after Rd3 Rb6 Black is a sound pawn up with the safer king. In the game you lashed out with Rxh6, but Bxf3! then won material anyway.

pv: Rd3 Rb6 Ne4 Rfb8 Nbc3 Bxc3 Nxc3 Qxg5 Rd7 Bc6 Rh5 Qg6 Qd3 Qxd3 Rxd3 Kh7
e: Rd3 challenges the intruder head-on: after Rb6 Ne4 the knight jumps in with Nxc5 and Nd6 ideas, Nbc3 finally untangles the queenside, and even Qxg5 runs into Rd7 with full counterplay - your pieces coordinate again. Activity, not pawn-grabbing, holds this together.
ep: Rxh6 grabs a pawn while the queenside caves in: Rfb8! wins the b1-knight - Rxb1+ Qxb1 Rxb1+ Kxb1 nets queen and knight for the two rooks, and Bxf3 picks up more. In the game the immediate Bxf3 hit your queen and won the exchange after Qc2 Bxd1.

pv: Nb5 Ke7 Qxc7 Qxc7 Nxc7 Rb8 Nb5 a6 Nc3 b5 Bd3 b4 Na4 a5 a3 e5
e: Nb5 goes straight at c7, which black cannot comfortably hold: after Ke7 Qxc7 Qxc7 Nxc7 Rb8 Nb5 you have won the pawn and, more importantly, black's king is stuck on e7 with the rooks disconnected. The knight then returns via c3 with a clear extra pawn (+1.4).
ep: Bd3 is a natural developing move but it lets black off the hook: ...c5 comes immediately, hitting d4, and the c7 weakness disappears along with your advantage.

pv: O-O c4 Be2 b5 a3 Bb7 Ne5 Nb6 f3 Ne8 Qxd8 Rxd8 b3 f6 Ng4 Nd6
e: O-O puts the king on the side where black has no pawns to throw at it. After c4 Be2 b5 a3 Bb7 the queenside advance costs black time and space in the centre, and Ne5 gives you a strong outpost, with Qxd8 available to trade into a healthy game.
ep: O-O-O castles straight into black's ready-made pawn storm: ...c4 hits the bishop, then ...b5-b4 and ...a5-a4 arrive with tempo while your own attack is still being assembled (the game saw ...c4 and ...b5 at once).

pv: Qh4 b5 g4 b4 Na4 Ne4 Qxd8 Rxd8 Rhf1 Rb8 Ne5 Nxe5 dxe5 c3 Bd3 Nd2
e: Qh4 keeps the queen on the useful diagonal, eyeing h6 and f6 and supporting g4-g5 to break black's kingside open. In the line Qh4 b5 g4 b4 Na4 Ne4 Qxd8 Rxd8 Rhf1 you get your attack rolling first and can even trade queens on favourable terms when black's pawns arrive.
ep: Qg3 puts the queen where it does nothing: after ...b5 you have to go to h4 anyway, so black gets a free tempo for ...b4 and Na4 leaves the knight stranded on the rim while the queenside pawns roll.

pv: g4 Bg6 a3 bxa3 bxa3 Bc2 Kg3 a4 f4 Bd1 Nc6 Be2 Nb8 Bd1 Na6 Ke7
e: g4 hits the bishop on h5 for free and gains vital kingside space - the bishop cannot take because the pawn is defended by the king on f3. After Bg6 a3 bxa3 bxa3 the queenside opens for your knight, Kg3 and f4 follow, and the black king is kept out of f5 (+2.9).
ep: Kg3 gives the bishop a free move and hands black the key square: ...Kf5 activates his king right in front of your pawns, and with f3 forced your winning attempt stalls.

pv: Ng4+ Kg7 Kxg5 Bd3 Ne5 Bf1 g3 a4 g4 Bg2 f4 Bf1 Nd7 Bd3 f5 Kf7
e: Ng4+ is the move order that wins the pawn: the check forces Kg7, and only then Kxg5 collects the g-pawn with your king safely in front of it. The knight on e5 and the extra kingside pawn then do the work - f4-f5 and g3-g4 create a runner black's bishop cannot stop alone.
ep: Nd7+ checks from the wrong square and chases the king exactly where it wants to go: ...Kf5 defends g5 and blocks your pawns, while your knight is offside on d7.

pv: g3
e: g3 is essential prophylaxis: it takes f4 away from the black king and keeps your f3-pawn defended, so your king on h5 stays safe and can keep pressing g5. Without it there is no way to make progress, because everything hangs on controlling the f4 square.
ep: Ne5 puts the knight on a square the black king attacks: ...Kf4 hits the knight and the f3-pawn at the same time while defending g5, so something has to fall.

pv: g3 Bc2 Kh6 Bd1 Kg7 Be2 Kf7 Bd1 g4+ Kf4 Kxe6 Bxf3 Nxf3 Kxg4
e: g3 again covers f4 and prepares to meet ...g4+ with Kf4, when your king walks in and takes the e6-pawn: g3 Bc2 Kh6 Bd1 Kg7 Be2 Kf7 Bd1 g4+ Kf4 Kxe6 is the whole plan. Keeping the black king out is worth far more than any pawn you could grab.
ep: Nc6 sends the knight pawn-hunting on the wrong wing: ...Kf4! and while you take on a5 the black king marches through e3-d3 and eats c3 and d4, so the race turns against you.

pv: g3 g4
e: g3 is still the move: it holds f4 and prepares to answer ...g4 with f4, keeping the black king out and your pawn structure intact. Everything in this endgame depends on that one square - your knight is only useful once the king cannot invade.
ep: Na7 is a journey to nowhere; the knight needs Nb5 to get back and by then ...Bd3 and ...g4+ activate black's pieces. The game showed the cost: ...e5! broke through in the centre immediately.

pv: Nb5+ Kd3 f5 d4 f6 c3 f7 c2 f8=Q c1=Q+ Kg4 Qd1+ Qf3+ Qxf3+ Kxf3 Ba2
e: In a pawn race every tempo is a whole move, and Nb5+ comes with check. After Kd3 f5 d4 f6 c3 f7 c2 f8=Q c1=Q+ you queen first, and the new queen holds with Qf3+, forcing the trade into a drawn king-and-pawn ending. That one check is the whole difference.
ep: Nc6 wastes the check and the knight lands where it can be taken: ...d4! and the pawns run - d3, d2, d1=Q comes a move before yours, so black queens with the initiative. The game went Nc6 d4 Nxd4 Kxd4 and the race was over.

pv: e6 Bd3 Ne7 O-O Qc7 Qe2 Nc6 Re1 Bd7 c3 Be7 Nd2 O-O
e: e6! shores up d5 before the bishop comes out. The point: d5 hangs by your queen alone, and any Bb5+ forces a block that cuts the queen off from d5 - so solidify first. After e6 Bd3 Ne7 you complete development with a sound structure (-0.4).
ep: Bf5? drops d5: Bb5+! and the forced block Bd7 shuts your own queen off from d5, so Qxd5! wins the pawn cleanly - a6 Bxd7+ Qxd7 Qxd7+ Kxd7 and White is simply a pawn up (-2.1). Your opponent played Qe2? after Bd7 and never took it.

pv: exf5 Nxd5 Qxb2 c3 Qb5 Rxf5 Rfe8 h4 Rc5 Qe4 Qc6 h5 Rxd5 Rxd5 Ne7 c4
e: Deal with the threat first: the f5-pawn attacks your g6-knight. exf5! removes it, and Nxd5 is met by Qxb2 anyway - the pawn grab arrives one move later with your kingside intact, and after c3 Qb5 Rxf5 Rfe8 you keep a clear plus (+1.1).
ep: Qxb2 grabs while g6 hangs: Nd1! first hits your queen, and after Qxa2 fxg6 fxg6 Rdf2 White doubles on the f-file with a dangerous attack - the advantage is gone (-0.3). In the game White took at once (fxg6) and Rxc3! kept you afloat.

pv: d2 Kg1 Qc1 h4 Qe1 Qd7 Qe2 h5 Kh7 a3 b5 h6 Kxh6 a4 bxa4 Qxa4
e: d2! - the passer decides: on d2, guarded by your queen, it chains White's rook to the back rank forever (it must watch d1), and Qc1-e1 escorts the pawn while White's lone queen can't blockade and defend everything at once (line: d2 Kg1 Qc1 h4 Qe1). +4.1 and White is paralysed.
ep: Qe2? lets the rook out with tempo: Rf2! hits the queen, and after Qe1+ Kh2 the rook swings Rf3 and Rxd3, rounding up your prize pawn (punish: Qa5 Rf3 Qxa2 Rxd3, only +1.0). The game began exactly Rf2 Qe1+ Kh2.

pv: e5 Nf3 d4 Nb1 Qc7 e3 dxe3 Bxe3 Nf6 a3 Bf5 Nc3 a6 Bd3 e4 Nd4
e: e5! kicks the d4-knight, and after Nf3 the push d4 hits the c3-knight too, driving it back to b1 - you build a big center with tempo and develop freely (Qc7, Bf5, Nf6) while White's queenside is still asleep.
ep: Bg4 bites on granite: f3! forces the bishop all the way home to c8, and e4 follows, giving White the strong center you could have had. In the game White played Bf4 instead - and after e6 e3 even lost the queen to Bxd1.

pv: h5
e: h5! is the consistent follow-up to g4/h4: strike at g6 before Black finishes developing. After gxh5 gxh5 the g-file opens for your rooks against g7, and Black must spend time on awkward defense (...Rh7, ...Bh6) - that fight is where White's chances live.
ep: Be5 puts the bishop on a square Black hits next move: Nbd7, and it must retreat to f4 having achieved nothing, while Black uses the free tempi for b4! Nb1 c5 on the queenside. In the game came Rh7 and Nbd7, and the bishop was traded off by Bh6 anyway.

pv: Nh3 Ne4 O-O-O Ke8 Bxe4 dxe4 Ng5 Bxg5 Bxg5 Kf7 Rd4 a5 Kb2 Rg8 Bf4 Rc8
e: Nh3! heads for g5, where the knight hits the e6-bishop and h7-rook at once. In the line Ne4 O-O-O Ke8 Bxe4 dxe4 Ng5, Black must hand over a bishop (Bxg5 Bxg5) and your rooks take the d-file - White keeps a solid +1.3.
ep: Nd1 does attack the c3-knight, but Bg7! defends it while activating Black's worst piece, and your knight crawls back (Nf2) two tempi poorer. In the game Black played Bxf4! exf4 Ne4 instead - your good bishop gone, the knight entrenched, and Rxh5 later won the h-pawn.

pv: Be2 a5 a3 bxa3 Nxe4 fxe4 Rxa3 Bd7 c3 Kd6 Kd2 e5 fxe5+ Kxe5 Rg1 a4
e: The h5-pawn is simply hanging to the h7-rook - Be2 finally defends it (Rxh5?? Bxh5) while keeping the f1-h5 diagonal covered. After a5 a3 bxa3 Nxe4 fxe4 Rxa3 the game trades down to a level ending (0.0).
ep: Nh3 blocks the h-file but doesn't guard the pawn: Rxh5! takes it anyway, and the knight becomes the next target - after Bf1, Ng3! forks the f1-bishop and h1-rook. In the game Rxh5 and Rah8 followed, and Black owned the h-file and the ending (-2.9).

pv: Bxf3 gxf3 Nxd4 Qd1 e5 f4 Bd6 fxe5 Bxe5 cxd5 Nxd5 Bg2 Nb4 O-O O-O Qg4
e: The point is that d4 is only held by the Nf3, so remove it: Bxf3 gxf3 and now Nxd4 wins the pawn and hits the queen on b3 at the same time, so after Qd1 you keep it and follow with e5 to build a big centre. As a bonus White's kingside is shattered and his king has no safe home, while your knights get the d4/e5 squares.
ep: Na5 hits the queen but she is happy to go: Qb5+ forces Bd7 and then cxd5 collects the d-pawn, leaving the knight stranded on the rim with no way back. That is exactly how the game went (Qb5+ Bd7 Qb4 dxc4).

pv: e5 Qxf8+ Kxf8 dxe5 Ne8 O-O-O Qc8 Be2 Nc6
e: e5 is the active break: it hits the Bf4 and challenges d4 at once, so White has nothing better than Qxf8+ Kxf8. After dxe5 your king is perfectly safe in the centre of a simplified position, the knight comes back into play with Nc6, and you keep the material.
ep: e6 is passive and shuts in the Bd7. White gets Bd6 in, trading off your good bishop after Bxd6 Qxd6, and with Ne5 to follow his pieces come alive while your a5 knight is still out of the game.

pv: exd5 Ne2 Nc6 Nxc6 Bxc6 Nd4 Bb7 Kd2 Nd7 Kc3 Nc5 a3 Na4+ Kc2 Rab8 Rhf1
e: Recapture with the pawn: exd5 keeps a pawn on d5 that blunts the Bg2 and shelters your own Bb7 on the long diagonal, and it holds the c4/d5 duo together. After Ne2 Nc6 you trade off the strong Ne5 and the bishop on b7 becomes the best piece on the board.
ep: Nxd5 invites the trade of your best piece: Bxd5 exd5 and now Nd7+ picks up the tempo, so after Kg8 Rxe8+ Rxe8 Rd1 the isolated d-pawn drops with Nxd5. The game followed that script almost move for move.

pv: Ke4 Nxb5 Kf3 Kd2 Kxg3 Nxd4 Nxd4 Kc3 Nc6 Kxc4 Kxf4 a4 Nb8 h5 Ke5 b4
e: In knight endings the king is the strongest piece: Ke4 walks straight into White's camp. After Nxb5 Kf3 you round up g3 and then f4, and your c- and d-pawns are so fast that the knight has to be given up to stop them.
ep: Kc5 steps onto a square the knight can hit: Ne6+ forks your king and the g7 pawn, so after Kd5 Nxg7 the kingside pawns fall and White gets counterplay with his own passers. That is what happened (Ne6+ Kd5 Nxg7).

pv: Kf3 Nxg2 Nxf5 Ne1+ Ke2 Ng2 Ne3 Nxe3 dxe3 Kc2 Kf2 b3 e2 bxc4 bxc4 Kc3
e: Kf3 is the square that does everything at once: it guards the far-advanced g2 pawn, attacks the knight on f4 and keeps the king in touch with h4 and f5. White has to solve two problems in one move, and after the knights come off your extra pawns on c4/d4 decide.
ep: Kf1 is a step backwards: the king stops attacking the f4 knight and gets shut in the corner, so White grabs on g2 and then repositions with Nf5, giving him time to attack your queenside pawns instead of just defending.

pv: cxb3 axb3 Kf3 Kb2 Ne5 Kb1 d3 h5 Ke2 Kb2 d2 f7 Nxf7
e: cxb3 first, forcing axb3, is the key finesse: it kills White's queenside majority, so he can never manufacture an outside passed a-pawn. After that you are free to run with Kf3 and Ne5, escorting the d-pawn home while the lone b3 pawn is no danger at all.
ep: Kg3 leaves the tension, and White immediately gets bxc4 bxc4 followed by a4-a5-a6 with a passer on the far side of the board. In the game that pawn ran (a4 bxa4 bxa4 Kf4 a5) and suddenly you had to race instead of just winning.

pv: Kf3 axb5 Ke2 b6 d3 Kb2 Nd7 f7 d2 b7 d1=Q b8=Q c3+ Ka2 Qd2+ Ka3
e: Ignore the wing and push your own trumps: Kf3 heads for the d-pawn's queening square, and after axb5 Ke2 b6 d3 the race is won by a tempo. The finish is worth remembering: d2 with b7 d1=Q b8=Q c3+ and the new white queen is lost to the check.
ep: bxa4 does White's work for him, handing him a ready-made outside passer on a4 and spending a tempo you needed for the race. Same position, one move worse: the game went bxa4 bxa4 Kf4 a5 and the pawn was already flying.

pv: c3 Qe8+ Kf1 Qb5+ Qxb5 Ka2 Qb2#
e: c3! is the quiet killer: the pawn covers b2, so the unstoppable threat is Qb2 mate against the cornered king. White's checks only accelerate it, as the line shows: Qe8+ Kf1 Qb5+ Qxb5 Ka2 Qb2#. Push the pawn first, check later.
ep: Qc3+ checks before the pawn arrives, and after Kb1 Qb3+ Kc1 the king walks out towards the centre. In the game Ka2 Qb3+ Ka1 c3 reached the same idea two moves too late, by which time White's f- and h-pawns gave him a queen and perpetual chances.

pv: Kf1 Qb7 Qxb7 Ka2 Qb2#
e: Your king on e2 is the only reason White is still alive: he checks down the e-file. Kf1! steps off that file and there is not a single check left, so the threat of Qb2 mate cannot be met. The line Qb7 Qxb7 Ka2 Qb2# shows White reduced to giving away the queen.
ep: Kd2 keeps the king in the open, and Qd6+ starts the checking spree that never ends: Kc2 Qh2+ Kd3 Qh3+ and so on. The game showed the same perpetual, throwing away a forced mate.

pv: Ke4 Qg2+ Ke3 Qg1+ Ke2 Qg2+
e: With only queen and c-pawn left the whole game is about avoiding lines with your own queen. Ke4 keeps the king and the b3 queen off any common file or diagonal, so White has nothing better than repeating with Qg2+ Ke3 Qg1+ Ke2 Qg2+.
ep: Kc4 puts your king on the a2-g8 diagonal with your queen right behind it on b3: Qg8+ skewers them, and after Kb4 Qxb3+ the queen is gone. The game version was Qf4+ Kb5 Qb8+ Ka4 Qxb3+, the same idea on the b-file.

pv: Kd5 Qf3+ Kd4 Qf2+ Kd3 Qf3+
e: The only safe square is Kd5. It keeps your king off every line through the queen on b3, so White cannot find a check that wins her, and after Qf3+ Kd4 Qf2+ Kd3 Qf3+ the game is a draw by repetition.
ep: Kb5 lines the king up with your own queen on the b-file, and Qb8+ skewers immediately: Ka4 Qxb3+ and it is over. That was the game finish.

pv: Bd6+ Ke8 Bg3 Kf8 Ned4 e5 Nc2 f6 Nd6 Rc7 Nf5 Ndc5 O-O-O Rcd7 h5 Rb8
e: Insert Bd6+! — the bishop is immune because the b5-knight guards d6, so the king must go back to e8 (Kf6 invites g5+). Then Bg3 retreats having pocketed the tempo, and Ned4! follows, piling on e6 and c6 with Black's king stuck in the center — Nd6 and Nf5 keep him tied up in the line (+1.5).
ep: g5? ignores the center and drops a pawn: e5! hits the f4-bishop, and after Bg3 comes Bxe3! — the f4-bishop was the e3-pawn's only defender, and once driven off, the pawn just falls. The game went exactly g5 e5 Bg3 Bxe3, and the advantage was gone (+0.1).

pv: fxe5 gxh4 Bxh4+ g5 Rh3 Rh8 Rxe3 Rxh4 Ng3 Rf4 Nxa7 Rc5 a4 Rcc4 b3 d4
e: fxe5 wins a central pawn with a tactical point attached: after gxh4 you recapture Bxh4+ with check, and then Rh3! attacks the loose bishop on e3 — Rxe3 wins it back (Black only regains the h4-bishop), and Nxa7 picks up a second pawn. Your buried g3-bishop springs to life in every line, and Black's center is gone.
ep: fxg5 grabs the wrong pawn: it leaves Black's center intact and concedes e4 — after Nac5 and Ne4 the knight hits c3 and g5 and towers over your g3-bishop. Even Rxd5 Ke6 leaves your rook and the b5-knight hanging in the air; in the game f6! simply regained the pawn with the stronger position.

pv: Rg4 d4 Nxf4 Na4 Nd3+ Kd5 Bxd4 e4 Rf5+ Kc4 Rxe4 Kb3 Kf1 Rd6 b6 Nxc3
e: Rg4! wins the f4-bishop outright: it is attacked three times — Rf6, Nh5 and now Rg4 — held only by the e5-pawn, and it has no escape square. After d4, Nxf4 takes it, and exf4 fails to Rgxf4+ regaining everything; so Black must simply concede the piece (Na4 Nd3+ and Bxd4 mops up the pawns too).
ep: Ng3+ turns a piece-winning position into a mere trade: Bxg3 Rxg3 swaps knight for bishop and Black's rooks and knight stay on the board. You were still clearly better (+2.6 instead of +5.8), but the free piece became a small edge — and the very next move gave back the rest.

pv: Rxg3 d4 cxd4 exd4 Rg4+ Ke5 Rh6 d3+ Kd2 Kf5 Rg5+ Ke4 Re6+ Kf3 Rgg6
e: The bishop just captured your knight on g3 — Rxg3! simply takes it back. After d4 cxd4 exd4 Rg4+ and Rh6 your rooks are dominant, you keep bishop against knight with an extra pawn, and the h-pawn becomes a real asset. A clean, technically winning position.
ep: Rg4+?? lets the bishop live: Bf4! blocks the check and keeps the extra piece. Worse, your f6-rook turns out loose — after Bd4 Nd3! (defending f4) Bxe5 Kxe5 Kxd3 Kxf6 the black king simply eats it: rook and bishop for knight and pawn. In the game Bf4 was played and the piece stayed on the board.

pv: Rfxf4+ exf4 Rxf4+ Ke5 Rxc4+ Kf5 Bxb8 Re7+ Kd3 dxc4+ Kd4 Rd7+ Kc5 Ke4 Kxc4 Rd1
e: Rfxf4+! cashes in: exf4 Rxf4+ Ke5 Rxc4! collects bishop, pawn and knight for one rook — and with e5 cleared, your g3-bishop suddenly sees all the way to b8, so Bxb8 wins a whole rook on top (dxc4 Bxb8 comes to the same). You emerge material up with connected pawns and an easy win.
ep: Re6?? walks into Kf5!: the king forks your rooks on e6 and g4 and neither defends the other. They must huddle with Rgg6, when Rxb6 wins your passed pawn and Black keeps all the trumps — the f4-bishop and the d5/e5 pawns dominate. Your opponent missed Kf5 in the game (Rf8?), but the position had already swung from winning to lost.

pv: Rxf4+ Rxf4 Rxb6 Rf3 Rg6 Rxc3 Be1 Rc2+ Kf1 Rh2 h6 Kd3 Bg3 Rh5 Kg2
e: You are a piece down and the f4-bishop keeps your g4-rook fenced in. Rxf4+! solves both problems: after Rxf4 Rxb6 you restore full material equality — and Nxb6? even fails to Bxf4!, when the h5-runner gives you a roughly level ending. Black's best is to decline with Rf3 and rely on activity, but you are fighting again instead of just lost.
ep: Rxb6? gets the order wrong: Nxb6! recaptures at once, and with the f4-bishop still alive your remaining rook stays entombed on g4. After Bf2 Na4 (hitting c3) Be1 Rh8 the h-pawn drops too — exactly the game's course (h6 Rh8 Rh4): a piece down with no counterplay.

pv: f5 g4 e6 Rad1 a5 Ng5 Rxd1 Rxd1 a4 a3 Rb8 Nxe4 Nxe4 Bc1 Nc5 gxf5
e: f5 makes your knight on e4 untouchable - the pawn defends it and the c2-bishop's diagonal is blocked at f5. The follow-up is clear: ...e6 and ...a5 gain space, the rooks take the d-file (Rxd1), and only then does ...Nc5 or ...a4 hit the queenside, with your knight still dominating the centre.
ep: Rab8 leaves the knight on c5 loose: b4! hits it, and after Bxc3 bxc5 Bxa1 Rxa1 you have given a piece for the exchange while White's knight and bishop clamp down on the dark squares.

pv: Rb1+ Bc1 Rxc1+ Rd1 Rxd1+ Ne1 Rxe1#
e: Rb1+ is mate in four, and it works because every block can be captured with check: Bc1 Rxc1+ Rd1 Rxd1+ Ne1 Rxe1#. Each white piece that steps onto the back rank is taken by the rook with another check, and after the knight goes to e1 the king has no escape square.
ep: gxf5 grabs a pawn and gives White the move he needs to defend the back rank. Your opponent then played Bh6 anyway and Rb1+ Ne1 Rxe1# followed - you found the mate two moves later than it was available.

pv: Re1 Kd8 Ra7 Nd6 Rxa5 Re8 Ra7 h6 h5 Rb8 Ra6 Nc8 Rb1 Rxb1+ Kxb1
e: Re1 seizes the e-file against the centralized king, pressuring e6 and keeping every piece on: after Kd8 Ra7 Nd6 Rxa5 you collect a second pawn while Black stays tangled. A piece up, avoiding trades is the fastest win (+3.1).
ep: Bb5 invites the simplification Black is begging for: Rc7! offers rooks (Rc8 Rxc8 Bxc8), and in the game Bxd7 Rxd7 Rxd7+ Kxd7 traded two pairs — every swap makes converting the extra piece slower and Black's defense easier.

pv: Ra7 h5 g5 Nxb5 Rxb5 f6 g6 Rh6 Rbb7 Ke8 Nc1 Rxg6 Nd3 Rg1+ Kb2 Rg2+
e: The d6-knight attacks both your b7-rook and b5-bishop — Ra7 saves the rook while hitting a5, and if Nxb5 Rxb5 recaptures cleanly. Then g5 and g6 create a runner, and Rbb7 doubles on the seventh (+2.8).
ep: Bxd7 meets the zwischenzug Nxb7! — Black takes the rook before recapturing, and after Bxe6 Kxe6 Rxb7 you have traded rook for knight and pawn, giving back nearly all of the advantage (-0.1). In the game Black just recaptured Rxd7, letting you off.

pv: Bd5 Nc3 Nf6 Nxd5 Nxd5 Bg5 Rc8 Rc1 Qd6 Bxd5 Qxd5 Bxe7 Rxc1 Qxc1 Re8 Bb4
e: Bd5! solves the b7-bishop's problem by force: it offers to swap off White's strong e4-knight and the light-squared bishops in one sequence — Nc3 Nf6 Nxd5 Nxd5 — after which the game is dead level. The point is contesting the long diagonal before White's Bf4/Rc1 setup gains time on your queen.
ep: Qc7 steps into Bf4!: after e5 Rc1! the queen is hit again (Qb8), and Bg5-e7 with Nd6 wins material in the punish line. In the game Bf4 e5 dxe5 Bxe5 Bxe5 Nxe5 walked into Nf6+! and the long-diagonal tactics cost you a piece.

pv: Nxe5 Rc1 Qe7 Bg5 f6 Bf4 Rad8 Qb3+ Kh8 h4 Rfe8 Red1 Ba8 Qb5 Rxd1+ Rxd1
e: Recapture with the knight: Nxe5! keeps the g7-bishop at home guarding f6, so Nf6+ never works, and the e5-knight is rock solid. After Rc1 Qe7 Bg5 f6 you consolidate with only a shade of pressure left to defend.
ep: Bxe5?? removes the defender of f6: Nf6+! wins on the spot — Nxf6 Bxe5 and the recapture hits your c7-queen, so after Bxg2 Bxc7 White has won the queen for a knight. The game's move order (Bxe5 Nxe5 Nf6+ Kg7 Bxb7 Qxb7 Rxe5) cost a clean piece the same way.

pv: Qxc5 Bd3 Qe7 Bxg6 hxg6 e4 c5 Qg5 Rxd4 Re3 Qc7 f4 Nh5 Qh4 Re8 Qg4
e: Qxc5! wins a full rook: c5 is 'defended' by the d4-pawn, but dxc5 opens the d-file and Rxd2 snaps off the queen - so there is no recapture. White gets nothing for it (line: Qxc5 Bd3 Qe7) and you're simply a rook up (+5.0).
ep: Ne4 forks queen and rook, but Qb4! meets both - stepping out of the attack while defending c5 - and after Nxc5 Rc1 the damage stays modest (+3.1 instead of a clean rook). In the game White inserted Nxg6 hxg6 and Qc1; you won the exchange, but the game later slipped away.

pv: Rd2 Qh4+ Qxh4 c8=Q Qxc8 Kg1 Qf2+ Kh2 Qxg2#
e: Rd2! forces mate in five: with the rook on the second rank, Qf2+ and Qxg2# cannot be parried. White's spite tries change nothing - Qh4+ Qxh4 (the e1-queen recaptures) c8=Q Qxc8, and then Kg1 Qf2+ Kh2 Qxg2#, queen and rook doubled on the second rank.
ep: Qh1+? releases the king: Kg3! and after Qe1+ Kf3 the checks run out while c7 is still queening. You were still winning on the board (+5.8), but the forced mate was gone - and this game eventually got away entirely.

pv: Qe1+ Kh2 Rd2 Qh4+ Qxh4 c8=Q Qxc8 Kg1 Qf2+ Kh2 Qxg2#
e: The mate is still there, one move longer: Qe1+! (the h1-queen) forces Kh2, and now Rd2! decides - Qh4+ Qxh4 c8=Q Qxc8 Kg1 Qf2+ Kh2 Qxg2#. Rook on the second rank, queen infiltrating on f2 and g2: mate in six no matter what White throws in.
ep: Rd7?? goes pawn-hunting and allows Qh4+! Kg8 Qd8+!: the rook must give itself (Rxd8 cxd8=Q+) and the brand-new queen checks forever - 0.0, down from mate in six. Your opponent missed it and just promoted (c8=Q), yet the game was still lost in the end.

pv: Bxf3 Bxf3 Rc8 Qc1 Qxc1 Rxc8+ Rxc8 Rxc1 Ba3 Rc3 Bb4 Rb3 Ba5 g4 Bb6 Rc3
e: Bxf3 Bxf3 and then Rc8! is the point: your c3-queen is so strong that White must allow mass simplification — Qc1 Qxc1 Rxc8+ Rxc8 Rxc1 — into an endgame a clean pawn up, where Ba3! and Bb4 chase White's rook while a2 and d4 stay chronically weak (+2.0). Trade pieces while material and structure favor you.
ep: Rb6 gives White the tempo for Ne5!, and the tactics turn on your deep queen: Bd6 is met by Bd2!, and after Bxe5 Bxc3 Bxe2 Rxe2 Bxc7 the queen has gone for rook, bishop and knight — roughly level (-0.4 from +2.0). In the game Ng3 let you play Bxf3 anyway, and you won.

pv: Qg6+ Kh2 Rxd1 h4 f4 Qxf4 Rxf2+ Kh3 Qg2#
e: Qg6+! forces mate in 5: Kh2 Rxd1 brings the rook into the attack, and White is helpless — h4 f4! Qxf4 Rxf2+ Kh3 Qg2#, the f2-rook guarding the mating queen. With the enemy king that bare, forcing moves come before pawn-grabbing.
ep: Qxe6 allows the queen trade Qxe6+ Rxe6 (or the game's Qxa7), and the mating attack is gone — still completely winning at +5.6, but a forced mate became a technical ending. In the game White even checked around until Qc7+ ran into Rxc7.

pv: Rc8 Nf3 Nh6 g4 Bg6 Be2 O-O O-O Kh8 Rc1 Ng8 b4 f6 Na4 Be4 exf6
e: Rc8 puts the rook on the file that will open and keeps every option. Black's plan in this Botvinnik-Carls structure is Nh6 (heading for f5 or g8-e7) and pressure on c3/d4: Nf3 Nh6 g4 Bg6 Be2 O-O O-O Kh8 Rc1 Ng8, roughly balanced at -0.4.
ep: Bg5 offers a trade that only helps White. Bxg5 Qxg5 and now h4 chases the queen (Qg4) while Nge2 and Nb5-d6 arrive with tempo; Black's dark squares around the king are permanently loose and he never castles in comfort. -0.4 to -1.6. The e7-bishop was not the piece to give away.

pv: Qh4+ Ke2 Bg4+ Nf3 Bxf3+ gxf3 Nge7 Qe1 Qh6 f4 O-O Kd2 Nf5 Qf2 f6 exf6
e: Qh4+! White has committed to e3 and g2 and his king is stuck on e1 — punish it now. Ke2 Bg4+ Nf3 Bxf3+ gxf3 wrecks his structure permanently, and after Nge7 Qe1 Qh6 f4 O-O Black castles into a completely safe position with a bind (+1.0).
ep: a6 is a useful move at the wrong moment. Nf3! plugs the hole, and after Nge7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 Nf5 O-O O-O White has castled and equalised. The h4-check only worked while f1 and g1 were undeveloped — one free tempo and the chance is gone. +1.0 to level.

pv: Qh4+ Kd2 Nxd4 exd4 Qxd4+ Ke1 Qxe5+ Kf2 Bc2 Qxc2 Qd4+ Kg3 Qxa1 Nf3 Qxa3 Bxa6
e: Qh4+ is still on, and now it is tactical: Kd2 Nxd4! exd4 Qxd4+ Ke1 Qxe5+ Kf2 Bc2 Qxc2 Qd4+ Kg3 Qxa1 and Black wins two pawns with check and then the a1-rook. The knight sitting on a4 is exactly why the defence collapses — it cannot come back. +1.7.
ep: Nge7 is natural but gives White the tempo he needs: Nc5 hits a6, b7 and e6, and after g4 Be4 Nf3 h6 Bg2 the king finally gets out of the middle. +1.7 down to +0.3. When the enemy king is stuck on e1 and one of his knights is on a4, check first and develop later.

pv: b6 Qe2 Nb8 Rac1 O-O Rxc8 Qxc8 Qd2 Bxf3 Bxf3 Qc6 Nc3 Rc8 Rc1 b5 e4
e: b6! takes c5 away from the a4-knight, which is White's only route back into the game, and shores up the queenside so a6 is covered. After Qe2 Nb8 Rac1 O-O Rxc8 Qxc8 the rooks come off and Black is completely fine (0.00).
ep: Nxe5 grabs a pawn that is defended twice — by the d4-pawn and the f3-knight — and Black has only the one attacker. dxe5 (or Nxe5) followed by Bxg2 Kxg2 leaves him a knight down for a pawn. In the game White preferred Nc5, hitting a6 and e6, but the position had already gone from 0.00 to -2.9. Count defenders before capturing a central pawn.

pv: Bxf3 Bxf3 Nc4 Qe1 b6 Nxa6 Ng6 a4 O-O Ra2 Qg5 Re2 Nh4 b5
e: Bxf3! Trade the bishop, not the knight. After Bxf3 the strong knight stays on e5, White's light-squared bishop — his best piece, aiming at d5 — is gone, and Nc4 Qe1 b6 Nxa6 Ng6 a4 O-O keeps the extra pawn with a much better structure (+2.5).
ep: Nxf3+ trades the wrong piece. Bxf3 puts White's bishop on the long diagonal hitting d5, and the e4-bishop is now loose against both Bf3 and Nc5, so Black must spend time on it: Qd6 Bxe4 dxe4 Nxe4 Qd5 and the extra pawn is gone. +2.5 to +1.1.

pv: O-O Nxe4 dxe4 Bxe4 Nd5 Bxd5 exd5 Rc1 Rxc1 Qxc1 Qd7 Qc2 Qe6 Rf3 Rc8 Qf5
e: O-O gets the king out of the centre and, just as importantly, keeps the f7-pawn where it is — that pawn is the only thing defending e6. After Nxe4 dxe4 Bxe4 Nd5 Bxd5 exd5 Rc1 Rxc1 Qxc1 Black trades into a comfortable position a pawn up (+1.1).
ep: f5 removes f7's guard of e6, and Nxe6! forks the queen on d8 and g7. After Qd6 Nxg7+ Kd7 Ra2 Rhg8 Nh5 White has two pawns and the black king is walking in the open. +1.1 to -0.5, and it got far worse from there. Before pushing an f-pawn, check what it was defending behind it.

pv: Bc2 Qe2 Nxf5 gxf5 Rhg8+ Kh1 Ke7 e4 Kd8 Rac1 dxe4 Bg4 h5 Rxc2 Rxc2 Qxc2
e: Bc2! The e4-bishop is attacked by Bf3 and nothing else is urgent — move it before capturing anything. After Qe2 Nxf5 gxf5 Rhg8+ Kh1 Ke7 e4 Kd8 the king finally reaches shelter with the bishop still alive. Still bad (-1.7), but a completely different game from -4.1.
ep: Nxf5 grabs the knight but leaves your e4-bishop hanging to Bf3. Bxe4! dxe4 Rxf5+ takes the piece straight back with check, and after d5 Qd6 Qd4+ Kg6 Rf4 the king is caught in a crossfire on the open f-file. -1.7 down to -4.1. When one of your own pieces is loose, deal with it before you start trading.

pv: Kg7 d5 Rhf8 Qd4+ Kg8 Raf1 Rxf5 Rxf5 Qd6 Qe5 Qxe5 Rxe5 Rc3 Kf2 Rxa3 Rxe4
e: Kg7 tucks the king off the f-file and away from the a2-g8 diagonal. After d5 Rhf8 Qd4+ Kg8 Raf1 Rxf5 Rxf5 Qd6 Qe5 Qxe5 Rxe5 Black at least trades a pair of rooks and the queens and can try to hold the ending (-4.2 instead of -7.6).
ep: Ke6 steps into the open and every White piece joins with tempo: Qb3+! Kd6 Rd5+ Kc7 Rxd7+ Kxd7 b5 and the queen is gone on top of everything else. -7.6. When you are already lost, walk the king away from the checks, not into the middle of the board.

pv: a3 b5 Nd2 Qa5 Bd3 Qc7 Rhf1 f5 Rde1 a5 Nb3 b4 axb4 axb4 c4 fxg4
e: a3! quietly fixes the queenside: it takes b4 away from Black's pieces, so ...b5 is met by the clean regroup Nd2, Bd3 and Rhf1 - in the line the a4-queen gets pushed all the way back to c7 while you keep a stable plus and the g4/f5 space to play with (+1.1).
ep: Kb1 does nothing about ...b5!: the c4-knight is hit, and after Ne3 e5! the center dissolves - Nxd5 cxd5 fxe5 fxe5 is dead level (-0.1). In the game Nd2 ran into ...Nxf4, and your queenside pawns fell with it.

pv: Ne4 e5 Qxf6 gxf6 Nxc3 Rxd4 Rxd4 exd4 Ne4 f5 gxf5 Bxf5 Bd3 Kg7 Rg1+ Bg6
e: Ne4! attacks the c3-queen and adds an attacker on f6. The critical ...e5 (hitting your queen) is answered by Qxf6! anyway: after ...gxf6 Nxc3 both queens are gone, Black's kingside is shredded, and Rxd4 exd4 Ne4 leaves you a clean pawn up with the healthier structure (+3.0).
ep: Rc1 attacks the queen but lets it grab your center on the way out: ...Qxd4! forces the trade (Qxd4 Rxd4), and with the d4-pawn and the queens gone, your winning chances went too (+0.1). Exactly this happened in the game.

pv: Bxb5 cxb5 Rc7+ Kf8 Rxb7 Rad8 Rxa7 e5 Rxh7 Rd1+ Rxd1 Rxd1+ Kc2 Rf1 Nd2 Ra1
e: Bxb5! wins material through the overloaded c6-pawn: if ...cxb5, then Rc7+! and Rxb7 wins the bishop back with interest, and the seventh-rank rook keeps eating - Rxa7 and Rxh7 follow, leaving you several pawns up (+3.0).
ep: Bh3? aims at e6 but lets Black consolidate: ...c5! and ...Be4+ activate the b7-bishop, and from h3 you no longer even attack b5 - the tactic is gone for good and +3.0 shrinks to +1.1.

pv: Bg2 Be4+ Ka1 Ke7 Nd2 Bxg2 Rxg2 Rad8 Nb1 e5 Rxc5 a6 Kb2 Ke6 Rg7 b4
e: Bg2! offers the trade Black cannot really avoid: after ...Be4+ Ka1 Ke7 Nd2!, the monster b7-bishop comes off (...Bxg2 Rxg2), and with the long diagonal neutralized your rooks take over - Rxc5 wins a pawn shortly after (+1.1).
ep: Nh4? heads for f5, but ...Be4+ Ka1 f5! takes that square away and shuts your h3-bishop behind the pawn. After ...Rg8 everything gets traded off (Bg2 Rg8 Bxe4 Rxg1 Rxg1 fxe4) and it is dead equal (0.0).

pv: Ka1 f5 Bg2 Rg8 Bxe4 Rxg1 Rxg1 fxe4 Rf1+ Ke7 Re1 Rd4 Ng2 Kd6 Re2 Ke5
e: Ka1! is the precise square: it sidesteps so that ...Rd2 no longer comes with check, which buys the tempo for Bg2!, trading off the e4-bishop. After ...f5 Bg2 Rg8 Bxe4 Rxg1 Rxg1 fxe4 Rf1+ your active rook holds everything comfortably (0.0).
ep: Kb2? walks into the little fork ...Rd2+!: the check picks up the h2-pawn (Ka1 Rxh2), after which the rook gnaws at your position and the h3-bishop, with ...f5 coming (-1.7). Your opponent missed it at first (...Rc8) but played ...Rd2+ two moves later anyway.

pv: Nf3 f5 Nxd4 cxd4 Bg2 Bxg2 Rxg2 Kf6 Rge2 Re8 Rd2 Rd8 Rc2 Rd6 Rc5 d3
e: Nf3! wins the exchange by attacking a rook that cannot run: the d4-rook is the only defender of the e4-bishop, which your e1-rook is attacking. After ...f5 Nxd4 cxd4 you are the exchange up, and Bg2 then swaps off Black's last active piece - a technical win (+2.4).
ep: Rg4? gets hit by ...f5! (or the game's ...Bf5): the rook must retreat, e4 is secured for good, and your h4-knight is stranded on the rim while ...Rcd8 doubles on the d-file - you are suddenly worse (-1.0). In the game you ended up giving the exchange back with Rxd4 yourself.

pv: Kb2 Ke5 Kc3 Ke4 Kd2 Rd6 Re1 Ra6 Nc2+ Kf3 Nb4 Ra3 Ra1 Kg2 Nd5 f5
e: The knight already blockades beautifully from e3 - what is missing is the king. Kb2! begins the march via c3 to d2: after ...Ke5 Kc3 Ke4 Kd2 the d3-pawn is surrounded, Black's rook goes passive, and with king, rook and knight all working your extra piece wins (+2.8).
ep: Ng4? abandons the blockade for nothing: ...Kf5! hits the knight, and after Nf2 d2! the pawn reaches the second rank - your rook is chained to the back rank forever and the win is gone (0.0). In the game ...Kf5 came at once and the knight got chased to g2.

pv: Nf1 Kf3 Rd2 f5 Kb2 f4 Kc1 Rg8 Kd1 Ke4 Rf2 Rg1 b4 f3 Ke1 h5
e: Nf1! is the only move because it keeps d2 covered: after ...Kf3 you have Rd2!, planting the rook on the blockading square where the knight protects it. The d-pawn is stopped dead, and ...f5-f4 is met by walking the king over via b2-c1-d1 - a dead draw (0.0).
ep: Ng2? gives up control of d2, and ...d2! decides on the spot: the pawn is taboo (Rxd2 Rxd2) and ...Kf3 and ...Ke2 escort it in - there is no defense (-5.4). In the game Black escorted with ...f5-f4-f3 instead and won just the same.

pv: Rf1 f3
e: Rf1! is the best try in a bad position: the rook gets in front of the f-pawn, the most dangerous runner, before it reaches f3-f2. You are still clearly worse after ...f3 (-2.2), but the pawns are contained for the moment and everything else loses faster.
ep: Kc3? invites ...Rc8+!, driving your king away from the pawns: after Kb4 f3! rolls with the king cut off, and Re1+ Kd4 Ne3 is refuted by ...a5+! Ka3 f2, when a pawn queens (-3.6). In the game ...f3 came immediately with the same effect.

pv: Re1+ Kf5 Ne3+ Kf4 Kd2 Rd6 Rg1 f2 Rg7 Ra6 Kxd3 Rxa2 Rxh7 a5 Rf7+ Kg5
e: Re1+! turns the tables with checks: ...Kf5 Ne3+! Kf4 and now Kd2! - the king reaches the pawns just in time. Then the rook swings: Rg1, and after ...f2 Rg7! it goes hunting - ...Ra6 Kxd3 Rxa2 Rxh7 and you emerge better (+1.9) in a position that looked lost.
ep: Nh4? goes after the f3-pawn one move too late: ...f2! simply runs past the knight, and with ...d2 to follow the pawns cannot both be stopped - one of them costs your rook (-5.9). In the game ...Ke3 escorted first, with the same result.

pv: Re1+ Kf4 Kd2 f2 Rf1 Kg4 Ng2 Rf8 Ke3 Re8+ Kxd3 Kf3 Nh4+ Kg4 Rxf2 Kxh4
e: Again Re1+! saves everything: after ...Kf4, Kd2! gets home - ...f2 is met by Rf1 and the blockade holds, while Ng2! and Ke3 start rounding the pawns up; the line ends with Rxf2 and real winning chances for you (+0.4).
ep: Nf5+? chases the king exactly where it wants to go: ...Ke2! attacks your d1-rook, and after Rd2+ Ke1 Black liquidates - rooks come off on d3, then ...f2 forces you to give the knight for the pawn - into a won king-and-pawn endgame for him (-2.9). In the game ...Ke2 duly followed.

pv: Rd2+ Ke1 Rxd3 Rxd3+ Kxd3 f2 Ng3 f1=R Nxf1 Kxf1 h4 Kg2 h5 Kh3 h6 Kh4

pv: Qa4+ Kd3 Nxe5+ dxe5 Qxg4 Nd6 Rf8 Re1 Qf3+ Kc2 Qf2+ Kd1 g4 c4 g3 e6

pv: Qb5 Ke1

ep: Qc4 puts the queen exactly where the knight jumps: Nd6! forks it while also hitting b7 and f7, so after Qa2+ Ke1 Nc2+ Kf2 you have been driven backwards for nothing. In the game Qe4 came instead and Black still ended up passive.

pv: Nc4+ Kd3 Qa6 Kc2 b5 Qe1 c5 Nd6 Nxd6 exd6 Qxd6 Rf1 Qxh6 Qe5+ Qg7 Qxc5

ep: Nc2+ is a check to nowhere: Kf3 and the knight must crawl back to a3, having gained nothing while White reorganises with Nd6 and forces the queens off. Two tempi thrown away in a position where the knight was already the problem piece.

pv: Nb1+ Ke1 Qxe2+ Kxe2 Nxc3+ Kd3 Nd5 Nd6 Rg6 Nxb7 g4 Nd6 g3 Rb1 Nb6 Nxf7+

pv: Nc4 Kd3 b5 Ne7 Re8 Nxc6 f6 Ke4 Kg8 Kf5 fxe5 dxe5 Kf8 Ra1 a5 Kf6
e: Nc4 recentralises the knight that has been buried on a3 since move 42. From c4 it hits e5 and e3 and covers a5, and the follow-up is clear: b5, Re8 and the rook gets active, with ...f6 breaking up the e5 pawn and the king coming to g8-f7.

pv: Be7 Bd2 a6 Rac1 O-O Na4 Rc8 g4 Nh4 Nxh4 Bxh4 Kh1 Be7 f4 f6 b4

pv: Qe5 O-O c3 f6 Qg3 Qc6 Kb1 e5 f4 Qc4 Qg2 exf4 Nxf4 Re8 Nxd5 Ra6

pv: g3 Nf3 gxf2+ Kxf2 Nd7 Nxd5 Bxd5 Rh3 e6 Qc2 Nf6 Rg3+ Kh7 Ne5 Nd7 Nf3

pv: gxf3 Nxf3 Nd7 O-O Qd6 Rae1 a6 Nh2 Kh8 Re2 c5 Bxf5 Bc4 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3

pv: Bd5 Be4 Nf6 Bxd5 Nxd5 Qd3 b4 Rc1 Nxc3 Qe3 Rab8 Nxc3 bxc3 Qg5+ Qg6 Qxg6+

pv: Rd2+

pv: Rb2 Qd4 a3 Kc5 Rc2+ Kb4 b2 Qd5+ Ka1 Qe5 a2 Kb3 Rd2 Qg7 Rf2 Qd4

pv: Re1 Nxg4 Rg1 Qf5 Rxg4+ Qxg4 Qxc7 Qg5+ Kd1 e5 Qxe5 Qxe5 dxe5 Kf5 e6 Kxe6

pv: a5

It also opens the a-file for the rook that is already sitting on a8. White's Bxh7+ trick still exists, but the pawn you win on the other wing pays for it.

pv: Bxf3 gxf3 Qd8 Bxh7+ Kh8 Bd3 g6 Kg2 Kg7 Rh1 Nc6 Qd2 Rh8 Na3 Qh4 f4

pv: f5 gxf5 Nxf5 Rh3 Rxh3 Qxh3 Qb6 Qf3 Qb2 Qxf4 Qxa1 Qc7+ Kh6 Qxb7 Qa2 Qb8
e: f5! is the freeing break. It hits g4 and, after gxf5 Nxf5, your worst piece finally leaves the rim and joins in, while the h-file opens for the rook that is already on h8. pv: Qe2 Qg3 Rc8 Rd3 Bf4 Qf3 Qxf3 Rxf3 Bc7 c4 dxc4 Rc3 Bd8 Rb4 bxa5 Rbxc4
e: Qe2 does two jobs at once: it attacks the rook on f3 and takes a square from which the queen still guards your bishop on d2. pv: Bxd4 b7 Qc7 Qh2 Be5 Qh1 Rb8 Rfb3 Bd4 g5 Nf5 h4 Qf4 Qh2 Qxh2+ Kxh2
e: Bxd4! rescues the bishop with profit. It steps off the c-file where Rc1 was coming, takes a pawn, and from d4 it rakes the long diagonal while eyeing b6 — so the passed b-pawn is under control, not running. After b7 Qc7 Qh2 Be5 the pawn is blockaded and your extra minor piece decides the game.

pv: Ng8 Qg3

e: The break you have to prevent is f4, kicking your king and then f5 prising the position open — g5! clamps it down at once, fixing the g4 and h3 pawns and denying the white king the f4 and g5 squares. pv: Bxg6 Rxg6 Qh3 Kh7 Rxg6 Nxg6 h5 Ngf8 Qg3 Qe8 Rg1 Qf7 Qf4 Qe8 Nh4 Qf7

e: Your queen on g3 stands behind the Bf4 on the b8-h2 diagonal, so c7 is only defended by the black queen — Bxc7 just wins a pawn, because Qxc7 Qxc7 is a plain trade with you a pawn to the good. After Qd7 Rd1 the bishop comes back via e5 with a fine game.

e: The knight on d5 forks queen and bishop, so move the queen to the square that solves both problems: Qe4 keeps f4 defended and attacks the knight itself. Black has to resolve it immediately with Nxf4 Qxf4, and your queen sits beautifully in the centre.

pv: Be3 h6 h4 a6 Nh3 b5 dxc5 b4 Ne2 Nxc5 Qxb4 Qc7 Bd4 Rc8 Qc3 O-O

ep: h4? ignores d4: cxd4! wins a pawn, because the trick Nb5 a6 Nxd4 runs into e5!, forking the d4-knight and the f4-bishop. After Bg3 exd4 Black is up material and Bxd6 only recovers a pawn - the center collapsed while the h-pawn was strolling.

pv: hxg6 fxg6 g5 Nh5 Kb1 Kd8 Rxh5 gxh5 g6 Kc7 g7 Rhg8 Bh3 b4 Nce2 Qb5
e: hxg6 fxg6 g5 is the moment: the f6-knight is booted, and after Nh5 comes the thematic exchange sac Rxh5! gxh5 g6 - the pawn marches with your queen already on h6, and after g7 Black's rook must blockade passively on g8 while you regroup. The attack only works while the knight has no square; one slow move and the chance is gone.
ep: a3 is too slow and doesn't even stop the b-pawn: in the game b4! came at once (Nb1 was forced), and in the engine line Rg8 followed by b4 gets Black's attack moving while yours stands still. The kingside breakthrough had a one-move window.

pv: b4 Na4+ Kc1 Nc3 Rd3 Rc8 Re1 h5 gxh5 Nxh5 Kd2 Na4 Rg1 Bb7 Rxg6
e: b4! kicks the c5-knight before Black consolidates. After Na4+ Kc1 Nc3 you have Rd3, and the knight on c3 attacks nothing while your extra exchange does the talking - the line ends with gxh5 and Rxg6 stripping the kingside, close to winning.
ep: c4? opens lines toward your own king: bxc4 bxc4 Rb8+ forces Nb5, and Bxb5 cxb5 Rxb5+ wins the pawn back with check and an active rook. In the game you recaptured with the knight instead, and after Rb8 and h5 your pieces went passive - the initiative changed hands for good.

pv: Na6 Rc8
e: The knight on c5 is also a blocker - it sits on the a3-f8 diagonal in front of b4. Na6 is the retreat that keeps things together: from a6 it still guards b4, so Bxb4+ is simply met by Nxb4, and it eyes c7/b8 while you finish development and get castled.
ep: Nxd7 opens the f8-b4 diagonal and the pawn drops with check: Bxb4+ Kf2 costs the pawn and the right to castle, leaving your king stuck in the centre - exactly the game continuation.

pv: Nce7 Rc1 Bc6 Nd4 Bd5 Nb5 Bb8 Nbd6 a6 Bb1 b5 Ne3 Nxe5 Bxe5 Bxd6 Ba1

pv: Nce7 h4 Bc6 h5 Nf4 Bb1 Rd8 Nd4 Bxg2 Qg4 Ned5 Ne2 Bh3 Qf3 Nxe2+ Rxe2

ep: b5 hits the c4-knight but fatally removes b7's protection of your own c6-knight: Bxg6! and if hxg6 then Qxd7! wins a piece, because the old defense Rd8 Qxc6 bxc6 no longer exists. In the game White played Nd6 instead, still with a winning bind after Bxd6 exd6 (-4.5).

pv: f6 h4 a5 Be4 Qe8 h5 Nf4 g3 Nh3+ Kg2 axb4 h6 bxa3 Ba1 e5 Qd5+

ep: Rd8 leaves f7 to its fate: Ng5! targeted it, and in the game h6 Nxf7! Kxf7 Bxg6+ ripped the king position apart (-5.2).

pv: Qxd6 Red1 Qe7 Qc3 f6 Bxb5 Nce5 Bf1 Rac8 Qe3 Nxf3+ Qxf3 Ba4 Rxc8 Rxc8 Rc1
