ep: Qb7 leaves the pawn alive and the kingside short of defenders: the game's Ng5! h6 Nxf7! Kxf7 Bxg6+ Kg8 Bh7+! crashed through, and Bxg6 followed by Qe4 (double attack on c6 and g6) was also winning material (-4.5).

pv: Qxd4 Nxf6+ Qxf6 g3 g6 Nf3 Bg7 Bg5 Qe6 O-O-O h6 Qxe6 Bxe6 Be3 Nd7 Be2
e: Qxd4! wins a clean central pawn. The only real try, Nxf6+, is met by Qxf6 - the queen recaptures, keeps g7 covered, and after g3 g6 Nf3 Bg7 White's development lead never turns into anything concrete. You consolidate a pawn up.
ep: Bf5? lets White wreck your structure first: Nxf6+ gxf6, and the bishop becomes a target - Nf3 and Nh4! hit it with tempo, forcing Bg6. You never win d4 cleanly; in the game f3 Qxd4 Be3 chased your queen from b4 to a5 while White developed for free.

pv: Qxb2 Nxf6+ gxf6 Rd1 e5 g3 Qxc2 Bh3 Bb4+ Kf2 Qxe2+ Kxe2 Be6 f4 exf4 Bxe6
e: Qxb2! is safe and strong: after Nxf6+ gxf6 Rd1 e5 the queen has escape squares whenever it needs them, and g3 Qxc2 collects a second pawn - the line finishes with Bb4+ and Qxe2+, trading into an endgame two pawns up.
ep: Qb4+? donates the tempo White needs: c3! hits the queen and defends b2 permanently. After Qa5 Nxf6+ gxf6 your kingside is damaged, b2 never fell, and Qf2 let White untangle - a large edge shrank to a small one.

pv: Rg8
e: Rg8! addresses the real threat: the d4-bishop x-rays your h8-rook along the empty long diagonal (g7 is gone). On g8 the rook is safe and sits on the half-open file against the g4-pawn, keeping your extra activity while f5 stays covered.
ep: f6? blocks the diagonal with a pawn that has no real defender: the e7-pawn is pinned by the e2-queen, so Bxf6! wins it outright (exf6 is illegal). The game showed the follow-up - Bxf6 Rg8 Qe6! Bf7 Qc8+ and b7 fell too, and White took over completely.

pv: Kf7 Bc4+ Bd5 Rd1 fxg4 Rxd5 cxd5 Bxd5+ Kg7 Bxg8 Kxg8 b4 h5 a4 h4 a5
e: You're in check from the e1-rook, and Kf7! is the right escape: it keeps your extra piece and prepares Bd5 to blunt everything at once. After Bc4+ Bd5 Rd1 fxg4, even White's best regaining attempt Rxd5 cxd5 Bxd5+ Bxg8 Kxg8 trades into an ending where you are simply a piece up.
ep: Be4 blocks the check but pins the bishop to your own king on the open e-file - it can never move again and becomes the target. In the game Bc8! Qc7 gxf5 kept it under fire and Rxe4+ eventually won the pinned bishop; Kf7 would have kept the piece.

pv: Qxf4+ Kd1 Qd6+ Kc1 Bh6+ Re3 Bxe3#
e: Qxf4+! is mate in 4: Kd1 Qd6+ (the queen switches to the d-file, still checking) Kc1 Bh6+ brings the f8-bishop in decisively - Re3 is the only block, and Bxe3# finishes. Every move is check, so White's Rxe4 resource never gets a turn.
ep: Rg2? forgets that your e4-bishop is pinned on the open e-file: Rxe4+! wins it with check, and after Kf7 Be6+ Kg7 the White queen and bishop swarmed (Qc8 in the game). One move earlier you had forced mate; one move later you were lost.

pv: Qb6 Qd7+ Kh6 Qd2 Rxd2 Kxd2 Qxb2+ Kd3 Qb1+ Kd4 Qd1+ Kc4 Qf1+ Kd4 Qb5 Re1
e: Qb6! does everything at once: it hits b2, keeps your king covered, and leaves White only Qd7+ Kh6 Qd2 to stave off the threats - and then Rxd2! wins queen for rook. After Kxd2 Qxb2+ the queenside pawns fall with checks and your queen dominates the rook and bishop.
ep: Rg1+? lets the king walk out: Kc2 Rg2+ Kb3!, and Qb6+ is answered by Rb4!. After Bxb4 comes the sting - Qg8+! (protected by the e6-bishop, so you can't take) forces Kh6, and Qxg2 wins your rook. The checks turned your most active piece into a target.

pv: Qb5 Rd2 Qa4+ Bb3 Qe4+ Qd3 Qxf4 Bc4 Rg4 Be6 c5 a3 c4 Qd4 Kg5 Qxf4+
e: Qb5! hits the e2-rook along the diagonal and keeps the checking network alive: after Rd2 Qa4+ Bb3 Qe4+! the queen forks its way through the light squares and Qxf4 regains a pawn, reaching a defensible position with your queen fully active.
ep: Qc5? attacks nothing and surrenders the light squares: Qd3! centralizes, your Qa4+/Qe4+ resources vanish, and the plan Qf3-h5 comes at your bare king while the g1-rook sits shut out of play. In the game Qd2 kept the same grip and your rook had to grovel.

pv: Qd6 b4 Kh5 a4 Kg4 Qxd6 Bxd6 Bd7 h5
e: Qd6! forces the queen trade while hitting f4: with your king on h6 and the rook stranded on g1, every piece White keeps is an attacker, so swapping queens is worth material concessions. The line even shows your king activating - b4 Kh5! a4 Kg4 - before Qxd6 Bxd6 reaches a grindable ending.
ep: Rg4? feeds the rook to the queen: Qd3! Rh4 Qg3! traps it - only Rh5 is left, where it stays buried while White's queen dominates. The game's Rg2 and h3 snared it the same way, and you had to bail out with the Qd6 trade anyway, worse off than before.

pv: Rxg2 Qxg2 Qe3 a3 Qxf4 Kb3 Qb8+ Ka2 Qc7 Bg8 Bd6 Qg4 Bxh2 Qh4+ Kg7 Qxh7+
e: Rxg2 Qxg2 trades off White's attacker, and then Qe3! is the point: it hits f4 and c3 at once, so after a3 Qxf4 you win the pawn back and reach a queen ending where your king is safe enough to hold on and fight.
ep: Rxf4?? puts the rook on the d2-queen's diagonal with your king exposed: Qxf4+! wins it with check - and it is actually mate in 2, since Kh5 is forced (g7 is covered by the g2-rook) and Bf7# follows. White missed it in the game (h3), but the mate was on the board.

pv: Rh2 Rxh2+
e: Rh2! forces the rook trade - Rxh2+ Bxh2, with your d6-bishop covering h2 from afar - and the opposite-colored-bishop ending is a fortress: the a-pawns are locked against each other, c6 is defensible, and White has no way through. A concrete route to the draw.
ep: Bc5? leaves the c6-pawn loose at the wrong moment: Bd7! wins it (Bd6 Bxc6), and after the same rook trade White is a clean pawn up with b4 coming - now the queenside pawns plus a6 decide instead of a drawn bishop ending.

pv: Kf4 Rg6 Ke3 Bc4 Rf2+ Kb3 Rxf5 Rh6 Kd2 Bf7 Kc1 Rxh5 Rxh5 Bxh5 f5 Kc4
e: Kf4! marches toward the action: after Rg6 comes Ke3, hitting the d3-bishop, and then Rf2+ followed by Rxf5 regains the pawn with everything active. With the rook loose on the fifth and your king central, the draw is well within reach.
ep: Kh4? heads for the corner where the geometry bites: Rh2+ Kg4 and Be2! pins your f3-rook to the king. In the game Kxf5 Bxf3 won the exchange and Rxh5+ took a pawn with it - all avoided by walking the other way with Kf4.

pv: Rh3 Re2 Re3 Rh2+ Kg5 Rg2+ Kf4 Rh2 Kg4 Rg2+
e: Rh3! blocks the check and offers a trade White can't dodge: on Re2 you reply Re3, and the checking attempts Rh2+ Kg5 Rg2+ Kf4 just repeat the position. Keeping the rook glued to the king holds the draw on the spot.
ep: Kg4?? steps onto the e2-g4 diagonal: Be2! pins the f3-rook to your king and wins it. The game continued Kxf5 Bxf3, leaving you the exchange down, and Rxh5+ soon followed - all from a position that was a dead draw one move earlier.

pv: Kg3 Bxf3 Kxh2 Bxc6 Ba5 b4 Kg3 bxa5 Kf4 Kd3 Kxf5 Kd4 Ke6 Bg2 h4 Bh3+
e: Kg3! counterattacks the h2-rook: now Bxf3 is answered by Kxh2, and you have traded rook for rook instead of rook for bishop. White still stands much better after Bxc6, but with level material there is real resistance left in the position.
ep: Kxf5 wins a pawn but deserts the f3-rook: Bxf3 nets rook for bishop, and in the game Rxh5+ picked up another pawn immediately. Kg3, hitting the rook on h2, would have kept the material balance and the fight alive.

pv: b5 Bd3
e: b5! hits the c4-bishop, the d5-pawn's key guard: after Bd3 you regain the pawn with Nfxd5 (Nxd5 Nxd5), reaching full equality (-0.3).
ep: Bg4 pins against nothing dangerous and loses time: Qa4+! forces the bishop straight back to d7 — exactly the game — and after castling White keeps the extra d5-pawn, with Qb4xb7 ideas in some lines (-1.9).

pv: Nxb5 Qb3 Qb6 Ne5 Nd4 Qxb6 axb6 Kd1 g6 Nxd7 Kxd7 b3 b5 Bb2 Bg7 Re1
e: Ncxb5! wins a piece: the bishop's protection is an illusion. If White recaptures Nxb5, then Qb6! attacks the knight again while hitting b2 — with a6 coming, it cannot be held (Nfd4 a6 Nc2 Qxb5 Qxb5 axb5). White's best is to decline with Qb3 and stay a bishop down (+4.1).
ep: Nfxd5 lets White liquidate everything: Bxd7+ Qxd7 Qxd7+ Kxd7 and the tension resolves into a level ending (+0.2) — the game followed exactly, and a whole free piece slipped away.

pv: Nxf4 g3 Nfd5 h4 h5 Ke2 a5 Rac1 a4 a3 Nxc3+ bxc3
e: Nxf4! — the f4-bishop is flat-out undefended, so the d5-knight takes it for free; after g3 the knight simply returns with Nfd5 and you are a clean piece up (+4.8).
ep: Bb4 lets White solve everything with Bxc7!: the hanging bishop trades itself for your c7-knight, and a3 then puts the question to your b4-bishop — the free piece became rough equality (+0.3). In the game White even left the bishop hanging with O-O, and the chance passed again.

pv: Nxf4 g3 Nfd5 Rfc1 Be7 h4 Kd7 Kg2 g6 Rc2 b6 Rac1 Rhc8 Nxd5 Nxd5 Rxc8
e: Nxf4 still wins the bishop — it has been undefended for two moves. After g3 Nfd5 the knight is safe and you are a piece up for nothing (+4.7).

pv: g5 Re1 Kd8 g3 g4 Nh4 Nh3+ Kg2 Ng5 c5 Ba5 Re2 Kc8 Re7 Rd8 f4
e: g5! anchors your best piece — the pawn defends the f4-knight — and prepares g4 to harass the f3-knight; White's b7-rook bites on granite while your knight dominates (+1.4).
ep: Ne2+ chases nothing: after Kf1 the knight must retreat, and grabbing d4 fails to R1xb6! axb6 Nxd4, with Nxe6+ forking next. In the game the knight drifted to a2 and c5 hit your b6-bishop, costing a piece (0.0 and worse to follow).

pv: Ne4 Re3 f5 Ra3 Bd8 Ra6 Bf6 Ke2 Rc8 c5 e5 Re6+ Kd8 Nxe5 Bxe5 Rxe5
e: Ne4! steps out of the rook's attack toward the center: supported by f5 next, the knight is untouchable, and Bd8 holds the queenside — Black keeps everything defended (-0.2).
ep: Nxa2 grabs a poisoned pawn: Ra3! boxes the knight into the corner with Rxa2 to follow, and meanwhile c5 hits your b6-bishop. In the game c5 and cxb6 won a piece for two pawns (-2.5).

pv: g5 g3 Nd5 Ra7 Nb6 Ra6 Nc8 Rxd6 Nxd6 Ke2 Nb5 Kd3 g4 Nb3 Nc7 Kc4
e: g5! secures the f4-knight — the pawn now defends it — and prepares Nd5-b6 to blockade White's queenside pieces; you hold comfortably (-0.3).
ep: Rxd4 walks into Nd7+!: the king has no square (e5 is covered by the knight, the 7th rank by the h7-rook), so Rxd7 Rxd7 is forced — rook for knight. White missed it with g3?? and was even mated by Rd1#, but the pawn grab was objectively losing material (-2.8).

pv: d5 Bg2 Nc6 h3 e5 c4 Be6 cxd5 Bxd5 Bxd5 Qxd5 Nf3 O-O-O
e: d5 takes the centre immediately, which is the standard antidote to 1.g4 — the g-pawn has done nothing for development and the bishop on g2 will bite on granite. After Bg2 Nc6 h3 e5 you have a big pawn duo, and ...Be6 holds d5 so c4 achieves nothing.
ep: b6 fianchettoes straight into the bishop White is about to place on g2, and after Bg2 d5 c4 White strikes at the centre you delayed occupying. In the game the b7 bishop was simply traded off and you were left with nothing to show for the tempo.

pv: Rh7 h4 Qd7 e4 dxe4 Qxe4 O-O-O O-O-O Kb8 Rhe1 Re8 Kb1 Nbd6 Qd3 Nxh4 Nxh4
e: Rh7 tucks the rook back to safety and, just as importantly, leaves the knight on f5 where it stands — that knight is the only thing blocking White's queen on the c2-g6 diagonal. After h4 Qd7 e4 dxe4 Qxe4 O-O-O you get the king safe and the position stays balanced.
ep: Nxg3 opens the c2-g6 diagonal, and Qxg6+ takes the pawn with check because it was shielded only by that knight; after Kf8 Qxg3 the knight comes back and your king cover is shredded. The game reached the same fork one move later.

pv: f5 g4 Rh8 gxf5 gxf5 h4 Nd6 h5 Ne4 Bf4 Qd7 h6 O-O-O e3 Rdg8 O-O-O
e: f5 plugs the c2-g6 diagonal with a pawn, which is the only way to save both the g6 pawn and the rook on h5 at once. After g4 Rh8 the rook steps off the loose square, gxf5 gxf5 leaves you a solid pawn wall, and ...Nd6-e4 gives a good blockading square.

pv: f4 Bd7 Rc5 f6 h3 Kh8 Kh2 Rcd8 Qc1 Qb4 Qc2 Bc8 Rc4 Qb8 Rxc6 Ne5
e: f4! gains space and threatens f5, hitting the e6-bishop and g6-knight at once. After Bd7 Rc5! the rook lands on the fifth rank, and White slowly piles up on the weak c6-pawn (Qc1-c2, Rc4) until Rxc6 wins it — all while the d4-passer stays firmly blockaded (+2.4).
ep: Qc5 offers the queen trade Black is praying for: Qxc5 Rxc5 (the game) releases all the pressure — without queens c6 is easy to defend and the d4-passer becomes real counterplay; even declining with Nf8-d7 lets Black regroup comfortably (+1.1).

pv: Rxh5 f5 exf5 h6 Re1 Nd5 f6 gxf6 Bf5 Rdc7 Bxc8 Rxc8 Rxh6
e: The h5-bishop is simply loose — Rxh5! wins a whole piece. Nothing defends h5, and the rook can't be trapped: after f5 exf5 h6 Re1 White consolidates a clean bishop up (+5.1).
ep: Bf2 pokes at d4 but walks past a free bishop: after f5! exf5 Bf7 it slips to safety for good, and Black gets c5 and the d4-passer moving (+2.6). In the game f6 and Bf7 saved it just the same — the chance never came back.

pv: Rxh5 Rcd8 Rhc5 f5 e5 Rf8 Bh4 Ng6 Bg3 Ne7 e6 Rd6
e: Still Rxh5! — the bishop is exactly as loose as it was last move, and the fifth rank is clear. After Rxh5 Rcd8 Rhc5 the rook comes straight back into play, and White is a full piece up with e5/f5 coming (+5.3).
ep: g4 attacks the bishop with the wrong unit — it simply retreats to f7 in safety, and the advance has loosened f4 and your king for nothing: h5! soon pries at the g4/h3 pawns you pushed (+2.7). Taking the bishop was free; chasing it wasn't.

pv: Bh4 Re8 f5 Nc8 Bg3 Ne7 Ra4 h5 Kf2 hxg4 hxg4 g6 Bh4 g5
e: Bh4! keeps the bind: the f2-bishop swings out to hit f6, and after Re8 f5! fixes the black pawns; then Bg3 and Ra4 — swinging the rook onto the blockaded d4-pawn — let you squeeze both weaknesses (f6 and d4) while Black can only shuffle (+2.8).
ep: e5 releases the tension a move too soon: Rcd8! first, and after exf6 Nd5! arrives with tempo on f4; Bf5 is met by Rd6, and fxg7 Nxf4 regains the pawn while the d-passer starts running (+1.2). The game's e5 fxe5 Rxe5 likewise let Black activate with Ng6 and Bd5.

pv: f5 g5 Bd4 Kc7 Kf3 Kd7 Be3 h5 f6 hxg4+ Kxg4 Ng6 Bd4 Nf8 Kf5
e: Leave the queenside alone — b5 is safe for now — and win where you are effectively a piece up: f5!, then Bd4 activating the buried bishop, Kf3-e4, and the f6/g5 breaks create a second passer that the knight can't stop while it also watches the b-pawn (+5.1).
ep: b6? pushes the pawn into the king's arms: Kc6! blockades, and Nc8! attacks both b6 and the cornered a7-bishop, so the pawn can't be kept; after Kb7 and d4 Black is right back in it. The game duly fizzled into a draw (+0.6).

pv: b7 Kxb7 Bd4 g6 fxg6 hxg6 Kf4 Kc6 Kg5 Kb5 Kxg6 Kc4 Bf2 d4 h4 Ne7+
e: b7!! deflects: after Kxb7 the entombed bishop escapes with Bd4, hitting g7, and your king marches Kf4-g5xg6 to eat the kingside — g6 fxg6 hxg6 and Kxg6 leaves the h-pawn running while Bf2 later holds up d5-d4. Giving the b-pawn back frees every white piece (+3.2).
ep: g5? keeps the pawn but leaves the bishop buried on a7: Nd6! hits f5, and in the game after f6 gxf6 gxf6 came the fork Ne4+! — king and f6-pawn — removing your last passer. The knight held the draw single-handedly (+0.3).

pv: Bd3 Bg7
e: Bd3 finishes development and keeps the king's destination open. With Black's pawn already on b5 and a fianchetto coming, the queenside is not a safe home; after Bg7 you can still castle short or stay flexible, and the bishop on d3 guards e4 so the centre holds.
ep: Castling long puts your king right in front of Black's advancing pawns: b4 hits the c3 knight, and once it retreats (Nb1 in the game) the e4 pawn falls to Nxe4. The attack comes with tempo because every pawn move gains time on a piece.

pv: Nxe4 dxe4 Bxe4 Be6 Qb4 Qb6 Qa3 a5 Nf3 Qb4 Bd6 Qxa3 Bxa3 f5 Bd3 Kd8
e: Nxe4 wins the d5 pawn outright thanks to the queen on e1 standing behind the file: after dxe4 Bxe4 Black cannot recapture, because Bxe4 runs into Qxe4+, hitting the uncastled king on e8 and picking up the bishop. So Black has to retreat with Be6 and your bishop sits on e4 raking b7 and c6 while Qb4 keeps him from castling comfortably.
ep: Be5 achieves nothing concrete: f6 kicks the bishop straight back to f4 and Black castles into safety, keeping the knight on e4 and the extra centre pawn. The free pawn on d5 was there for one move only.

pv: Nxe4 Qxe1 Nd6+ Kf8 Rxe1 Bxd3 cxd3 Ke7 Nf3 Na6 Rhf1 Nc5 Re3 Ne6 d4 Rab8
e: Nxe4 works because the pin on the d2 knight is an illusion. Qxe1 is answered by Nd6+! — a family fork of the king on e8 and the bishop on f5 — and after Kf8 Rxe1 you have recovered the queen, planted a monster knight on d6 and left Black's king stranded with his rooks disconnected.
ep: a3 gives Black exactly the move he needs, Nxd2, trading the knight off before the fork ever appears. After Bxf5 the position is still pleasant, but the chance to win with the Nd6+ trick has evaporated.

pv: Qxa5 exd3 Nf3 dxc2 Rd6 O-O Nd4 Bg4 h3 Nxe5 Qxe5 Rfe8 Qf6 Bd1 Nxc2 Bxc2
e: Qxa5 just takes the undefended queen. Black's e4 push attacked your bishop on d3, but the bishop is the cheaper piece: after exd3 Nf3 you finish development, and Rd6 plus Nd4 round up the loose c2/d3 pawns while you are a queen for a bishop up.
ep: Bxe4 saves the bishop and forgets that both queens were en prise to each other: Qxe1 forces Rxe1, and then Bxe4 Rxe4 restores material equality. The game followed exactly this, and a winning material edge became an ordinary advantage.

pv: Na4 Rc8
e: Count the defenders: b5 is already covered by the f1-bishop, but c5 hangs. Na4! is the one move that holds the queenside — it defends c5, eyes the b6 hole, and keeps your space-gaining pawn chain intact.
ep: a4 defends the wrong pawn — b5 was never hanging, the f1-bishop watches it — and abandons the one that was: Bxc5 wins it on the spot, exactly as happened in the game. After that the dark squares around c5 belonged to Black.

pv: Rad1 Qb6 Nac3 Rc4 g5 Nd7 Nxd5 exd5 Qxd5 Qc7 Rd4 Rc5 Qe4+ Re5 Qg4 h5
e: Rad1 finally puts your worst rook to work and sets up the central counter: after Qb6 Nac3 the a2-knight rejoins too, and Nxd5! exd5 Qxd5 becomes a real resource — the queen recaptures hitting the loose c4-rook with Rd4 right behind her. Slightly worse either way, but every piece plays.
ep: Nf4 improves one piece while two others rot: Rc4! ties you to the a4-pawn, and the only plan left is the grovel Nc1-b3 while Black reroutes Nc8-b6 at your queenside. In the game g5 hxg5 hxg5 Rxh1 traded away your one active file.

pv: Nc3 Rc8 Rh7 Qc5 Nce2 Qxc2 Qa3+ Qc5 Qxc5+ Nxc5 Rxg7 Kf8 Nh5 Nxa4 Rh7 Rc2
e: Nc3! brings your worst piece back — it hits d5 and defends both b5 and a4. After Rc8 Rh7 your rook takes the seventh with Rxg7 in the air, and the g5-pawn stays where it is useful, as a cramping wedge. Advancing it only creates a target.
ep: g6 hands Black Ne5!, forking your queen and the freshly advanced pawn: after Qb3 fxg6 the pawn is gone and the knight is a monster on e5. In the game f6 kept things closed and blunted your rook, and the g6-pawn never achieved anything.

pv: Rg8 Nc5 Qd2 Nc8 Rxg7+ Ke8 Rg8+ Kd7 Qxa5 b6 Rg7+ Ke8 Qa8 Ne4+ fxe4 Rxc2+
e: Rg8! wins a pawn by force — nothing defends g7 — and turns g6 into a monster: after Nc5 Qd2 Nc8 Rxg7+ Ke8 Rg8+ Kd7 Qxa5 you have grabbed two pawns and the g-pawn is ready to run with the rook escorting from behind.
ep: Ra8 attacks nothing that matters: Nc8! leaves the rook biting on a5 while Ndb6 comes to harass it and hit a4 — and the g7-pawn survives, so your passer stays stuck. In the game Qc5 came, and after c3? Rxf4! you even lost the f4-knight.

pv: Ne2 Nc8 Nd4 Qc7 Kg2 Nc5 Qd2 Nxa4 Rxa5 Kd7 f4 e5 Ne2 Nab6
e: Black's Qc5 set a trap: Rxf4! exf4 Qe3+ forks king and queen the moment the e3-pawn leaves. Ne2 is the calm answer — the knight steps off the target square and heads for d4, where after Nc8 Nd4 it stands beautifully centralized with everything defended again.
ep: c3 walks into the point: Rxf4!, and you can't recapture because exf4 Qe3+ wins the queen — so the sac simply wins a clean knight. The game saw exactly that: Rxf4, and after Rg8 Rxa4 Black was a piece and pawns to the good.

pv: Rxd7+ Kxd7 g7 Rxa2+ Kg3 Ra1 Kh2 Nc8 g8=Q Qa3 b6 Qb3 Qg3 Qxb6 e4 Ne7
e: Your rook stands in the g-pawn's way, so clear it with tempo: Rxd7+! Kxd7 g7 and nothing catches the pawn — Rxa2+ Kg3 Ra1 Kh2 comes a move short, and after Nc8 g8=Q the new queen outweighs the rook you invested. In a bad position, this was the fighting chance.
ep: Nc1 gives Black time for Ne5!, hitting your queen and attacking the g6-pawn at the same time; after Qd1 Qxb5 Black wins a pawn and coordinates. In the game Ne5 came, and after Qf1? Ra2+! Nxa2 Qxc3 the position collapsed.

pv: Qd1 Qxb5 f4 Qb2+ Kg3 Re4 fxe5+ Rxe5 Ne2 Nc6 Rg8 Ne7 Rd8+ Kc7 Ra8 Nxg6
e: With the queen attacked, the square is everything: Qd1 steps away while still covering g4, so the knight check fails — Ng4+? fxg4 Rxg4 runs into Qxg4 down the opened diagonal. Black's best is Qxb5, met by f4! kicking the knight: Qb2+ Kg3 Re4 fxe5+ Rxe5 and you fight on.
ep: Qf1 loses to Ng4+!: fxg4 runs into Rf4+! (Kg2 Rxf1 Kxf1 Qxe3 wins the queen), and Kg3 into Qxe3 with your king stripped bare. In the game Black found Ra2+! Nxa2 Qxc3 instead, which also won material.

pv: Nxc3 Nc8 Rxb7 Nd7 Qd3 Ke7 g7 Nd6 Rxd7+ Kxd7 g8=Q Nc8 Qgh7+ Ne7 b6 f5
e: Black's queen just landed on c3 — inside your a2-knight's range! Nxc3 wins the queen for a knight on the spot. After Nc8 Rxb7 Nd7 Qd3 you are a queen for rook ahead and the g6-pawn marches with g7 and g8=Q; the game is effectively over.
ep: Rxb7 wins a pawn but leaves the queen on the board: Nd3+! Kg1 Qd2 gives Black real counterplay with Qxe3+ and Nf2+ tricks coming. In the game Qc2+ Qe2 Qc8 saved the queen — you were still better, but a whole queen was there for the taking.

pv: e4 cxd4 Qxd4 Qb6 b3 Qxd4 Nxd4 Ne3 Rd3 Ng2 Nde2 h5 g5 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd5
e: e4! stakes the center at the right moment: on cxd4 you recapture Qxd4 with a centralized queen, and after Qb6 b3 the c4-knight must justify itself — the ending after Qxd4 Nxd4 is clearly pleasant for white, with Rd3 chasing the strays (+1.2).
ep: Nf4 aims at d5 and e6, but nothing there can be won: black simply continues Rc8, Qb6 and b5 — queenside play with tempo — while the knight bites on granite and the c4-knight stays the best minor piece on the board (-0.6). The game's Qb6 and Qa5 kept you tangled.

pv: Nxc5 O-O-O g5 hxg5 Nb3 Qc7 hxg5 Rxh1 Rxh1 Ne8 g6 Ned6 Kb1 Kb8 gxf7 Qxf7
e: Nxc5! wins a pawn for free: the natural Qxc5?? loses the queen to dxc5, since your d4-pawn covers c5. Black must decline with O-O-O, and then g5! hxg5, Nb3 (tempo on the queen) and hxg5 open the h-file with the attack and the extra pawn (+1.9).
ep: Qb3 pokes at the c4-knight — which d5 defends anyway — and lets black liquidate with cxd4. After exd4 the knight is secured by b5, as in the game, and the free pawn on c5 plus the initiative are gone (-0.4).

pv: Rhg1 Kh8 Rxg5 e5 dxe5 b4 Qxb4 Qxb4 axb4 Nc7 e6 Nxe3 Rd3 Nc4 exf7 Rxf7
e: Right idea, wrong rook: Rhg1! doubles against g5 while the d1-rook keeps covering d2, the invasion square for black's queen. After Kh8 Rxg5 you win the g5-pawn with the attack in full flow — e5-breaks and Qxb4 trades lead to a winning position (+4.5).
ep: Rdg1 abandons d2: Qd2+! invades with tempo, and after Kb1 Kh7 Rxg5 Qxe3 black forces the queens off (Qxe3 Nxe3) and the attack fizzles to a much smaller edge (+2.8). In the game black missed it with f6 and you crashed through anyway.

pv: Bf5 Rc1 Bg6 g4 Rc8 h3 Ne7 Nxe5 Rxc1 Rxc1 Bc7 Nf3
e: White's Qd3/Bb1 battery is loaded against h7 with the e4-knight ready to join — Bf5! meets it head-on. After Rc1 Bg6 the bishop permanently plugs the b1-h7 diagonal, and with your extra pawns and Ne7 rerouting to cover the king, the attack is over and the material tells.
ep: Bc7 tends the queenside while the kingside burns: b5 kicks the c6-knight to the rim, and the winning margin evaporates. In the game the battery detonated — Nc5! b6? Qh7+ Kf8 Nxe6+! Rxe6 Qh8+ and the king hunt decided the game.

pv: g6 b5 Bf5 Qd2 Bxb1 bxc6 Bf5 cxb7 Rb8 Qxh6 Qf6 Ng5 Qg7 Qh4 Bd6 g4
e: g6! finally closes the b1-h7 diagonal for good. The c5-knight is then left without a target: after b5 you hit back with Bf5!, trading off White's key attacking bishop, and even the sharp bxc6 cxb7 lines burn out to balance. King safety first — the b7-pawn was never the point.
ep: b6? attacks the knight, but Nxe6! lands first: fxe6 Qh7+ Kf8 Bg6! wins material by force — Ne7 Bxe8 Qxe8 Nxe5 leaves White the exchange and pawns up. The game version was even faster: Qh7+ Kf8 Nxe6+ Rxe6 Qh8+ Ke7 Qxg7 and the king was run down.

pv: Qg8 Qxg8 Rxg8 Rc1 Rf6 Kf1 Kd8 h3 a6 Bd3 b5 Rc5 Re8 Rec1 e4 Rxc6
e: Qg8! meets the invader head-on: it offers the queen trade, and after Qxg8 Rxg8 White's attack is over — f7 is no longer a target and your rooks (Rg8, Rf6 in the line) coordinate again. You stand only slightly worse (-0.6) with the d4-passer as a long-term trump. When you are under attack, trading off the attacking queen is worth a small concession.
ep: Rg6 attacks the queen but hangs the rook to the b1-bishop: Bxg6! — and fxg6 is illegal, because the f7-pawn is pinned along the seventh rank by the g7-queen. The game ended exactly Rg6 Bxg6: a whole rook, gone for nothing.

pv: c6 Ne5 Nbd7 Ndc4 Qd8 Qb3 Nb6 Na5 Qc7 Bf4 Nbd5 Bh2 Qxa5 Qxb7 O-O Nxc6
e: c6 sorts out your queen before White's knights arrive with tempo: it opens the d8/c7 escape route. In the line c6 Ne5 Nbd7 Ndc4 Qd8 every jump is met calmly, and when Na5 comes later, Qc7 keeps her safe while your development continues normally.
ep: Ne4 ignores the queen's problem: Nc4! hits her at once, and after Qd5 Bf4 Qd8 Qb3 White develops with one tempo after another. In the game it was worse still - when the queen went to d5, Ne3 forked her and the f5-bishop, and Nxf5 won a piece.

pv: c6 Rc2 Rae8 Rce2 Qd8 a3 a5 Qc2 Bd6 bxa5 Bxe5 dxe5 Rxe5 f3
e: c6 shores up the queenside and gives your queen the d8 square: after Rc2 Rae8 Rce2 Qd8 you contest the e-file, the e5-knight has nothing to bite on, and White's edge stays small. The closed d-file could wait - the fight is on the e-file.
ep: Rfd8 walks away from the kingside just as Qb3! comes, eyeing b7 and f7. After Qe6 Bc4 the queen is harassed, and the trick Ng6! hxg6 Rxe6 wins queen for rook and knight. In the game White's Nc4, Qf3 and Bxe4 targeted the loose e4-knight instead.

pv: Qe7 Qe3
e: Qe7 keeps the queen in touch with the kingside, where Ne5, Qf3 and both rooks are aimed: she covers f7 and keeps the e-file tricks toothless - the exchange sac Rxe4 achieves nothing with f7 defended. After Qe3 nothing in your camp hangs (-0.1).
ep: Qa4 wanders offside and abandons f7: Rxe4! wins material, since fxe4 runs into Qxf7+ - exactly the game (Qxf7+ Kh8 and White took over). Even the grovel f6 leaves White a clean extra pawn after Re2 fxe5 Rxe5.

pv: h4 Rfe8 Kf2 Kf7 c3 Nb3 Bb5 Rh8 h5 Nc5 Be5 Rhg8 Kg3 Bd5 Kh4 a6
e: h4 improves the kingside and prepares Kf2 followed by c3, which is the right order: the bishop on d3 must stay put because it is the only defender of c2, so you fix the king first and challenge the knight afterwards. Then Bb5 and Be5 give the bishops real scope against the loose black pawns.
ep: Bc4 abandons the c2 pawn, and Nxc2+ takes it with check so the knight is never trapped: after Ke2 Bd5 Bd3 Nd4+ it returns to the centre a pawn up. The same Nxc2+ arrived a move later in the game.

pv: Bg2 f5 h4 Nf7 Nc1 Nd7 Nd3 Be7 Qe2 c6 O-O-O Bf6 Rdg1 O-O Bg5 e5
e: The g5-knight threatened mate on f3, and every detail matters: your g-pawn is gone, the d1-queen's path to f3 is blocked by your own e2-knight, and Bb4 covers the d2 escape square. Bg2 guards f3 with the bishop and prepares h4, when the knight finally has to retreat (f5, h4 and Nf7 in the main line).
ep: Rg1 does nothing about Nf3#: nothing can capture on f3 — e2 is blocked by your own knight and there is no g-pawn — and the king has no square, since the knight and Bb4 cover d2. The game ended on the spot.

pv: g6 Qd2 Kg7 Ne5 Bf5 Bxf5 exf5 Qf4 Nc6 Nd3 Rad8 a4 Qf6 g4 fxg4 Qxg4
e: g6! comes first: it gives the king air and blunts the c2-h7 diagonal before White's queen lands on it. After Qd2 Kg7 Ne5 Bf5! you trade off the dangerous light-squared bishop and the kingside holds — only then should the knight think about f5.
ep: Nf5? runs into Qd3!, stacking queen and c2-bishop against the knight: you are forced into Bxf3 Qxf3 Nh6, conceding your good bishop and retreating, and Qh5 with g4-g5 keeps chasing while your king still has no luft. The game's Qd2 was kinder, but g6 and Kg7 came a tempo late anyway — Qg5! and the g4-bishop fell.

pv: Nh6 Ne5 Bf5 Re3 Kg8 Rae1 Rfe8 Bxf5 exf5 Nd3 Re4 Nc5 Rxe3 Qxe3 Qb6 Qd2
e: Nh6! keeps everything covered: the knight guards the g4-bishop, watches f5, and prepares Bf5 to swap off White's dangerous c2-bishop — Ne5 Bf5 Re3 Kg8 and the attack is contained. The one thing you must not do here is touch the pawns in front of your king.
ep: g6?? invites Bxf5!, winning a piece: after Bxf3 White has Qh6+! Kg8 Bxg6! — fxg6 Qxg6+ Kh8 Qh6+ and the king cannot escape the checks while gxf3 also recovers the bishop; White ends a piece and pawns up with the king stripped bare. In the game Qg5? let you cover with Kg7, though the g4-bishop still dropped.

pv: Bxf3 Bxf5 exf5 Qh6+ Kg8 gxf3 Rfe8 Kg2 Qf8 Qf4 Kg7 Qc7 b5 Qd7 Red8 Qb7
e: Bxf3! saves the attacked bishop by cashing it in — the queen on g5 was simply threatening Qxg4. After Bxf5 exf5 Qh6+ Kg8 gxf3 the minor pieces have traded evenly, and with Rfe8 and Qf8 you cover the dark squares and keep a defensible game.
ep: Kg7? defends nothing that matters: Qxg4 pockets the bishop for free, exactly as happened in the game. When a piece is attacked and can trade itself off (Bxf3), do that before anything else.

pv: Nf3 b5 e3 Rf7 a3 Bb7 c4 Nc5 cxb5 axb5 Bxb5
e: Nf3 develops the last minor piece and - the key point - physically blocks the f-file: Rxf2 is no longer even possible. With f2 secured, White calmly plays e3, a3 and c4, and after b5 cxb5 axb5 Bxb5 even picks up a pawn while converting the extra material (+2.0).
ep: e3 leaves f2 hanging: Rxf2! grabs it, and the rook cannot be trapped - after Nh3 Rf5 Be2 it slides out with its pawn. The game went Rxf2 as well, and that rook camped on your second rank for the rest of the game.

pv: Nf3 b5 Bb3 h6 e4 Bb7 Nxc7 Bxc7 Rxd7 Bf4+ Kb1 Bxe4 Re1 Bxf3 gxf3 Rf8
e: Nf3 covers e5 - shutting out Ne5, Black's main idea against your c4-bishop - and finally develops the kingside. It also readies the trick Nxc7! Bxc7 Rxd7, exploiting the loose d7-knight and c7-bishop to grab material back (+0.4).
ep: g3 gives Black time for Ne5!, hitting the c4-bishop with tempo. Bb3 is met by Bg4, harassing the d1-rook, and with your Ng1 and Rh1 still asleep every Black piece plays - the game's a5 and Bd7-c6 squeeze followed, and the eval tipped to -0.8.

pv: Rf1 Rxf1+ Bxf1 Bc5 Bg2 c6 Nc3 Bxe3+ Kb1 Nc4 b3 Nd2+ Kb2 Bg4 Bh3
e: The f2-rook is the piece strangling you - Rf1! challenges it head-on. After Rxf1+ Bxf1 the invader is gone, Bg2 contests the long diagonal and Nc3 finally develops; Black keeps an edge (-0.9), but you're untangling instead of suffocating.
ep: Bb3 lets Black keep building: Bg4! hits the d1-rook, and after Re1 comes Raf8, doubling on the f-file with total domination (-2.4). The game's slow squeeze - a5, Bd7, Bc6 - flowed straight from this; the f2-rook was never challenged again.

pv: a3 g5 Nc3 Raf8 h3 Bf5 g4 Bg6 Nge2 Nf3 Ref1 Bc5 Rxf2 Bxe3+ Kd1 Bxf2
e: a3! is prophylaxis against ...a4, which would trap the b3-bishop (a2 is occupied by your pawn and c4 is covered by the e5-knight). Moving the a-pawn vacates a2 as an escape square; then Nc3, g4 and Nge2 slowly untangle, and White stays afloat at -1.0.
ep: h3 hits the g4-bishop, but a4! is stronger than any retreat: the b3-bishop is trapped, and Bxa4 runs into Bf5 (hitting c2) and Rxa4! - after Nc3 Bd7 Nxa4 Bxa4 material is level again but every Black piece dominates (-2.4). In the game Nd3+! struck two moves later instead.

pv: Nc3 Raf8 a4 Bc5 Kb1 Rf1 Nge2 Rxe1+ Rxe1 Bxh3 Nf4 Bg4 Ne4 Bb4 c3
e: Nc3 regroups the d5-knight to guard the key squares around your stuck king (d1 and e2), preparing Kb1 and at last Nge2 to challenge the f2-rook. Black stays on top (-1.1), but there is no breakthrough - as long as you keep d3 under control.
ep: c3?? abandons the c2-pawn's guard of d3: Nd3+! forks in with check, and the knight feasts - Kd1 Nxb2+ Kc1 Nd3+ Kd1, and after a4! overloads the b3-bishop, Nxe1 even wins the rook (-6.5). The game followed those exact checks and collapsed.

pv: Be2
e: Be2 is modest but safe — it keeps the bishop off the square the e5-pawn can attack. White can then finish development with O-O and the position is about level (-0.3). Sometimes the whole job of a developing move is to not stand on a pawn's advance square.
ep: Bd3 walks into a pawn fork. Bxf3 Qxf3 and now e4! hits the bishop on d3 and the queen on f3 at the same time. After Bxe4 dxe4 Qxe4 Qd5 Qxd5 Nxd5 White has given a bishop for two pawns and stands clearly worse in the ending. -0.3 to -3.3. With a black pawn on e5 ready to advance, keep pieces off d3 and f3.

pv: Qg2 Ne5 Rb4 Re8 Re4 Rff8 f3 Kg8 Rf2 Ng6 Rxe8 Rxe8 f4 Rf8
e: Qg2 is pure damage control: the g-file is the whole position. Black's Qh5 and Rf3 are pointing at g1, and your queen on g3 is the only body in the way — but on g3 she can be shoved with ...Rxg3. On g2 she is defended by the king and plugs the file permanently, so the b7-rook is freed to come back (Rb4, Re4) and f2-f3 kicks the rook. You are still clearly worse, around -3.8, but that is a game rather than a mating net.
ep: Qxc7 wins a pawn and vacates the g-file with the king still on g1. Qg4+ is check straight down the file and the queen has to trudge back with Qg3, when Rxg3+ fxg3 Qxg3+ Kh1 Qxh4+ Kg1 Qg4+ strips the king naked with check throughout. In the game it came the same way: Rg8 Rfb1 Qxh4 Qxc6 Qxf2+ Kh1 Rh3#. When the enemy queen and rook are lined up on your king, a pawn on the other wing is not a currency you can spend.

pv: Qh2 Rgf8 c4 Qg4+ Qg2 Qxh4 c5 Qc4 g6 h6 Rfb1 Qxc5 R1b5 Qxa3
e: Qh2 brings the queen home to the only square that matters. From h2 she covers g1, g2 and g3 at once, so the ...Qg4+ resource is answered by Qg2 and the checks run out. The engine line shows the difference: Qh2 Rgf8 c4 Qg4+ Qg2 Qxh4 c5 — Black wins the h4-pawn, but the king is walled in and White gets counterplay with the c-pawn and the b-file rooks. Around -3.6 and still playing.
ep: Rfb1 doubles rooks where nothing is happening and leaves g1 defended by the f2-pawn alone. Qg4+ forces Qg3 (nothing else blocks the file), and Rxg3+ fxg3 Qxg3+ Kh1 Qf3+ Kg1 Qg4+ collects material with check while the king stays in the box — -3.6 becomes -7.7. Your queen on c7 was doing nothing useful; with Qh5, Rf3 and Rg8 all aimed at your king, every move you make has to be a defensive one.

pv: Qh2 Qxg5+ Qg2 Qf6 Rd1 Ne5 Rd4 Ng6 Rbd7 Rf8 R4d6 Qxc3 Rxg6 Qe1+ Kh2 Rxf2
e: Qh2 is forced. It guards f2 — the square Black is mating on — and covers g1 and g2, and it offers the trade of queens down the h-file, which is exactly what a defender wants. After Qxg5+ Qg2 the checks stop, and the b7-rook plus the d-file give White something to hold onto. About -4.1, i.e. probably lost, but a position with moves in it rather than a forced mate.
ep: Qxc6 grabs the knight and gets mated in two: Qxf2+ Kh1 Rh3#. The f2-pawn was the only guard of g1, so once it falls with check the king is stuck on h1 and Rf3-h3 finishes. This is the third move in a row where the queen went hunting on the queenside instead of covering the king; when your opponent has queen and rook on your castled king, count his checks before you count his pieces.

pv: Ng7 Rcd1 Rfd8 g4 Be8 Kh1 hxg4 Nxg4 f5 Nf6+ Kf7 Bg2 Bc6 Nh7 Bxf4 Rxf4
e: Ng7! keeps the kingside stitched together: the knight covers e8 and h5, so White's g4 can be met by hxg4 Nxg4 f5!, hitting the knight — later in the line Bxf4 even nets the f-pawn. Meanwhile Rfd8 and Be8 complete a tidy setup, a solid pawn up (+1.6).
ep: Be7 lets the queenside tension resolve in White's favor: c4! hits b5 and d5, and after axb4 cxd5 the center opens with b4 hanging both ways — the extra pawn dissolves into near-equality (+0.4). In the game White chose Nxd7 and Qe5 instead, also comfortable for him.

pv: Nxd2 Qxd2
e: Nxd2 releases the tension on your terms: the knight on e4 is your best piece but it can be challenged at any moment, so trading it for the Bd2 leaves you with a solid centre, no weaknesses and easy development after Qxd2.
ep: g5 loosens your own king's cover and simply drops a pawn: Nxe4 dxe4 clears the way for Nxg5, and White also gets Nxe6 ideas against your queen. In the game fxg5 followed at once and the kingside came apart.

pv: Bxg3 hxg3 Qh1+ Kf2 Rh2+ Ke1 Rxe2+ Kxe2 Qh7 Nb5 Kd7 Rh1 Qg7 Rh2 Kd8
e: Bxg3! rips open the h-file: hxg3 Qh1+ Kf2 Rh2+! Ke1 and now Rxe2+ Kxe2 nets the queen for the rook, leaving you with Qh7 dominating an open board and the white king stuck in the centre. The bishop is worth far more as a battering ram than as a piece.
ep: Nd7 is a normal developing move that gives White the tempo he needs: Be1 shores up the h4-e1 diagonal and after f5 Nb5 the attack is gone and he starts playing on the queenside instead.

pv: Nxe3 Rxe3 Rad8 h3 Rd7 Ne5 Bxe5 Rxe5 Red8 Rde1 Rd5 Ne4 Nxe4 Qxe4 h6
e: Nxe3 removes the bishop that guards white's dark squares and does it before c4 can kick your knight off d5 for free. After Rxe3 Rad8 h3 Rd7 the d4 pawn is fixed as a target, and if Ne5 you simply answer Bxe5 and stay completely solid.
ep: Re7 leaves the e3 bishop alive and the knight on d5 loose: Bg5 h6 Bxh6! gxh6 c4 strips the king bare. In the game Bg5 and Ne4 traded off your defenders and the f6 point collapsed.

pv: Nxe4 Rxe4 f6 Bd2 b5 h3 Nb6 Rde1 a5 h4 Qd7 Bf4 Nc4 b3 Nxa3 R4e2
e: Nxe4 takes off white's best-placed piece before it lands on d6 or f6. After Rxe4 f6! chases the g5 bishop away and breaks the pin on your knight, and with b5 and Nb6 to follow the position is completely level.
ep: e5 opens lines while your f6 knight is still pinned against the rook on e7: Nxd6 Qxd6 dxe5 wins a pawn and c4 kicks the d5 knight. In the game Nxf6+ Nxf6 Bxf6 gxf6 Qxf6 stripped the king and cost material.

pv: Bg3 f3 Qf4 Nc5 Rh6 Qg4+ Qxg4 fxg4 Bxe1 Rxe1 Rh1+ Kf2 Rxe1 Kxe1 Re7 Ke2
e: Bg3! rescues the bishop from the corner while keeping it aimed at the rook on e1 — and it covers the g4 square where white's queen wants to check. After f3 Qf4 Nc5 Rh6 the attack arrives in the right order: Bxe1 followed by Rh1+ picks up a whole rook.
ep: Rh6 first allows Qg4+, and with g4 still uncovered the rook has to trudge back: Rg6 Qf5 Rf6 Qg4+ is a repetition, which is precisely how the game ended.

pv: a4 Qb6 Ra3 Qa5 Kf1 Ne8 Nf3 Nd6 g3 Nf6 Kg2 Nf7 Ne5 Nxe5 Bxe5 Ne4
e: a4 takes b5 away from Black's queenside expansion and keeps the flexible setup: Ra3 is available to swing the rook along the third rank, and you keep the option of Nf3, Bd3 or the kingside advance. Nothing is committed yet, whereas the bishop trade on h6 is a one-way decision.
ep: Bh6 trades your good dark-squared bishop and, because the recapture would be with the h1 rook, that rook ends up stranded on h6 where ...e5! hits back with tempo. In the game Black played ...e5 straight away and after Bxg7 Kxg7 the ...exd4 and ...Ng4 sequence handed him the initiative.

pv: Ne5 Qe7 Qg5 Nxf2 Rh4 Ng8 Rxh7+ Kxh7 Qxg6+ Kh8 Qh5+ Kg7 Qg6+
e: Ne5 hits the knight on g4 and, more importantly, clears the way for Qg5 with a real attack. That gives you the saving resource: after Qe7 Qg5 Nxf2 Rh4 Ng8 comes Rxh7+! Kxh7 Qxg6+ Kh8 Qh5+ with a perpetual, because the king on g7 has no cover on the h-file and g6 squares.
ep: Ng5 leaves f2 undefended with your king still on e1: ...Nxf2 Rf1 N6g4 wins the pawn and after Bxg4 Nxg4 the king can never settle. The knight on g5 generates no threat of its own to compensate.

pv: Rf1 N2g4 O-O-O Qc7 Rde1 Bd7 Bxg4 Bxg4 b3 Rae8 Kb2 Rxe1 Rxe1 Qd6 Re5 Nd7
e: Rf1 confronts the intruder: the knight on f2 is hit by the rook and has to go back (N2g4), and that single tempo lets you finally solve the king with O-O-O. From there Rde1 and Bxg4 untangle everything and the extra pressure on the e-file gives you a game again.
ep: Rh2 leaves the f2 knight sitting in your camp for free and puts the rook where a second knight can hit it: after Qd6 Nf3 N6g4 the rook on h2 falls (Nxh2), and in the game Bg4 followed by ...Qd6 and ...Qxg3+ tore the position open.

pv: Nxh7 Bh5 Nxf8 Qxf8 Qf4 N6g4 Qxf8+ Rxf8 Bxg4 Nxg4 Rh3 Rf2 O-O-O Rxg2 Rdh1 Nh6
e: Nxh7! is a fork, not a pawn grab: from h7 the knight attacks the rook on f8 and the knight on f6 at the same time. After Bh5 Nxf8 Qxf8 Qf4 you have won the exchange and the queen on f4 keeps hitting both black knights, so Qxf8+ Rxf8 Bxg4 wins another one back.
ep: Bxg4 releases all the tension and takes the piece that wasn't the point; ...Qd6 then brings the last black piece into the attack against your stranded king, and g3 N2xg4 Re2 Qxg3+ followed in the game.

pv: Ne6+ Kg8 Rxh7 N2xg4 Rg7+ Kh8 O-O-O Qxe6 Rxg6 Rf7 Re1 Qf5 Rg5 Qh7 Ne2 Ne4
e: Ne6+ comes with check and forks the king and the rook on f8, which is exactly the tempo you need. After Kg8 Rxh7 you pick up a pawn and threaten Rg7+; then O-O-O finally gets the king out of the centre, and Rxg6 gives real counterplay for the material.
ep: The bishop on g4 is attacked by both black knights and defended by nothing, and g3 doesn't change that: ...N6xg4 simply takes it. In the game ...N2xg4 came, and after Re2 Qxg3+ your king had no cover left.

pv: Qxa2 Qc1 Qa4 Qc8+ Kh7 Qc6 Qa1+ Bc1 f6 g4 Be4 Nd7 Kg6 h4 Bf4 Nf8+

e: The g-pawn is the fastest thing on the board, so start it: g4, and after d5 g3 a7 g2 Kc2 g1=Q a8=Q Nxa8 your knight takes the new queen off and the bishop stops the d-pawn. Played that way it is mate in 9.
ep: Kf2 escorts the pawn but costs the tempo the race cannot spare — after Kd2 white's king reaches the pawn's path and the forced finish is gone. The position is still winning, just far slower.

pv: e5 Nh5 Bh6 dxe5 dxe5 Bxe5 Nf3 Qc7 Nxe5 Nxe5 Be2 Be6 Rhe1 Nf6 Bg7 Rg8
e: e5! strikes at f6 before Black's queenside play exists: after Nh5 Bh6 trades the g7-bishop, and dxe5 dxe5 Bxe5 Nf3 regains the pawn with a big lead in development and pressure on the d-file (best line, +1.3). In mutual-attack setups, the first central break sets the pace.
ep: h4 gives Black a free move for b5!: after e5 b4 the c3-knight gets booted to b1 before your attack lands a blow (punish line), and the game's b5, Qa5 and b4 told the same story — the race slipped away one tempo at a time, from +1.3 to dead level.

pv: Na2 Rb8 Ne2 c5 Kb1 Qb6 axb4 cxb4 Bh6 Bxh6 Qxh6 a5 Nac1 a4 h5 Rg8
e: Na2! is the retreat that fights: it attacks b4 immediately, so Black must spend time on the pawn, and after Rb8 Ne2 c5 Kb1 you untangle and capture on b4 under good conditions (best line, +0.1). A retreating piece should still bite something.
ep: Nb1 bites nothing: Rb8 comes with a free hand, and the h5/c5 clamp in the punish line shows Black taking over on both wings (-1.1). In the game axb4 Qxb4 Qxb4 Rxb4 traded into an ending where the b1-knight was still looking for a square.

pv: g4 Nxd4 cxd4 c5 Bc3 cxd4 Bxd4 Rc6+ Kb1 Nxe5 Bb5 Rc7 h5 f5 h6 Bh8
e: g4! puts the question to the f5-knight. The desperado Nxd4 doesn't save it: cxd4 c5 Bc3! cxd4 Bxd4 keeps everything together, and after Rc6+ Kb1 Nxe5 comes Bb5!, hitting the c6-rook — White emerges a piece for two pawns up with h5 rolling (+1.7).
ep: Bxf5 gxf5 hands over your best minor piece and repairs Black's structure: the new f5-pawn controls e4 and g4, and the punish line's h5 h6 Kh7 shows the attack hitting a wall (+0.4 from +1.7). Keep the bishop and make the knight move instead.

pv: e6 fxe6 Nxe6 Rg8 Re1 Bf6 Rxg8+ Kxg8 h5 Kh7 Bf4 Kg8 Nc2 Bc4 Ne3 Bd3
e: e6! is what the e5-pawn was for: after fxe6 Nxe6 the knight lands on a monster square hitting g7 and f8 — best line Rg8 Re1 Bf6 Rxg8+ Kxg8 h5! and White's pieces pour in (+2.0). A pawn that opens lines for every piece behind it is never a sacrifice.
ep: Nh5 attacks g7 once — and it's well defended; Rg8 shores everything up and the knight becomes the piece that gets neutralized (the game's Rxg8+ Kxg8 released all your pressure, +0.7). The e6 break had to come while f7 was still tied to defense.

pv: Rg1
e: Rg1 saves the attacked rook and loads the g-file behind the g4-pawn: now Bxf3? loses to gxf5+! — a discovered check from the g1-rook — and after fxe6 and Nf4 you win the material back with interest. Black's stray e2-bishop is left misplaced deep in your camp (+0.3).
ep: gxf5 concedes the exchange: Bxd1, and even the correct recapture Nxd1 leaves you worse after c5! (punish line). In the game Kxd1 followed and Rxb2 made it two problems — down rook for bishop with an enemy rook loose on your second rank (-1.5).

pv: Nxd1 c5 Kc2 cxd4 cxd4 Nb8 Ne3 Be7 Ng4 Nc6 Bc3 Bxh4 Nxh6+ Kf8 f4 Nb4+
e: Nxd1! recaptures while keeping b2 covered — the knight guards b2 from d1 and later reroutes via e3 to g4, hitting h6 (the best line ends with Nxh6+). Down the exchange you're worse (-1.4), but the position stays closed and the b6-rook has no entry square.
ep: Kxd1 drops b2 on the spot: Rxb2! plants the rook on your second rank, where it teamed up with the a-pawn to eat the queenside — the game's fxe6 fxe6 didn't slow it down (-2.8). When two recaptures exist, count what each one stops defending.

pv: Kh8 Nb3 f6 Ne1 Nf5 g3 Nxe3 fxe3 g5 Nd3 Ne7 Bf3 e5 dxe5 fxe5 Bg2
e: Kh8 is the professional move: it steps off the g1-a7 diagonal and prepares f6 — the plan is f6, Nf5 and Nxe3, trading White's good bishop, with e5 to follow and the centre opening on your terms (+0.9). In this symmetric Exchange Caro structure, small preparing moves beat committal pawn pushes.
ep: b5? just gives up a pawn: Bxb5 takes it, and the pressure on b2 and the b-file never adds up to full compensation (-0.3). The game showed it — Bxb5 Qb6 Qa4 Rfb8 Bxc6 Qxc6 and after the queen trade White simply kept the extra pawn while you ground uphill.

pv: Nb5 Nhf3 Nxa3 Ra1 Nb5 Rfc1 f6 g3 Bf8 Nf1 Rc8 Bd2 a3 Ra2 Be4 Rca1
e: Nb5! converts your worst piece into the hero: from b5 the knight attacks a3 and c3, and a3 cannot be held — Nxa3, and after Ra1 the knight returns to b5 while your a4-pawn becomes a protected passer (+3.0). The route a7-b5-a3-b5 looks slow, but White has no counterplay to punish it.
ep: Rc8 gives White the tempo for c4!, when c5 pushes your d6-bishop around and seals the queenside with your knight still stuck on a7 — the a3-target and the b5-square, the whole basis of your advantage, both disappear. In the game White missed it with Nhf3 and your Nb5 landed anyway.

pv: dxe5 Nxg4 Nf3 f6 Rg1 Qe7 Qd4 Bf5 exf6 Nxf6 O-O-O Nbd7 e4 dxe4 Nh4 Be6
e: dxe5! recaptures with the pawn, hitting the f6-knight and keeping the f4-bishop. The g4-pawn is only lent out: after Nxg4 Nf3 and Rg1 the g4-knight itself becomes the target, and your rook takes over the open g-file with a strong initiative (+1.3).
ep: Bxe5 wins the same pawn on a square black can hit: Nxg4! grabs your g-pawn and attacks the e5-bishop in the same breath. After Nf3 Nxe5 Nxe5 the game had simply traded back to equality (+0.1).

pv: Bxe6 fxe6 Qh5+ g6 Qg4 O-O-O Ne2 Rhe8 h5 gxh5 Rxh5 d4 Nxd4 Qxa2 Nb3 Rxd1+

ep: e4 allows the freeing sequence Bxc3 Qxc3 Qxc3 bxc3 — the queen trade drains your initiative — and dxe4 then nets a pawn while your c-pawns sit doubled (-0.7). In the game black castled instead and the chances stayed balanced.

pv: Qe2 Ne7 O-O-O Qd6 Qe3 Nd7 Re1 Nb6 Kb1 Kd7 a3 Rae8 Nge2 Kc7 Nc1 Kb8
e: Qe2 keeps developing toward O-O-O and leaves the kingside tension alone: with pawns on f4, g4 and h4 you keep both gxh5 and g5 as options, and Black has to stay ready for both. Committing the pawns was the only way to go wrong here.
ep: g5 hands over f5 forever: Ne7-f5 lands on the hole, attacking d4 and h4, and no pawn can ever chase it away - exactly what happened in the game (Ne7, then Nf5 after the bishop trade). One push turned your space into a permanent weakness.

pv: Qxf8 Rxf8 Rhe1 Rxe5 fxe5 Nc7 Rd1 Ne6 a3 Nf4 Rd2 Ra8 Kb1 Rb8 Kc1
e: Qxf8 Rxf8 gets your queen out of the far corner with a trade: after Rhe1 Rxe5 fxe5 the e5-wedge and your active rooks hold everything level. The g7-queen had done its job - one more move there and it becomes a liability to tactics on e5.
ep: Qf6 leaves the e5-rook overloaded: Rxe5! fxe5 Re8, and since Qd6+ Qxd6 exd6 Kxd6 trades queens anyway, Black simply emerges a clean pawn up in the ending. In the game Black played Rae8 instead and let you keep fighting.

pv: Rxd5+ Kc7 Qd6+ Kb7 Re5 Rxe5 Qxf8 Rxf8 fxe5 Re8 Re1 Nc7 Rd1 Kb6 Ne2 Nd5
e: Rxd5+! wins a central pawn with check, and capturing loses more: cxd5 opens the sixth rank, so Qxa6! scoops the stranded knight and Qxb5+ with Qxa4 strips the queenside, all with check. After the better Kc7, Qd6+ Kb7 Re5 forces the queen trade a healthy pawn up.
ep: Nxd5 drops material to Rxe5!: after fxe5 Re6 your queen is trapped - every escape square loses it - so Qxe6+ fxe6 is forced, leaving you rook and knight against the queen. Nf6+ wins a tempo, nothing more. In the game Black played Re6 at once and you escaped the worst.

pv: Qxa8+ Kd7 Rd1+ Bd6 Qb7+ Qc7 Qxc7+ Kxc7 Kxf1 c4 Kf2 Bc5 Ne2 a5 f4 Re8
e: Take the rook first, the bishop is not going anywhere: Qxa8+ Kd7 Rd1+ Bd6 Qb7+ Qc7 Qxc7+ Kxc7 and only now Kxf1. You come out a full rook up with queens off, which is the cleanest possible version of the position.
ep: Kxf1 grabs the bishop but gives Black the move he needs: Rd8 saves the rook and activates it, and after Qc6+ his king runs to safety while your extra material has shrunk to almost nothing.

pv: Rd1 Qc7 Qxc7 Rxc7 Ne2 c4 Rg1 Bc5 Rg4 Rd7 Nd4 Rd5 Ke2 f5 Rg5 Bxd4
e: With extra material the recipe is to trade: Rd1 contests the only open file and offers the exchange of Black's active rook. After Qc7 Qxc7 Rxc7 Ne2 you develop the last piece, the king walks out, and the extra piece decides the ending.
ep: Qxf6 wins a pawn but takes the queen away from the defence and hands Black the initiative: Rg8 and Rd2 flood the second rank, and after Ne2 Qb5 Kf2 Rd2 in the game the attack was worth far more than the pawn.

pv: Qf5 Be7 Qxh7 Rg6 Qh8+ Bf8 c4 Qxc4 Qc3 Qh4 Nf4 Rgd6 Re1 Rd1 Ke2 R7d2+
e: Qf5 hits two things at once: the rook on d7 along the f5-d7 diagonal and the h7 pawn. Black must block with Be7, and then Qxh7 wins a pawn while harassing the g8 rook with Qh8+, keeping your queen active instead of drifting.
ep: Kf2 steps onto the g-file in front of the rook and allows Rg2+, when capturing runs into Qxe2+ picking up the knight with check. The game's Rd2 was just as unpleasant, with the rook on the seventh forever.

pv: Rae1 Qd3 h4 Rg6 c4 Re6 Qc3 Rxe3 Qxd3 Rexd3 Kg3 Kd7 Kg4 Rxb2 Nf4 Rd4
e: Bring the other rook: Rae1 supports the pinned knight on e2 while leaving the h1 rook guarding the corner and h2. After Qd3 h4 Rg6 c4 your king is safe and the extra pawn structure holds, whereas the kingside is the one place you cannot afford to strip.
ep: Rhe1 leaves h1 and the corner completely unguarded, and Black went straight at it: Qxb2 Rab1 Rxe2+ Rxe2 Qxb1 and finally Qg1 mate. Every defender of the first rank near your king was gone.

pv: Re1 Qxa2+ Re2 Qb1 Re1 Qc2+ Re2 Qc1 Re1 Qd2+ Re2 Rg2+ Kxg2 Qxe2+ Kg1 Qe1+
e: The immediate threat is Qg1 mate, supported by the rook on g8, so the rook must cover g1: Re1 does it. Black can chase with Qxa2+ Re2 Qb1 Re1 but nothing more, and the repetition keeps you alive in a position where the alternative is instant defeat.
ep: c4 is a developing pawn move in a position where you were being mated: Qg1# ends it at once, the queen protected by the rook down the g-file and the king with no square on e1, f1, g2 or g3.

pv: Bxd6 Nd7 Bxc5 Nxc5 Nxc5 Qxc5 Qd4 Qxd4 cxd4 h5 e3 Rh6 Bd3 Rb6 b3 a5
e: Recapture order matters: Bxd6 keeps the knight on e4 where it hits c5 and d6, and after Nd7 Bxc5 Nxc5 Nxc5 Qxc5 Qd4! forces the queens off with a clean extra pawn and a much better structure. Trading your worst piece for black's best is the wrong way round.
ep: Nxd6+ lets black recapture with the bishop, Bxd6 Bxd6, giving up his worst piece; then Qxb2 grabs the pawn and trades queens on c1, and a nearly winning edge shrinks to a small pull. That is how the game went.

pv: Rd1 Rc8 Nf6+ Nd6 Ne4 Rxc2 Nf3 Rxb2 exd6 g6 e3 Bg7 Bd3 Bxa2 O-O a5
e: Rd1 lines the rook up on the d-file behind the d5-knight, so every knight move becomes a discovered check on the d8-king. After Rc8 Nf6+ Nd6 Ne4 White keeps all three extra pawns while Black's rooks never get organised (+3.8). Develop the last rook to the file the enemy king is stuck on.
ep: Nf4 abandons the d5 outpost and invites Bb4+ with tempo: c3 Nxc3 and the knight is loose in White's camp chewing on a2 and e2. White still untangles with Nxe6+ fxe6 a3 Ba5 e3, but +3.8 has become +1.9 — a lot of the win handed back for one knight move.

pv: Nxe6+ fxe6 a3 Ba5 Nf3 Ke7 e3 Rhd8 b4 Bb6 Rc1 Rac8 Be2 h6 g3 Nd5
e: Nxe6+! Take the bishop with check first — the king on d8 has to recapture fxe6, shattering Black's kingside and leaving him with three pawn islands. Only then a3 kicks the b4-bishop, and after Ba5 Nf3 e3 White is a pawn up with the far better structure (+1.9).

pv: Bxf3 Qd2 f6 Bh4 Bg4 O-O Bf5 g4 Bxg4 exf6 Nxf6 f3 Bh5 Bxc6+ bxc6 Rae1
e: Bxf3! removes the g5-bishop's only defender: however White recaptures, ...Qxg5 follows — your d8-queen sees g5 down the cleared diagonal — and wins a full piece. White's best is to desert the knight with Qd2 (guarding g5), when ...f6 and ...Bg4 keep the extra piece with an easy game (+3.6).
ep: Qb6 steps off the d8–g5 diagonal and defuses your own threat — with the queen gone from d8, Bxf3 no longer wins a piece because the recapture isn't met by ...Qxg5. White consolidated with Be3 in the game and the chance never came back (+0.5).

pv: Rxc3+ Kb2 Qa3+ Kb1 Nxe3 fxe3 O-O Rc1 Rd3 Qb2 Qxb2+ Kxb2 Rxe3 Rhd1 Re2+ Rc2
e: Capture with the rook: Rxc3+! wins the pawn with the queens staying on — after Kb2 Qa3+ Kb1 Nxe3 fxe3 you castle, double with ...Rd3, and White's bare king faces a permanent attack from queen and rooks (+4.2). The point of the capture order is that White never gets to trade queens.

pv: Nxe3 Rxc4 Nxc4 Nh5 Nc6 f4 Na3 Rf1 Kf8 f5 exf5 Rxf5 Nb4+ Kd2 Nc4+ Ke2
e: Nxe3! wins the bishop clean, courtesy of the doubled c-file rooks: fxe3?? loses a rook to ...Rxc1 Rxc1 Rxc1 — the last capture on c1 has no reply — and Kxe3 meets the same. White's best is Rxc4, but your e3-knight recaptures with Nxc4: bishop banked, rooks traded evenly, a full piece up (+5.3).
ep: Rxc1 lets the bishop off the hook: the game's Bxc1! recapture rescued the loose e3-bishop — the piece the whole position was pointing at. You stayed better (+2.8), but ...Nxe3 first won it outright; release the c-file tension only after cashing in on e3.

pv: Rc4 Bb2 Nc6 Ne2 Nb4+ Kd2 Nxa2 g4 Nh4 f4 Nb4 h3 g5 Rc1 a5 fxg5
e: Rc4! puts the rook on its dream square: it presses d4 and ties White down, and only then do the knights maneuver — ...Nc6, ...Nb4+ and ...Nxa2 wins a pawn while White's pieces are stuck guarding d4 (+4.0). Activity in the right order: rook first, knights second.
ep: Nc6 lets White coordinate with Ne2, after which d4 is solid and your knights need a long, slow tour (...Nh4–f3 and ...Na5 in the line) to create anything (+2.1). You found ...Rc4 two moves later in the game, but Be3 and a4 had already stabilized White's position.

pv: Kg7 Nf6 Kg6 Kd3 Nh4 Ke3 Nf5+ Kf4 Nxd4 Nd7 Nf5 Nc5 Ne7 Nb7 Kh6 Ke3
e: Kg7! turns the tables on the stranded d7-knight: after Nf6 Kg6 it's attacked again and must keep running, while your own knight reroutes ...Nh4–f5+ and removes the d4-pawn (Nxd4). With the extra pawns and the dominant king the win is routine (+5.5).
ep: h4? allows Nf6+, forking your king and the g4-pawn: ...Kg7 Nxg4 and the stray knight rescues itself with a pawn in the bargain — exactly the game (+3.4). One quiet king move first would have left it with no way home.

pv: Kg5 Ke3 Ng2+ Kf3 Ne1+ Ke2 Nc2 Kd3 Na3 Kd2 Nb5 Nd3 Nxd4 Ke3 Nc2+ Kd2
e: Kg5 covers h4, keeps White's h3-pawn fixed, and frees the knight for the winning journey: Ng2+–e1–c2–a3–b5 and Nxd4 — White's lone knight and king cannot guard d4 and cope with your advancing d- and e-pawns at the same time (+4.7).
ep: Ng6? lets the f2-knight out: Nd3 (or the game's Ng4) reaches the checking circuit around your king, and in the game Nh6+/Nf7+ forked king and e-pawn over and over — the piece that was passively tied down became a permanent nuisance, and the win shrank to +1.2.

pv: Kg5 Ke3 Nf4 Nf2 Ng2+ Kf3 Ne1+ Ke2 Nc2 Kd3 Na3 Nd1 Nb5 Ke3 Nd6 Nb2
e: Kg5! steps off the fork square and keeps the plan alive: ...Nf4 next, then the knight's march Ng2+–e1–c2–a3–b5 rounds up the d4-pawn while White's knight can only watch (+4.6). With d5 still defended by e6, White has no checks and no counterplay after this one accurate king move.
ep: e5?? abandons d5 — the e6-pawn was its only defender — so Ne3+! forks your king and the now-loose d5-pawn: Nxd5 follows and White suddenly holds (+0.5). The game's Nh6+/Nf7+ checking carousel (the f7-jump hitting e5 too) rescued White the same way.

pv: Kf6 Nd8 exd4 Nb7 Kg5 Nc5 Nf4 Nb3 d3 Ke3 Nxh3 Kxd3 Kg4 Nd2 Ng5 Nf1
e: Kf6! hits the f7-knight and only then takes: Nd8 exd4, and the knight's trek home (Nb7–c5–b3) costs so much time that ...d3! and ...Nxh3 win a second pawn — the d-pawn drags White's king away (Kxd3) while your knight cleans up the kingside (+5.2). Chase the knight first; grab d4 second.
ep: Kf5 stays on the checking grid: Nd6+! comes at once and the knight checks from d6 and f7 forever — the line even wins a pawn back with the fork Nxe4+ after ...e4 (+0.6). The game's Nh6+/Nf7+ merry-go-round was the same story; Kf6, gaining a tempo on the knight, was the way to break it.

pv: Nf3 Nc6 Be2 Qe7 O-O Rd8 h3 a6 Rb1 Ba7 b3 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bd3 Bf5
e: Nf3 brings the knight back before the center strikes: from f3 it covers d4, and Be2 with O-O follows quickly. The e5-outpost was never secure with the c5-bishop and the d5-pawn ready to roll - solid regrouping preserves your small plus.
ep: g3 invites d4!: exd4 Bxd4 hits both your knights - e5 and c3 - at the same time, and after Nc4 Nc6 Black develops with threats while Re8+ hangs over your uncastled king. In the game Re8 came first with the same effect, and you never untangled.

pv: Bg2 Nc6 h3 Bf5 O-O Qd7 Ndf4 Rad8 Nd4 Nxd4 exd4 Qa4 c3 Bc2 Qd2 Ne4
e: Bg2 was the piece that had to move: it blunts the light-square pressure, prepares O-O and frees the h1-rook. After Nc6 h3 Bf5 O-O everything is connected and the d4 break can be met in comfort.
ep: h3 is answered by Bf3! anyway: the bishop plants itself, hitting the h1-rook and tying down the e2-knight, and you are reduced to Rg1 while d4 breaks open the center against your king in the middle. The game followed exactly: Bf3, Rg1, Bxg2 and d4.

pv: e4 Nxe4 Kf1 Qd7 h4 Nf6 Bf4 Ng4 Ng1 Re6 Nf3 Rae8 Nh2 Ne3+ fxe3 dxe3
e: e4 keeps the lid on: it denies the c6-knight the d4-square and keeps the b6-bishop's diagonal blocked, and with your king stuck in the center, closed lines are everything. Even after Nxe4 Kf1 you are worse but still playing - this was damage control, and it works.
ep: exd4 opens the game at the worst moment: Nxd4 centralizes with Nf3+ looming, and after Be3 Nf3+ Kf1 Bxe3 you cannot even recapture cleanly - fxe3 Nd2+ lets the knight out with check. In the game f3 lost instantly to Nxf3+ followed by Qd7 and Qxh3.

pv: e5 Ng8 Qe1 Nb6 h3 Bf5 Rh2 h4 Bg5 Nd7 Nge2 dxe5 dxe5 Bxe5 f4 Bf6
e: e5 is the thematic break and it has to come before Black organises ...b5. It kicks the knight from f6 (the main defender of the dark squares near his king) and after Ng8 Qe1 the queen swings across to join the Bf4 in an attack while Black's pieces are stuck on the back rank.
ep: Be2 is a slow developing move in a race, and Black uses the time for Rb8 and b5, opening lines against your king on c1. In the game his queenside expansion arrived first while your own break was still a move away.

pv: e5 Ng8 Bd3 Nf8 Qf2 Bf5 Bxf5 gxf5 Be3 Qd7 Nge2 b5 Nf4 b4
e: e5 is still the move: strike in the centre while Black's rook has gone to b8. After Ng8 Bd3 Nf8 Qf2 your pieces flow to the kingside, the black knights are pushed to the back rank, and Bxf5 followed by Nf4 gives you a lasting bind.
ep: g4 is a wing move that does not stop Black's plan: b5 comes anyway and after b4 the attack on your own king on c1 gains the tempo. In the game g4 b5 g5 Ng8 a3 e5 let Black free his position while your attack never got going.

pv: e5 Nb6
e: e5 is the move the whole setup was built for: the pawn hits d6, gains space and starts opening lines while black's king still sits on e8 and his pieces are tangled on the queenside. After e5 Nb6 you keep the initiative and black never gets his own central break in on his terms. Space in the centre is what justifies the pawn storm you have started with g5.
ep: a3 is a slow luxury move in a position where every tempo counts: black gets ...e6 and then ...d5, blocking the centre and killing your attack, and in the game he simply hit back with ...e5 and traded off your strong dark-squared bishop.

pv: Bd3 Qd8 Qf2 Ne7 Nh4 Bg4 Rd2 b4 a4 b3 c3 Qc8
e: Bd3 attacks the knight on f5, which is the piece holding black's kingside together, and it does so without releasing any tension. After Qd8 Qf2 Ne7 Nh4 you keep the e5 wedge, the monster knight on f6 and the g5/h-pawn mass all pointing at the king on h8. The whole edge here comes from the pawn on e5 cramping black - keep it.

pv: Bd3 Qc7 Bxf5 Bxf5 Nd4 Bxf6 gxf6 Qc5 b3 a5 Kb2 b4 a4 Bg4 Ra1 Rbe8
e: Bd3 again goes after the f5 knight, the key defender: Qc7 Bxf5 Bxf5 Nd4 hits the bishop and keeps the bind, with the knight on f6 and the pawn on e5 still strangling black. You do not need material here - you need the black king's defenders removed.
ep: The pawn on b5 is defended by the a6 pawn, so Bxb5 simply drops a bishop. Black did not even have to hurry: ...Qb7 piled up on the b-file first, and in the game the a-pawn eventually took the bishop anyway.

pv: Kxh4 Rxf4+ Kg3 Rxf6 Rxb5 Rf1 Rb6 Rg1+ Kf4 Rg2 h4 Rxb2 b5 Kg7 Rb8 Rb1
e: Kxh4 grabs the free pawn and, more importantly, keeps your king off the a8-h1 diagonal. After Rxf4+ Kg3 Rxf6 Rxb5 you liquidate and get the b-pawn rolling with Rb6 and b5 - the passed b-pawn plus the h-pawn are the only practical chances in a position this bad.
ep: Kf3 steps straight onto the long diagonal, and Bd5+ forks your king and the rook on b7 - which is exactly what happened in the game. After Kg4 Bxb7 you are a whole rook down with nothing to show.

pv: Nc6 Qb3 Qc7 Bd2 a6 Re1 b5 Bd5 Bb7 Ng5 Nd8
e: Nc6 develops and, crucially, covers e5 — the springboard for White's Bxf7+/Ne5+ tricks against your king. With the f7 tactics ruled out you keep the extra d4-pawn, and after Qb3 Qc7 holds both f7 and b7 while you finish development with a6, b5 and Bb7.
ep: Bg4 runs into Bxf7+! Kxf7 Ne5+ — the knight check forks your king and the g4-bishop. After Ke7 Bg5+ Nf6 Qxg4 White has won a pawn and dragged your king to e7 with a raging attack. In the game White missed it and played Qb3.

pv: Bxf3
e: Bxf3! removes the piece that holds White's play together: the f3-knight supports both the e5 break and the Ng5 jump. White has to take back with gxf3, wrecking the king's pawn cover, and you stay a healthy pawn up with clear targets on the g-file.
