e: The d5-pawn is the whole endgame, and stopping it is the king's job: Ke7 heads for the blockade so the rook stays free. Even the critical Nxe5+ fxe5 Kxb5 is met by e4!, when your own passer and active rook give just enough counterplay to hold.
ep: For one move nothing stopped the pawn, and d6! would have exploited it: after Rd8 Nxe5+ fxe5 Kb4 the passer stands one step from d7, your rook is glued to d8, and White's king collects b5. Your opponent played Rd3 instead and let you back into the blockade.

pv: Kd7 Nxe5+ fxe5 Kxb5 e4 Re3 Kd6 c4 Rb8+ Ka4 Ke5 Re1 Kd4 d6 Kxc4 Rxe4+
e: Kd7 keeps the king on the d-pawn's path, which is all that matters: after Nxe5+ fxe5 Kxb5 you get e4!, and with the king harassing both white pawns the reduced material is a draw. The rook belongs on defense, not chasing checks.
ep: Rc4+ hangs the b5-pawn: Kxb5! attacks the rook, and after it retreats, Nxe5 fxe5 c4 gives White connected passed c- and d-pawns. Your opponent retreated Kb3 instead and returned the favor.

pv: Ra4 c4 Bxh2 g3 Bg1 cxb5 Rd4 Rxd4 Bxd4 Kc4 Bb6 Ne4+ Ke5 Nc5 Kd6
e: The d2-knight attacks your rook, and the escape square decides the game: Ra4! stays active on the fourth rank and out of every knight fork. If c4 next, you have Bxh2 and then Rd4!, forcing the rook trade into a dead-drawn minor-piece ending.
ep: Rc5 steps onto the one square where the knight wins it outright: Ne4+! forks king and rook, and after Kc7 Nxc5 the knight can't even be captured — a whole rook gone for nothing. That is exactly how the game continued.

pv: f5 Nf2 c5 Nd3 Nxe3 Nxb4 cxd4 Rc1+ Kb8 g3 Rc8 Rxc8+ Kxc8 Kd3 a5 Nxd4
e: This is a race for the f5 square. ...f5! stops white's own f4-f5 forever, freezes the e5 pawn and takes the g4/f5 squares away from his knights; then ...c5 hits d4 and after Nd3 Nxe3 Nxb4 cxd4 black's pieces are the active ones. The knight on d5 is a monster only as long as white cannot dislodge it.
ep: Rhd8 is natural but a tempo too slow: white plays f5! himself, and once he owns that square his knights get e4-d6/g5 and black's kingside pawns are frozen for good.

pv: f5 exf6 gxf6 Rf1 Rg7 Rf2 Re7 Ne5 c5 dxc5 fxe5 f5 Nxe3 Kxe3 Rc7 Rc2
e: ...f5! again: after exf6 gxf6 black gets a mobile central mass and the half-open g-file, with the rook swinging to g7 and the knight on d5 still untouchable. Keeping that knight and opening a file toward the white king is the plan - white's whole position hangs on the e5 pawn.
ep: Nc3+ trades off your best piece for white's passive knight, and after Nxc3 Bxc3 the bishop gets chased by Rc1 while white gets g4 and f5 in for free. Both happened in the game and the advantage vanished.

pv: d3+ Ke3 Re8 Bf4 Bxe5 Nxe5 f6 Rc1+ Kb8 Bg3 fxe5 Rd1 d2 Rxd2 Rxd2 Kxd2
e: d3+! pushes the passed pawn with check and, crucially, denies the white king the d3 blockade square. After Ke3 Re8 Bf4 Bxe5 Nxe5 f6 the pawn on d3 ties white down completely - Rc1+ Kb8 and ...d2 forces material. Passed pawns must be pushed, especially when the push comes with check.
ep: Re8 hands white the square he needs: Kd3! plants the king in front of the pawn, and after Bf4 the d-pawn is dead and white's own f/g/h pawns start rolling - just as in the game.

pv: b5 g5
e: b5! is a queenside pawn move with a defensive point: it takes c4 away from the white king before it can march to c4 and b3, and it gains space so the bishop on a3 keeps its support. Your trump is the passed d4 pawn - it only survives while white's king stays out and the bishop keeps guarding it from a3.
ep: Kd7 does nothing about white's plan: Kc4! heads for b3, when the bishop on a3 runs out of squares and ...Bxb4 is forced. In the game Rb1-b3 achieved the same thing and the d-pawn fell soon after.

pv: a5 bxa5 Kc8 h5 Be7 Rb3 R8d7 Rb5 Rd8 Rxd5 Rxd5 f6 gxf6 Bxh6 fxe5 Bg7
e: a5! hits the b4 pawn while your bishop on a3 still has something to do: after bxa5 Kc8 the a-pawns are weak and the rooks get the open b-file, so black stays in the game. The problem to solve is that the bishop on a3 has almost no squares, so you must create play for it now rather than wait.
ep: Ke7 ignores Rb3, which traps the bishop on a3 - ...Bxb4 Bxb4+ is then forced, and after Bd6 white's bishop dominates the board while the b7/a6 pawns drop off. That is precisely the game continuation.

pv: Bxf6 exf6 Bd3 axb5 Rxh7 Rxh7 Bxh7 Bd6 Qd3 Nb4 Qf5 c5
e: Bxf6! removes the defender of the h7-bishop: after ...exf6 Bd3 lines up against it, and if ...axb5 (taking your knight) then Rxh7! Rxh7 Bxh7 wins the piece straight back — you emerge with the better structure and the safer king (+2.1).
ep: Nc3 saves the knight but leaves c2 loose: ...Bxc2! hits the queen, and after Rxh8 Bxd1 Rxd1 White has traded queen and pawn for rook and bishop — most of the advantage gone (+0.9). In the game ...Nb4! hit the same weak square and a3? Nxc2+ forked king and rook.

pv: Bxf6 exf6 Bd3 Nxd3+ cxd3 f5 gxf5 Qg5 Qe2 Qxf5 O-O-O Qf6 Qg2 c6 f4 Bf5
e: Black threatens ...Nxc2+, and Bxf6! answers with a counterattack: after ...exf6 you have Bd3!, offering the trade that removes the b4-knight — ...Nxd3+ cxd3 — and the c2 fork is history. Your grip on the h-file against the h7-bishop then gives a clear pull (+1.9).
ep: a3 attacks the knight a tempo too late: ...Nxc2+! forks king and rook anyway — the a3-pawn doesn't cover c2 — and after Kf2 Nxa1 Black has won rook and pawn for the knight (-1.2). The game continued exactly so (Qxa1 Bg7).

pv: Nh5 Ne4 dxe4 Bxe3 Bxf3 Rf2 Bxg2+ Rxg2 exd3 d5 Ng3+ Kg1 Ne2+ Rxe2
e: Nh5! tightens the net: the g4-bishop pins the f3-knight (hxg4 runs into Nxg4 with Nf2+ in the air), and the knight adds Ng3+ - grabbing with Qxb7?? even loses to Ng3+ Kh2 Nxf1+ Kh1 Qh2+! Nxh2 Ng3 mate. White's best is Ne4, but dxe4 Bxe3 Bxf3! still wins material: after Rf2 Bxg2+ Rxg2 exd3 you're pawns up with a passer on d3 (+5.0).
ep: Qf4 covers the bishops but lets White unpin with Ne1!, when the g4-bishop really is hanging to h3 and the attack stalls (+0.1). In the game Qxb7! made the same point another way: it forked the c6-knight and a8-rook, and after O-O Qxc6 the advantage was gone.

pv: Nh5 Rf2
e: You're a piece down, so the attack is everything. Nh5! keeps it alive: the knight covers g3, renewing Qg3 and Ng3+ threats against the h1-king, and White must find Rf2 just to survive - even then you stand better (+1.2). Any slow move lets White unpin and cash the piece.
ep: Qh6 trades the mating attack for a threat against c1 that White parries with Nb3 - or the game's Ng1!, unpinning. After the d2 trades you grabbed Qxd2, but Bxh7+! Kxh7 hxg4 won both bishops back: compensation gone, White simply up material (-2.6).

pv: Qh6+ Kg1 Qe3+ Kh1 Rh8 Qxa8 Qh6+ Kg1 Rxa8 Rae1 Rh8 Rf2 Rb8
e: Qh6+ wins by force: after Kg1 Qe3+ Kh1 Rh8! the queen, rook and g4-knight surround the bare king, and the threat of Qh6+ Nh2 (forced block) Qxh2# cannot be met. White's only try is the desperado Qxa8, and after Qh6+ Kg1 Rxa8 you emerge a full queen for rook ahead (+6.3).
ep: Nf2+ trades away the piece the attack runs on: after Kg1 the knight has no follow-up — Nh3+ gxh3 just loses it, as happened in the game — and without the g4-knight there is no mate on h2. Best case is bailing out with Qxb2 into a queen-shuffle draw.

pv: Qxb2 Ng5+ Kg6 Rab1 Qc2 Nxf7 Rxf7 Qxa8 Qxc3 Rb7 Rxb7 Qxb7 Qxd4 Rxf2 Qd1+ Kh2
e: Qxb2 grabs a pawn and, crucially, defends your f2-knight along the second rank. After Ng5+ Kg6 Rab1 Qc2 Nxf7 Rxf7 Qxa8 Qxc3 the tactics burn out to rough equality — the knight was never actually trapped.
ep: Nh3+ simply loses the knight to gxh3: the follow-up Qe3+ never regains the piece, and the game's Qe3+ Kg2 left you a knight for a pawn down with White's king walking to safety.

pv: Kh7 Qb5 f6 Qd3+ Kg8 Ng4 Qh4 Re2 a5 Kh2 Rab8 Rg2 Kh8 c4 dxc4 Qxc4
e: Kh7 retreats before White's pieces coordinate: the h4+ tricks lose their sting, and after Qb5 f6 the e5-knight gets evicted. You are a piece down either way (-4.2), but the king stays out of the mating net and you can keep resisting.
ep: On g5 the king is snared by h4+!: after Kh5, Qa6 leaves no useful move — Kxh4 walks into Rh1+ Kg5 Rxh6, winning your queen. In the game White grabbed Rxf7 instead, but the attack crashed through regardless.

pv: Kh5 Qa6 Qg5+ Kh1 Qh4 Qe2+ Kh6 Rg1 Qxh3+ Qh2 Qxh2+ Kxh2 Rxf7 Nxf7+ Kh7 Ne5
e: Kh5 steps out of the knight checks and heads for a queen trade: Qg5+ comes next, and after Qa6 Qg5+ Kh1 Qh4 Qe2+ Kh6 you pick up h3 and force Qxh2+ Kxh2; Rxf7 Nxf7+ then reaches an endgame a piece down (-5.0) but with every mating idea extinguished.
ep: Rh8 allows Nf3+! Kg6 Rxe6+ — the checks strip the king bare, and Ne5+ followed by Qxa8+ and Rxh6+ wins rook and queen, with mate in 10 behind it. The game's Re3 was slower, but Qxe6+ and Qxg6# arrived all the same.

pv: Kh5 Qxe6 Qe4+ Kf1
e: Kh5 leaves the sixth rank, so Qxe6 comes without check — and you answer with the counter Qe4+, hitting the e5-knight and forcing Kf1. Still lost a piece down (-4.6), but the immediate mating attack stalls out.
ep: On h6 Qxe6+ lands with check along the sixth rank and it is mate in 4: g6 was met by Qxg6# in the game, and the block Qf6 fails to Rxf6+ Kh7 Rf5 with Qg6# next.

pv: Nxd5
e: Just take the central pawn with Nxd5 while Black is still undeveloped. It removes the pawn that gives his position its shape, and any recapture leaves you with the pleasant c5 wedge and the Bf4 raking d6 without Black having a single active piece.
ep: Nb5 chases an outpost instead of a pawn, and Black frees himself with e5!, hitting the Bf4 with tempo. Nd6+ is no threat at all since Bxd6 cxd6 just leaves a weak pawn on d6 and Black's centre solved, as the game confirmed.

pv: Nc4 Bb6 Qd6+ Ke8 O-O-O Be6 Bd3 Bc7 Qa3 Qe7 Ne2 h5 Ng3 Qxa3 Nxa3 Rg8
e: The bishop on e3 has no defenders, so hit it: Nc4 attacks it and simultaneously brings the knight out of the awkward d6 outpost. After Bb6 Qd6+ Ke8 you have gained the time you needed to castle long and connect the rooks with an extra piece on the board.
ep: Rd1 ignores the loose bishop and lets Black take over: Be6 hits your queen, and after Qb5 Nd4 the knight lands with tempo while your Nd6 and Ng1 both hang in the air. The game version Be6 Qe4 Bxg1 cost you material straight away.

pv: Ke1 Rc8 Qd6+ Ke8 Ba6 h5 Rf1 h4 c4 Bxc4 Bxc4 Qxb7 Ba6 Rc1+ Kf2 Rxf1+
e: You are a piece up, so the only job is to find the square where the queen has no checks. Ke1 tucks the king behind its own pieces; after Rc8 Qd6+ Ke8 Ba6 you develop with tempo and the extra knight simply wins.
ep: Ke3 walks into the open board and Black gets a stream of checks: the game showed Qc1+ Kf2 Qd2+ Kg3 Qf4+ with a repetition, and the whole extra piece evaporated because the king had no shelter.

pv: Be2 Rc8 Qa4 Qxc3 Qxa7 Rc7 Qb6 f5 Rd1 h5 h4 Qc6 Qb4+ Kf6 Nd8 Qc5+
e: Block the check with the piece that also stays useful: Be2 interposes, guarded by the king, and after Rc8 Qa4 you get Qxa7 or Qb6 with your extra knight still on b7 and the black king exposed. Everything holds together and there are no more checks.
ep: Kg3 walks into Qe1#: the bishop on e6 covers g4 and h3 along the c8-h3 diagonal, and the e5 pawn takes f4, so the king has no flight square. Black missed it and played Qf4+ instead, but the escape was pure luck.

pv: h4 f4 Nd6 fxg3+ Kg2 Qxh4 Ne4+ Kg6 Rh1 Qf4 Nxg3 Bb3
e: h4 is the useful move before pushing pieces: it props up g3, the only shield in front of your king, and stops the black queen from using g5. Then after f4 you have Nd6, hitting f5 and f7, with Ne4+ coming and Rh1 joining the attack.
ep: Kg2 is a wasted tempo and lets Black in first with Qe3: after Kf1 Rc8 Qd6 Rxc3 the c-pawn drops and his rook is suddenly active behind your position, which is exactly the counterplay h4 was meant to prevent.

pv: Qf3
e: Qf3! puts the question to the stray g4-knight while developing: the queen eyes d5 and f7, the f1-bishop keeps its natural d3 square, and nothing is committed. White keeps a small, clean pull (+0.4) - the knight was never worth chasing with a piece you actually need.
ep: Bh3 commits the good bishop to a chase that wins nothing: Bxc3+! bxc3 wrecks your queenside first, and the knight can simply drop back (the punish line has Nf6 and your bishop retreating to f1). In the game h5! propped the knight up and you traded the bishop off instead (-0.8).

pv: a4 Qe7 Qe2 Bf5 f3 Nh6 e4 dxe4 Bxf5 Nxf5 Qxe4 O-O Qxe7 Nxe7 Kd2 Nf5
e: Don't take - the g4-knight is propped by h5 but attacks nothing. a4! gains space and keeps the light-squared bishop for the real fight: after Qe7 Qe2 Bf5 f3 Nh6 e4! you open the centre on your terms and trade bishops only on f5 (-0.3, fully playable).
ep: Bxg4 hxg4 is what Black wants: his rook gets the half-open h-file, your only light-squared bishop is gone, and e3 turns tender - the punish line ends with Bf5, Qe7 and Qxe3+ winning the pawn (-1.5). In the game f3 Bf5 followed and Black sat comfortably on the light squares.

pv: exd4 Nc7 Re1+ Kd7 Re5 Kc8 Rxf5 gxf5 Qg7 b6 Qxf7 Qd7 Qxd7+ Kxd7 Ng6 Rhg8
e: Recapture with the e-pawn: exd4 keeps the c-file closed in front of your king and opens the e-file for your rook instead. After Nc7, Re1+ Kd7 Re5 hits d5 and f5, and even Rxf5 gxf5 Qg7 works, winning back the kingside pawns with Ng6 hitting the h8-rook at the end. Which file opens is a king-safety question: your king lives around c1-d2, so the e-file is the right one to open (-0.8 but fully playable).
ep: cxd4 opens the c-file straight at your own king: Rc8! seizes it, and after Kd1 Nb4 the invasion plays itself — c3 Rxc3! wins the pawn anyway, since Be1 Rc4 Bxb4 Rxb4 leaves your queenside falling apart. In the game Qa5+ and Rc8 gave Black the same c-file attack.

pv: Rae1 g5 e4 dxe4 fxe4 gxf4 exf5+ Kd8 Qb3 Rc7 d5 Rd7 Rd1 Qxd5+ Qxd5 Rxd5+
e: Rae1 puts a rook behind the e-pawn and makes the central break work: after g5, e4! dxe4 fxe4 gxf4 exf5+ regains the piece — that last capture is a discovered check from the e1-rook down the freshly opened file, so Black never gets to keep the extra knight. The a1-rook was the one without a job; the c-file is blocked by your own c3-pawn.
ep: Rhc1 develops a rook onto a file your own c3-pawn blocks, and it abandons the centre: g5! kicks the f4-knight, and after e4 dxe4 fxe4 Bxe4 the pawn simply falls — without a rook on e1 the e4-push has no discovered-check punch. In the game g5 came at once and gxf4 soon won the knight.

pv: Nd3 Bxd3 Kxd3 Qa6+ c4 dxc4+ Kd2 Rh6 e4 Rf6 d5 Ne7 Rc3 g4 Rd1 Rxf3
e: The g5-pawn attacks your f4-knight — deal with that first. Nd3! removes the attacked piece and offers to trade off Black's strong bishop: after Bxd3 Kxd3 your king blockades the centre and the c4/e4 breaks give real counterplay. Down about a pawn (-1.5) you are still fighting; down a piece you are not.
ep: Qxb7 grabs a pawn while your f4-knight hangs: gxf4 just takes it, and after e4 Rc7! the queen is kicked with tempo (Qb1) while Black keeps the extra piece. A knight for two pawns is a terrible version of the b7-grab — and in the game gxf4 landed immediately.

pv: Qb4 Qxb4 cxb4 Nf3 Rxc8+ Bxc8 b5 f6 a4 Nxh2 a5 Ng4
e: With your king on d3 under fire, trading queens is worth almost anything: Qb4! forces it — Qxb4 cxb4 removes the attacker, and after Nf3 Rxc8+ Bxc8 b5 your passed queenside pawns give practical chances even though the position stays lost (-5.7). With queens on, the king on d3 cannot survive the coming checks.
ep: cxd4 grabs the knight but opens the f1-a6 diagonal at the worst moment: Bf1+! forces Rxf1, and Qc3+ Ke2 Qe3+ Kd1 Qxd4+ Ke1 Qxa1+ collects everything with checks — mate in 10. Your opponent missed Bf1+ and played Rxc1 instead, letting you escape with the win.

pv: Qe5+ Kd8 Qxh8+ Kd7 Qc8+ Ke7 Rc7+ Kf6 Qd8+ Kg6 Qg8+ Kh6 Qf8+ Kg5 Qg7+ Kh5
e: Qe5+! is the right check: the king must go to d8, and Qxh8+ wins the whole rook with check — then Qc8+ Ke7 Rc7+ Kf6 Qd8+ and the checks never stop, the queen herding the king into the open (mate in 20). Grab the rook with check first; the attack keeps running by itself afterwards.
ep: Rc7+ lets Black block with Bd7!, when the bishop parries the check and shields the king at once — after d6+ Kf6 Qxh8+ Kg6 there is nothing better than perpetual: 0.0 from a mating position. In the game Kf6? was played instead of Bd7 and Qxh8+ kept you winning.

pv: Qg8+ Kh6 Qf8+ Kg5 Qg7+ Kh5 Qxf7+ Kg4 Qe6+ Kf3 Qxh3+ Kf2 Rc2+ Qxc2+ Kxc2 f3
e: Qg8+ hunts from behind: Kh6 Qf8+ Kg5 Qg7+ Kh5 and now Qxf7+ — the pawn falls with check, then Qe6+ and Qxh3+ strip every shelter square; the rook only appears at the end (Rc2+) to remove Black's queen. Mate in 14, and every gaining check comes in the right order.
ep: Rc6+ allows the same defensive resource as before: Be6! blocks, and though dxe6 wins the bishop, Black's queen finally gets its say — Qb3+ Rc3 Qb1+ and your king starts running. Still winning (+4.1), but the forced mate is gone. The game went exactly this way, checks and all.

pv: Kd2 Qe3+ Kc2 Qxe4+ Kb3 Qd5+ Rc4 fxe6 Qh7+ Kg4 Qd3 f3 Kb2 Kh3 Rc5
e: Kd2 walks out of the checks: Qe3+ Kc2 Qxe4+ Kb3 and they are already drying up — Qd5+ Rc4! blocks with the rook defended by your king, and after fxe6 the queen swings to h7 and d3 with mating threats against the h5-king. Converting here is purely about ending the checks; the material is already banked (+3.4).
ep: Rc3 attacks the queen but hands Black a new check: Qb5+! forces Rc4, tying the rook to blocking duty while the queen slips away — in the game Qd1+ Kc4 Qa4+ Kd5 Qa5+ dragged your king across the board and gave back most of the advantage.

pv: c3 Be7 Nd6+ Bxd6 Bxd6 Ne4 Bf4 Qh4 Be3 Nb8 Nf3 Qe7 Bd3 Nc6 O-O O-O
e: c3 keeps everything protected before you commit: it bolsters d4 and vacates c2, so the d1-queen now defends a4 along the diagonal. Then Nd6+ Bxd6 Bxd6 becomes a real achievement - the dark-squared bishop lands on d6 with nothing hanging anywhere.
ep: Nd6+ Bxd6 Bxd6 loses a pawn to Bxa4!: your queen's path to a4 is blocked by the c2-pawn, and Rxa4 fails to Qxd6 - the d6-bishop was hanging. The pawn is gone for nothing; one preparatory move (c3) would have kept it covered.

pv: Kd2 Be8 Ra3 a5 bxa6 Ra7 Rb1 Rxa6 Rab3 Rb8 a5 b5 Ra3 Rba8 Rba1 Bg6
e: Kd2 improves the king without giving anything up - crucially, the a2-rook stays on guard duty for the a4-pawn. The plan is Ra3 and a5 (met by bxa6 and Ra7xa6) to liquidate the queenside weaknesses and hold this slightly worse endgame in comfort.
ep: Rac2 walks the a4-pawn's only defender away from it: Rc4! - protected by the d5-pawn and the c8-rook, so the king cannot take - hits a4 and d4, and after Kd2 Rxa4 Black is a clean pawn up. In the game a6! won the same pawn by deflection: bxa6 Bxa4.

pv: Rd2 Bg6 Nc2 Rf8+ Ke1 g3 Re2 Kf4 Nb4 Be4 Kd2 Rb8 Nd3+ Kf5 Nb4 Rb7
e: Rd2 keeps the rook on defense and attacks the d3-bishop: after Bg6 Nc2 the knight heads back toward e1, the g-pawn is stopped, and the position still holds (+0.0). With your king this exposed, the rook must stay close to home, not wander to the sixth rank.
ep: Rb6 abandons the king: Re2+! Kg3 Be4 sets up Rxg2# - the bishop, the g4-pawn and Black's king cover every flight square - and Rg6+ Bxg6 only postpones it: mate in 9. The rook on b6 attacks nothing and defends nothing.

pv: Nc4 dxc4 Rb5+ Bf5 Rb4 Rd2 Rxc4 Rd3+ Kf2 Kf4 d5+ Be4 g3+ Ke5 d6 Rxd6
e: Nc4! is the only fighting try: dxc4 Rb5+ and then Rb4 regains the c4-pawn and activates the rook - you give the knight to break the mating net and keep checking chances. Passive moves all lose to the attack on g2; activity was the last practical resource.
ep: Nb1 spends the tempo that lets Be4! decide: mate cannot be prevented (mate in 8), since Rg6+ Bxg6 buys only a move. In the game Rb3 allowed Rxg2# on the spot - rook, bishop, the g4-pawn and the king cover every square.

pv: O-O Be5 Rfd8 Nc4 c5 b3 Rd5 Re1 Rad8 Qf3 Nd7 Bc3 Nb6 Ne3 R5d7 Qxb7
e: Castling is the move: the knight on f6 is the only thing blocking White's queen on c3 from the g7 pawn, so the king must get out of the centre before that knight ever moves. After O-O Be5 Rfd8 the rooks come to the open d-file, ...c5 and ...Rd5 give the pieces squares, and Black is close to equal.
ep: Nd5 lifts the blocker off the long diagonal and Qxg7 just takes the pawn: after Bf6 Qh6 Be7 Be5 the king cover is gone for good. In the game it cost g7 and f7 within two moves.

pv: Bc7 Rb7 Qa1+ Kg2 Qa5 Rxc7+ Qxc7 Qd4+ Ke7 Qxh8 Qd7 Ne5 Qd5+ f3 a5 Qxh7+
e: Bc7 blocks the deadly Rb7+ check in advance while hitting the rook on b8, which is what buys the time. After Rb7 Qa1+ Kg2 Qa5 the queen keeps checking and covers the c7 bishop, so White has to spend moves on the exchange instead of mating. The king on d7 has no shelter, so every tempo goes into stopping the checks, not grabbing pawns.
ep: Rf8 leaves the b-file check open and it is mate: Rb7+ Bc7 (forced) Qxc7+ Ke8 Qxc6 mate, with the knight on f7 covering the escape. The game ran into the same net from a move later.

pv: Bxd6 Qxd6 c4 Nf6 Be2 O-O Nf3 Rd8 O-O Qe7 Nb6 dxc4 Qc2 Rb8 Nd2 Ne5
e: Trade first: Bxd6 Qxd6, then c4! challenges d5 before Black settles. White develops naturally with Be2, Nf3 and O-O, and the a4-knight gets the b6 outpost hitting the c8-bishop — a small, stable plus instead of loose pieces.
ep: Qf3 leaves both the f4-bishop and the a4-knight dangling: e5! hits the bishop, and after Bg3 h5! h3 Qa5+! the check picks on the a4-knight too — Nc3 Nf6 Qd1 and White's pieces have all been chased backwards. Black missed it in the game with Nf6.

pv: Qg3 e5 Nb6 Rb8 Nxc8 Rxc8 Bd3 h5 Nf3 Ke7 Be2 Ne4 Qh4+ f6 Nd2 Nxd2
e: Qg3! eyes both the d6-queen and g7 — and when e5 blocks the trade, Nb6! forks the a8-rook and c8-bishop: Nxc8 Rxc8 converts the offside knight into the bishop pair and disrupts Black's queenside before b5-b4 ever gets rolling.
ep: Castling queenside invites b5! — now Nb6 Rb8 Nxc8 Rxc8 happens with Black's attack already running: c3 is met by b4! axb4 Nxb4 and the files open straight at your king. In the game Black castled instead and let you off.

pv: Nb6 Rb8 Nc4 Qc7 e5 Nd7 Qg3 b5 Nd2 Bb7 Ngf3 b4 a4 Nc5 Nb3 Nxb3+
e: Nb6! rescues the offside knight with two tempi: it forks the a8-rook and c8-bishop, and after Rb8 it hops to c4, hitting the d6-queen. From c4 the knight finally participates, and e5 with Qg3 gives White kingside play in a difficult position.
ep: Qe2 wastes the moment: b5! comes, and Nb6 now happens on Black's terms — after Rb8 Nxc8 Rfxc8 his rooks are perfectly placed and the b5/e5 pawns roll. The game's e5 Nf3 Bg4 h3 Be6 c3 b5 gave Black everything he wanted.

pv: Nb6 Rab8 h4 Qc5 Nd5 Bxd5 exd5 Qxd5 Kb1 e4 Nd2 Rfe8 f3 e3 Nb3 Qe5
e: The a4-knight must move NOW, and Nb6! does it with tempo on the a8-rook. After Rab8 it heads for d5: Nd5 Bxd5 exd5 trades off Black's powerful e6-bishop — the piece gluing his position together. You shed a pawn to Qxd5, but in a bad position that trade is the best damage control.
ep: c3 leaves a4 and d1 exposed to one move: Bb3! forks the a4-knight and the d1-rook, and after Nb6 Bxd1 Qxd1 Black has won the exchange outright. In the game Black played b5 instead — strong, but the fork was stronger.

pv: Bxd2+ Qxd2 Nxe4 Bxd8 Nxd2 Kxd2 Kxd8 Ne2 Ke7 Rac1 Rd8 Ke3 Bg4 Rhd1 cxd5 Bxd5

ep: Qa5 lets White defuse it with Bxf6!: the forking knight disappears, and ...Bxd2+ Qxd2 Qxd2+ Kxd2 gxf6 merely doubles your f-pawns for equality at best (-0.7). In the game White played Nf3? and you got ...Nxe4 after all.

ep: Nxd2? trades off your only attacker of the loose bishop: White recaptures Nxd2 and g5 is no longer hanging. After ...cxd5 Bxd5 the position is level (-0.1) — in the game the same trades happened via Bxd2, and the free piece was gone.

pv: Qh2 Qe7 R8xe7 f4 Qxg2#
e: Qh2! sets up mate on g2 that cannot be parried: your e2-rook defends the queen and covers e1, so ...Qxg2 will be mate — Kxg2 is illegal and the king has no square. White's only try, Qe7, drops the queen to ...R8xe7, and after f4 Qxg2# lands anyway: mate in 3.
ep: Qe7 offers a trade at the very moment the king was caught: Qxe7 R2xe7 pulls your rook off the second rank and the mating net is gone. You were still winning (+4.9), but the game later slipped away — look for the forcing line first.

pv: Qe2+ Kg1 Qxd1+ Nf1 Re1 Qc4 Nf8 f3 Qd2 Qc5 Qxb2 Qxa7 Qc1 Kh2 Rxf1 Qxg7+

ep: Ref8 lets the moment pass: Nf3 gives the first rank a blocker on e1, and the rook-winning fork is gone. You were still clearly better (+4.8), but this game was eventually lost — cashing in with ...Qe2+ would have ended it.

pv: Re8 Rc1 Rd6 Qc7 Qe2+ Kg1 Rd1+ Rxd1 Qxd1+ Kh2 Qd5 Qxa7 Ne5 Nh4 Nd3 Nf3
e: A full rook up, your plan is the e-file and trades: Re8! takes the open file, and after Rc1 Rd6 Qc7 you have the clean finish ...Qe2+ Kg1 Rd1+! Rxd1 Qxd1+, liquidating with a decisive material edge (+4.8).
ep: Ne5? steps onto the open file: Re1! pins the knight against your queen, and after ...Rf5 Rxe5 Rxe5 Qxe5 White wins knight and rook for rook, handing back most of your material (+1.7). The game's follow-up ...Rxf3 made it worse still.

pv: Rf5 Rxe5 Rxe5 Qxe5 Re8 Qf5 Qe4 Qxe4 Rxe4 b3 Re6 g3 Kg8 h4 Re7 a4

pv: Nce2 b4 Kb1 a5 g4 a4 Ng3 Qa5 gxh5 Nxh5 Nxh5 Qxh5 Bg5 b3 cxb3 axb3

pv: dxe5 Ng8 exd6 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Bxa6 Rxa6 Qd4 Kh7 c4 Qc8 cxd5 cxd5+ Kd2 Qf5

e: Two tactics hang over you: Nf2+ forking king and h3-rook, and any c5-knight move discovering the c8-rook's attack on your c6-queen. Qb6! solves the discovery — off the c-file, still attacking the c5-knight and hitting b4 — and keeps the game close (-0.6).

pv: Qxe8+

pv: Qa7 Qf6 Kc1 Qf4+ Qe3 N4g5 Bb5 Rb8 Qxf4 Nxf4 Re3 Rxb5 Re7 Rb8

ep: Qxa5 grabs the pawn on a fatal square: Nf2+ Ke1 Nxh3 wins the h3-rook, and after Qb5 Qc1+! Bd1 the block opens the e-file — Nc7+! discovers check and hits your queen, so Qxe8+ Nxe8 leaves black completely winning (-7.6). The game followed move for move.

pv: Qd8 Rfb1 b6 a4 Na5 Qb5+ Qd7 Bb4 Nc4 Qxd7+ Kxd7 a5 b5 a6 Kc6 Ng5
e: Qd8 brings the queen home before it gets shut out on a5, and keeps the d6-bishop in its sights. After Rfb1 b6 a4 Na5! the knight reroutes toward c4, and White has nothing better than trading queens (Qb5+ Qd7 Qxd7+ Kxd7) into a manageable ending.

pv: Nf6 Rxb7 O-O Qb1 Rcd8 c4 dxc4 Ne5 Qd5 Rxc4 Ne8 Rb5 Qxd6 h3 Nf6 Rb7
e: Your king in the centre is the real problem: Nf6! develops and castles next move. Even Rxb7 O-O leaves you fine — Rcd8 follows, and the d6-pawn falls later (Qd5 and Qxd6 in the line) while your rooks finally join the game. King safety before pawn moves.

pv: Qxa2 d7 Qd5 Qxa7 h6 h3 b4 Qc5 h5 Rb1 Rd8 Qe7 Rxd7 Nxd7 Qxd7 Qxd7
e: Qxa2! keeps the queens on — the key to stopping the d-pawn. The pawn never touches d8, and your queenside pawns become the long-term trumps.

pv: Nf5 Bf4 Qf6 Kh1 Qxg6 Qe2 O-O-O Rg1 Qh5 Nbd2 Re8 a4 Be7 Rg2 Rhf8 Rag1

ep: Rg8 defends g6 passively and gives White time for Nh4 to prop the pawn up; the rook is misplaced and your king stays in the centre. You did win the pawn back later with Nxg6, but with far less activity.

pv: Qg4 Ne2 a5 Rg1 Qh4 Qe3 Qf6 Qf4 Rf8 Qxf6 Nxf6 Rg6 Ne4 Rxh6 Rf1+ Ng1

Qg4 stays active and off White's tempo-gaining squares; after Ne2 a5 Rg1 Qh4 the queen sits in front of the weak pawns, and only later, on your terms, do you allow the trade with Qf6.

pv: c5 Rf4 cxd4 Nd3 Nd7 Kg2 b6 Kf3 Ra5 Rxd4 Rxa3 Ke4 Rxa2 Nf4 Nc5+ Ke5

pv: Kxa3 dxc6 bxc6 Rc4 Rc7 Rc2 c5 Kf2 c4 Ke2 Kb4 Kd2 Rd7+ Kc1 Rd3 Rb2+

pv: Bh2
e: The f4-bishop is attacked by the h5-knight, and Bh2! is the one retreat that keeps everything: the bishop stays on its b8–h2 diagonal, out of the knight's reach, and the knight is left stranded on the rim with nothing to do. Bg3 would concede it to Nxg3, and passive defense of f4 invites e5 breaks.

pv: Nxf5+ Kf8 Qd8+ Rxd8 Rxd8+ Qe8 Rxe8+ Kxe8 Nxg7+ Kf8 Nge6+ fxe6 Nxe6+ Kf7 Nc5 Re8

Rxd8 Rxd8+ Qe8 Rxe8+ Kxe8 Nxg7+ then Nge6+ — White emerges a piece and a pawn up (+5.4).

pv: g5 Nh5 Qh4 g6 dxc5 Nxc5 Nf3 Bd7 O-O-O b5 Ne5 Rc8 Bxb5 Bxb5 Nxb5 Qb6

pv: Qd2 e5 h5 e4 Be2 Qd6 Nb5 Qe7 hxg6 fxg6 f4 Ba6 Kb1 e3 Qe1 Rac8

pv: Bxd3

pv: Nec3 Qa5 g6 O-O-O gxf7 b5 b3 e5 bxc4 exf4 cxb5 Rh6 bxc6 Rxc6 Qb5 Qxb5

pv: Nxd4
e: The knight on e2 is pinned to the king by your queen on e7, so the d4 pawn is only defended on paper - Nxd4 just wins it. As a bonus the knight on d4 attacks the queen on b3 and the pinned knight itself, so White has no time to punish you. A healthy pawn for free.

pv: Qd7 Nfe6 Re8 Nxg7 Kxg7 d4 h6 Nf3 Nc6 dxc5 Nxe3 fxe3 bxc5 Rac1 Qd6 Qc3+

ep: Nd7? ignores the standoff: White trades first — Qxb2 Bxb2 — and then Rab1! gains the decisive tempo on the bishop; after Bf6 Bxa8 Rxa8 White has won rook for bishop. In the game Bxa8 came at once and the exchange never came back.

pv: Qxd2 Bxd2 Bxa1 Bb7 Bf6 Kg2 Ne5 Ne4 Bg7 d4 cxd4 Rc1 Rd8 Bg5 Kf8 f4
e: Take the queen, not the bishop: Qxd2! Bxd2 Bxa1 wins the whole rook — the g7-bishop does double duty — and although the cornered a8-bishop slips out via Bb7, material returns to level (-0.5). The queen capture works because every move in the sequence forces a recapture.
ep: Rxa8 wins only the bishop and hands White the tempo he needs: Rae1! saves the a1-rook, your Qb2 runs out of targets, and you stay a clean exchange down (-2.5). In the game Ne6! came first, and the desperate Qxa1 that followed made everything worse.

pv: Qxd2 Bxd2 Bxa1 Rxa1 Ne5 Nf4 Rd8 Bc3 N7c6 Bxe5 Nxe5 Kf1 Nxd3 Rd1 c4 Nxd3
e: One more time the queen capture is right: Qxd2! Bxd2 Bxa1 Rxa1 — queens off, and your bishop bought White's rook. That restores full material equality, and Ne5! next hits d3 while N7c6–d4 activates the knights; you would even stand slightly better (+1.1).
ep: Qxa1?? nets both rooks but leaves White's queen alive: Rxa1 Bxa1 Qd1! hits the stray bishop, and after Bg7 Qb3 comes Nxc5+ — a discovered check from the b3-queen. Queen, knight and bishop overrun your scattered pieces (-4.7); the game's Rxa1 Bxa1 d4 won similarly.

pv: Bxe5 Nxe5 dxe5 Ne7 e4 Bxe5 f4 Bxc3 Qxc3 O-O f5 Qb8 Qf6 Qe8 Ng3 dxe4
e: Resolve the tension in your favour: Bxe5 Nxe5 dxe5 wins a clean pawn, since e5 is attacked as often as it is defended and your d-pawn ends up on e5 as a wedge. That wedge shuts the g7 bishop out of the game and takes f6/d6 from the knights; e3-e4 next fixes d5 and keeps a real bind.
ep: Bg3 retreats and hands the centre back - Black solves all his problems with exd4 Nxd4 and then dxe4, as in the game, and the g7 bishop comes alive on the long diagonal.

pv: Ne6 Qa5 Nxg7 Nd5 Nxd5 cxd5 Qxd5 Qxd5 Rxd5 Nb6 Re5 Kxg7 Re7 Nc4 Rxb7 Ne3
e: Ne6! lands on the one square only the f7 pawn covers and forks Qd8, Rf8 and the g7 bishop. fxe6 is no answer because Qxe6+ tears the black king open with your rooks already on d1 and h1, so Black has to abandon material: after Qa5 Nxg7 you win the dark-squared bishop and the squares round his king with it.
ep: Rhe1 is slow and allows the freeing Nd5: after Nxd5 cxd5 Qxd5 pieces come off and the e6 jump is gone forever. In the game Re8 followed and everything was traded on e8.

pv: Ne6 Bxc3 Nxd8 Bxe1 Bc7 Bxh4 Rxd7 Bxg5+ f4 Bf6 Nxf7 Kxf7 Qc4+ Kf8 Qe6 Bh4
e: Ne6 again: the knight drops into the hole hitting Qd8 and Bg7 at once, and fxe6 loses to Qxe6+ against the bare king. Black's best try Bxc3 does not save him - Nxd8 takes the queen, and after Bxe1 the quiet Bc7! covers the knight on d8, leaving you a queen for rook and bishop.
ep: Bd6 walks into Nf5, which hits the bishop and the d4 knight at once; after Qxe8+ Qxe8 Rxe8+ Rxe8 Nxf5 gxf5 every attacker has been traded off - precisely the game continuation.

pv: Kg3 axb3 axb3 Bc3 Ne3 Be1+ Kf3 h4 Ng2 Bg3 c3 c5 c4 b4 Ne3 Be1
e: Kg3 is the multi-purpose square: it guards f4, blocks the f2-h4 diagonal so the bishop has no checks at all, and frees the knight to reroute Ne3-g2 where it blockades h4 and holds f4. After axb3 axb3 there is simply nothing to attack and the position holds.
ep: Nd2 leaves the king on the checking diagonal and puts the knight on a square the bishop hits: Bf2+ Kh3 Be3 attacks d2 and f4, and after Nf3 Bxf4 the pawn goes. The game confirmed it - Nd2 Be3 Nf3 Bxf4 Nd4 Bxg5+ and two pawns were gone.

pv: Kf3 Bf6 Nxc6 Kg5 c4 bxc4 bxc4 f4 Nb4 Kf5 c5 h3 Nd3 Be5 c6 h2
e: Keep the king in front of the f-pawn. From f3 it covers f4 and the e-file, which is what lets White go pawn-hunting: Kf3 Bf6 Nxc6 Kg5 c4 bxc4 bxc4 and the passed c-pawn gives genuine counterplay.
ep: Kh3 buries the king in the corner behind the h4 pawn, out of touch with the f-pawn - in the game f4-f3 simply ran (Kh3 f4 Nxc6 f3 Nd4 f2) and the knight had to be handed over to stop it.

pv: Kg4 a3 Nxc6 h3 Ne5+ Kf6 Nf3 Bh6 Kxh3 Kf5 Kg2 Ke4 Kf2 b4 Ke2 Bf8
e: Kg4! marches into the black camp and hits f4, the bishop on g5 and h4 all at once, so Black must spend time saving the bishop while your king mops up: Kg4 a3 Nxc6 h3 Ne5+ Kf6 Nf3 and Kxh3 collects the last runner. The kingside pawns are the danger here, not c6.
ep: Nxc6 grabs the wrong pawn and lets the connected f- and h-pawns go: after Kf5 the black king escorts them and the knight is far away. In the game f3 came immediately and the knight had to be given for the f-pawn.

pv: Ne5+ Kf5 Nxf3 Be3 Nxh4+ Ke4 Kg4 Bc5 bxa4 bxa4 Nf5 Bb6 Kg5 Kd5 Kf4 Kc4
e: Ne5+ is the same capture with check, and the check is the whole point - the knight attacks the king on g6 and the f3 pawn in one move, so Black gets no time to support it. Kf5 Nxf3 Be3 Nxh4+ removes both passed pawns and the knight ending is a comfortable draw.
ep: Nd4 attacks f3 as well, but without check, and f2! is exactly one tempo faster: Kg2 Be3 Nf3 h3+ and the pawns cannot be stopped - the game's Nd4 f2 Kg2 Be3 Nxb5 h3+ shows it.

pv: Bxb3 axb3 Bb4+ Bd2 Bxd2+ Nbxd2 Ne7 Qe2 O-O Qc4 c5 Qxc5 Nbc6 O-O b6 Qh5
e: Bxb3! starts cashing in your extra d4-pawn: after axb3 comes Bb4+!, forcing the dark-squared bishops off too (Bxd2+ Nbxd2), and every trade brings the pawn-up endgame closer (+0.3).
ep: Bc5 invites Bxe6! fxe6, wrecking your structure — then Ng5! hits e6 and Qh5+ g6 Qh3 keeps hammering the weakened light squares, with Ne6 landing in some lines (-1.0). In the game White retreated Bf4 and missed the whole idea.

pv: Bxb3 axb3 Nf6 O-O Nbd7 Qd3 O-O Nbd2 Bb6 Bd6 Re8 e5 Nd5 Nc4 Nc5 Qf5
e: Bxb3 axb3 removes White's most dangerous piece: the b3-bishop is the only attacker of e6 and f7, and once it is gone you consolidate your extra d4-pawn with Nf6, Nbd7 and O-O. White is left with doubled b-pawns and no targets - a stable edge for you.
ep: Ne7 gives White time for Bxe6 fxe6 Ng5!, hitting the weak e6-pawn: after e5 the knight jumps into the vacated square with Ne6, forking your d8-queen and c5-bishop, and Qd6 Qh5+ Kd7 Nxc5+ wins the bishop. In the game White retreated Ne5 and missed the whole idea.

pv: Bxb3 axb3 Ng6 Nxg6 fxg6 O-O O-O Qd3 Qe7 Bxb8 Rxf1+ Kxf1 Rxb8 Kg1 Rd8 Nd2
e: Bxb3 axb3 is still the point: the bishop that pressures e6 and f7 disappears, and Ng6 then challenges the e5-knight - after Nxg6 fxg6 and castling you are a clean pawn up, with the half-open f-file for your rook as a bonus.
ep: Castling first allows Bxe6 fxe6, wrecking your structure while the e5-knight stays dominant - most of your extra pawn's value evaporates. In the game White pulled the knight back to d3 instead of taking.

pv: Ng6 Bg3 Bd6 Bxe6 fxe6 Qg4 Qe7 Nd2 c5 Nc4 Bxg3+ hxg3 Nd7 a4 Nf6 Qh3
e: Ng6 hits the f4-bishop and gains the tempo that Bd6 gives away: after Bg3 Bd6 you trade on your terms - Bxe6 fxe6 leaves you the half-open f-file, and Bxg3 hxg3 doubles White's pawns. Same plan as the game, but with a free useful move thrown in.
ep: The immediate Bd6 lets White simplify unbothered: Bxe6 fxe6 (or the game's Bxd6 Qxd6) releases the tension while the d3-knight sits comfortably, and your advantage shrinks. Kicking the bishop with Ng6 first would have cost White something for every trade.

pv: fxe5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 Rxe5 dxe5 Qc5+ Kf3 Qd5+ Kf2 Qxa2 e6 Qd5 h4 a5 Qe5
e: Take the pawn: fxe5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 Rxe5 dxe5 liquidates almost everything, and then Qc5+! Kf3 Qd5+ Kf2 Qxa2 collects the a2-pawn with checks. White's e-pawn is easily stopped by Qd5, and only you can press in the queen ending.
ep: g5? drops the f6-point with the e-file loaded: exf6! Rxe3 fxe7! — the little pawn eats through to e7, and after Rxe2+ Rxe2 Kf7 the passed e7-pawn ties your king down while d5! and Nd4 pick off f5. The game saw exf6 Rxe3 fxe7 Rxe2+ Rxe2 Kf7 Ne5+! — even stronger.

pv: Kf6 g4 f4 Rf5+ Kg6 Ra5 a6 Re5 Kf6 Rf5+ Kg6
e: Kf6! forks the e5-rook and the e7-pawn — the king does the work here. The rook can only check and come back (g4 f4 Rf5+ Kg6 Ra5 a6 Re5 Kf6 repeats), because leaving the fifth rank loses e7. A draw by repetition is the fair result, and this is the only move that secures it.
ep: Rxe7 wins the pawn but overlooks the zwischenzug Rxf5+! — White grabs one back with check, and your g5- and h6-pawns become lasting targets: after Kg6 g4 h5 Re5 they start to fall. In the game Rf8 and Rf3 mopped up and White won the rook ending.

pv: O-O-O
e: O-O-O. With Bf4, Bd3 and Qe2 you have built the classic queenside-castling setup against the English Defence, and the king has to go there before Black gets ...d5 in. The rook lands on d1 opposite Black's d-pawn, the rooks connect, and only then do you start e4-e5 or an h-pawn advance. The engine keeps it near equal at +0.3 — nothing else in the position improves until the king is settled.
ep: Be3 offers a trade of your best-placed piece and leaves the king in the centre, and Black hits back at once with ...d5. The engine's line shows the cost: Bg5 h6 Bh4 and now Bd4 plants a bishop on the hole in the middle of the board; after e5 Bxc3+ bxc3 Qc7 your structure is wrecked, the c3-pawn is weak and the king is still on e1. +0.3 to -1.1. In the game the trade came immediately (Bxe3 Qxe3 d5) with the same problem.

pv: Nf3 Kf8 Rad1 Rxd1 Rxd1 Ke7 g4 f6 b4 h5 gxh5 Rh8 Rg1 Kf8 Rd1
e: Nf3 first. The g1-knight is the whole traffic jam — it blocks the h1-rook, so no rook manoeuvre works while it sits there. From f3 it covers d4 and e5 and prepares Rad1, and crucially the a1-rook stays home guarding a2, so ...Nb4+ can simply be met by chasing the knight (after ...Nxa2 Rxa2 wins a piece). The engine line Nf3 Kf8 Rad1 Rxd1 Rxd1 Ke7 g4 is a balanced ending, 0.0.
ep: Rd1 walks the a1-rook off the only square defending a2, and Black has Nb4+! forking king and pawn. Kc1 Nxa2+ Kc2 Nb4+ Kc1 Rxd1+ Kxd1 Nd3 and the knight lands in the middle of your camp hitting b2, with the h1-rook and g1-knight still asleep — from equal to about -3.8. Before contesting a file, check what the rook you are moving was holding; here it was the a2-pawn.

pv: Qxh5 Qb6 Rb1 Nd7 Nge2 Qa5 a3 O-O Bh3 b5 O-O
e: Qxh5! wins a whole piece: the knight jumped to h5 to attack your f4-bishop but is completely undefended there, and the d1-queen sees it along the diagonal. Taking it first means the bishop never falls (+4.2).
ep: h4 ignores both threats: Nxf4 exf4 trades off your strong dark-squared bishop, and instead of being a piece up you're slightly worse, with Qb6 hitting b2 and d4 next (-0.8). The game continued Nxf4 exf4 and the chance was gone.

pv: dxc5 Nc6 Nf3 Bxc5 Qe2 Qe7 O-O-O Bd7 Kb1 O-O-O Ne5 Be8
e: dxc5 resolves the central tension cleanly: after Nc6 Nf3 Bxc5 you finish developing (Qe2, O-O-O in the main line) with only a small disadvantage (-0.6).
ep: Nb5 drops the initiative: Qb6! hits the knight and b2 at once, and after dxc5 Bxc5 the knight gets chased with a6 while Black takes over. In the game a6 drove it straight back to c3 — two lost tempi — and cxd4 dismantled your center (-1.9).

pv: Nf3 h6 Bg2 Bd6 Rb1 Qc7 Qd2 hxg5 hxg5 Rxh1+ Bxh1 O-O-O a4 Na7 Ra1 Kb8
e: Nf3 finally develops the kingside — Bg2 and short castling follow — and keeps the fight going at -2.1. The d4-pawn cannot be won: it's attacked twice (Ne2, Qd1) but defended twice (Qb6, Nc6), and Black recaptures last.
ep: Nxd4 loses a piece for a pawn to the capture count: Qxd4! Qxd4 Nxd4 and Black's knight makes the final capture — exactly what happened in the game (-5.0).

pv: Qd6 Qe2+
e: Qd6! develops the queen, clears d8 for ...O-O-O and leaves nothing loose; the check Qe2+ is comfortably met by ...Be6 and White has nothing (+0.6).
ep: b5? loosens a pawn while your king still sits on the open e-file: Qe2+! forces ...Be6, and after f4 Be7 Qxb5 White has won a clean pawn (-0.9). Your opponent missed it (Ne2?) and you took over with ...a5-a4 anyway.

pv: a3 bxa3 g6 f4 Qc7 f5 Bxg3 Qxg3 Qxg3 hxg3 Nxf5 g4 Ne3 Rxf6 Rfc8 Rd6
e: a3! fixes White's queenside as a permanent weakness: b2 must capture (else ...axb2), and bxa3 leaves doubled, isolated a-pawns to attack all game. The line shows the payoff: ...g6 and ...Qc7, and when White overpresses with f5, ...Bxg3 and ...Nxf5 net a pawn (+1.9).
ep: Qc8? invites a trade that only helps White: Qxc8 Rfxc8, and now he gets a3! in first - your a4-pawn is fixed, the ...a3 break is gone forever, and with it most of your queenside pressure (+0.6).

pv: Nf4 Qg4 g6 Qxc8 Raxc8 Rfd1 h5 a3 Rfe8 Nh1 Ne2+ Kf2 Bxh2 g3 h4 Nf1
e: The fifth rank is the problem: White's queen attacks d5, with b5 hanging behind it. Nf4! defends by counterattack - it hits the h5-queen and guards d5 at the same time. After Qg4 g6! White has nothing better than Qxc8 Raxc8, an endgame where your a4/b5 pawns squeeze his crippled queenside (+2.7).
ep: Qc7? leaves the rank: Qxd5! grabs the pawn, and after ...Nf4 Qxb5 a second one goes. Your ...Rfb8 and ...Rxb2 activity earns some of it back, but most of the edge is gone (+2.7 down to +1.2). In the game White took d5 at once.

pv: Qd2 Nc5 Kb1 Nb7 Nc3 a6 Qe3 Nc5 Bf2 Ne6 Qb6 Nf4 Bh4 Be6 Rd2 Ng6
e: Qd2 keeps the queen active while leaving the pawn on b2 in place as the defender of a3. That single detail holds the whole queenside together; then Kb1, Nc3 and Bf2 tidy up and the pressure against Black's loose c4/b5 pawns gives you the better game.
ep: b3 removes the only guard of a3, and Qxa3+ snaps the pawn off with check. After Qb2 Qxb2+ Kxb2 the queens come off with Black a clean pawn up, which is exactly how the game went.

pv: Nb5 c3+
e: Nb5 keeps the knight out of an exchange Black wants and puts it on a square where it covers both c3 and d4, so the coming c3+ can simply be captured. From b5 it also hits a7 and supports the rook on d6, holding the balance.
ep: Nd5 offers the trade that helps Black: after Nxd5 the recapture is forced and c3+ then arrives with no knight covering the square. The pawns on b4 and c4 cramp your king and the bishop on a2 stays out of play.

pv: Ra5 Nd7 Bxa7 f5 Ra4 fxe4 fxe4 Ke7 Rd1 Rd8 g4 Rf8 Bc5+ Nxc5 Rxa8 g5
e: Ra5 keeps the bishop pair and swings the rook to the a-file, where a7 is genuinely loose: after Nd7 Bxa7 you win the pawn without opening a single line for Black's rooks, and the rook on d6 keeps its clamp on the sixth rank. Take pawns in a way that does not activate the opponent.
ep: Bxb6 trades your strong bishop for the knight and, worse, hands Black the open a-file with axb6. After Rxb6 Be6 the rooks come to a8 and d8, the c3 pawn sits in your king's face, and the extra pawn is meaningless.

pv: Rd7+ Ke8 Bxe6 Ra6 Ka2 Rxe6 Rb7 h5 Kb3 g5 a5 Kd8 Kxc3 Kc8 Rb6 Rxb6
e: Rd7+ is a matter of move order: the check drives the king to e8 first, so you take the bishop on e6 with a tempo in hand instead of allowing counterplay. After Bxe6 Ra6 Ka2 Rxe6 Rb7 your rook owns the seventh rank and the passed a-pawn, supported from behind, decides the ending.
ep: Rc5 lets Black strike first with Bxa2+!: Kxa2 drags your king onto the a-file and Rxa4+ takes the passed pawn with check. The winning position turned into a level rook ending, exactly as in the game.

pv: Bb4 Qd3 Ne4 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 Qd7 d5 Bg6 Bxa7 b5 Be3 bxc4 Qxc4 cxd5 Qb4
e: Bb4! pins the c3-knight and prepares Ne4: after Qd3 Ne4 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 White's queenside pawns are wrecked and your knight is superb on e4. Just as important, keeping the pawn on c6 keeps the g2-bishop's long diagonal firmly closed.
ep: c5? opens the long diagonal with b7 still loose: Bxb7! wins a pawn, and after Rb8 dxc5 Bxc5 Qxd8 Rexd8 Bxc5 Rxb7 Be7! White emerges a healthy pawn up with the initiative. In the game White chose Nd5 instead, kept heavy pressure, and your position collapsed soon after.

pv: Qxe7 Rxe7 Rxe7 h4 h6 Qxa7 Rce8 a4 Re2 b4 Be4 Qd4 b6 Qc3 Rd8 b5
e: Capture with the queen: Qxe7! Rxe7 Rxe7 gives queen for rook and knight — the best deal on offer. Your rooks and bishop then coordinate: after h4 h6 Qxa7 Rce8 you own the e-file, and Re2 with Be4 keeps White's queen tied to defense. Worse, but very much alive.
ep: Rxe7?? misses the in-between move: Qxd8+! deflects your rook first, and only then Rxe7 — you got a knight for a rook instead of rook and knight for the queen. After Rb8 White's rooks invaded (b4 and Rc7 in the game) and the ending was hopeless.

pv: Nc3 g4 O-O-O d6 Nd5 Qa5 Ng5 g3 Qb5 Qxb5 Bxb5 O-O Bxg3 Nxg3 fxg3 Bxe5
e: Nc3! develops the last minor piece, covers d5 and prepares O-O-O - the calm answer to Black's pawn-grabbing setup. The critical ...g4 is met by O-O-O!: after ...d6 Nd5! arrives with tempo on the b4-queen, and following ...Qa5 Ng5 your pieces flood in while Black's king is stuck in the middle (+2.5).
ep: Qc3? posts the queen on your knight's best square and invites the trade Black wants. After ...g4 the position unravels: Bd3 d6! Nd4 Nfxd4 exd4 dxe5 and White must swap queens on b4 having lost the e5-pawn (-0.5). In the game Nd4 dropped e5 to the same mass exchange.

pv: Nd2 hxg2
e: Nd2! develops and, above all, keeps f3 covered so that ...Nf3+ can always be answered by Nxf3. You concede ...hxg2, but the g2-pawn falls to Rg1 next and the damage stays limited - you are worse (-1.1), not lost.
ep: gxh3? removes the g2-pawn, your only cover of f3, and ...Nf3+! forks king and h2-bishop: after Ke2 Nxh2 Rxh2 Bxe5 Black has swapped knight for bishop, grabbed e5 and owns every dark square (-2.5). The game went exactly this way.

pv: f4 d6 Rxh2 dxe5 Nc3 exf4 Nd5 Bxb2 Re1 Kd8 Rf1 c6 Nxf4 Re8+
e: f4! keeps the g7-bishop locked out by defending e5 - and the h2-knight is not going anywhere: g4, f3 and f1 are all covered by your h3-pawn and king, so Rxh2 can wait a move. After ...d6 Rxh2 dxe5 Nc3! you get counterplay toward d5; still worse (-2.6), but fighting.
ep: Rxh2? recaptures at the wrong moment: ...Bxe5! takes the pawn with tempo on the rook, and after Rh1 Bxb2 the same bishop forks your a1-rook and b1-knight - ...Bxa1 Rxa1 costs you the exchange and two pawns (-4.7). In the game ...Bxe5 duly landed.

pv: Kb1
e: Black's rook was already glaring at a2, and once that pawn falls the rook camps on the second rank next to your king. Kb1 defends a2 with the king and tucks it away from checks — only then are central captures like exd5 playable on your terms.
ep: exd5 ignores the threat: Rxa2!, and after Nd4 Qxd5 Black regains the d5-pawn with the rook entrenched on your second rank. In the game Rxa2 Nc3 Ra1+ followed and your king stayed rattled, though you won the scramble.

pv: Qf5 Rc7 Rxd5 Qf6 Qxf6 gxf6 Rxh6 Kg7 Rh2 Kxg6 b3 Re7 Kb2 Nc7 Rdh5 Ra8
e: Qf5 hits the c8-rook before taking anything, so after Rc7 you capture Rxd5 with a full extra tempo. When Black finally forces the queen trade with Qf6, Qxf6 gxf6 Rxh6 collects a second pawn — a far better version of this ending than an immediate trade on d5.
ep: Qxd5+ Qxd5 Rxd5 lets the e8-knight jump to c7, kicking your rook, and Black untangles completely — the ending is level. The check made the trade feel safe, but it gained nothing that Qf5 wouldn't have gained with interest.

pv: h4 c5 dxc5 Nxc5 h5 Qa5 Nge2 b4 Nd5 Na4 Nd4 Bxd5 exd5 Nc3 Bc4 Nxd1
e: h4 is the standard plan against the fianchetto: get the h-pawn moving before black gets counterplay. After c5 dxc5 Nxc5 h5 the h-file opens toward g6 while your bishop on f4 keeps hitting d6, and Nge2-d4 adds a piece. Speed matters more than a tidy setup here - whoever's attack lands first wins.
ep: Bd3 is a tempo the attack cannot spare. Black hits back at once with ...c5 and ...Qa5, and once the queenside opens against your king on c1 it is his attack that arrives first - exactly the course of the game.

pv: Nxd4 exd4 Bxd4 Nf6 h4 O-O h5 Rfc8 g4 Rab8 h6 Bh8 g5 Ne8 Bxh8 Kxh8
e: The knight on d4 is black's best piece and the reason his position holds; Nxd4 exd4 Bxd4 removes it and puts your bishop on the long diagonal opposite his fianchettoed bishop. That is the green light for h4-h5 and g4-g5: after Nf6 h4 O-O h5 Rfc8 g4 h6 the pawns crash through and Bxh8 strips the king.
ep: Na2 is a retreat that undoes your own coordination and hands black the initiative: ...Qxd2 Rxd2 takes the queens off, and with them the attack, while the knight on d4 keeps sitting in the middle of your position.

pv: Ne3 Bd6 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 Qd7 Nc4 Be7 Qe4 Bf6 Ne3 Rae8 Qd5+ Rf7 Qxd7 Rxd7
e: Ne3 solves both problems at once: it guards g2, so the e4-bishop loses its tricks, and it prepares Bd3 to trade off Black's monster - Bd6 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 and you consolidate two pawns up (+3.0) with Nc4 and Qe4 to follow.
ep: Bf3 invites Bxf3! gxf3, wrecking your king's cover: Qd7! hits h3, and after Kh2 Bd6+ f4 Black crashes through with Bxf4+! Bxf4 Rxf4 - the attack outweighs your extra pawns (-0.4). In the game Black retreated Bg6 and let you keep everything.

pv: Nc6 Qa4
e: Nc6! hits the centralised queen and develops for free: after the forced Qa4 you have gained a clean tempo and can continue e6 and Bd7, asking the queen questions again. White's early queen outing should cost time - but only if you punish it now (+0.3).
ep: e6? gives White time for Bxb8! - removing the knight before it ever hits the queen from c6 - and after Rxb8 e4! the d5-pawn comes under fire, exd5 and dxe6 winning a pawn in the line (-0.9). Your opponent played e4 without that preface, and you got Nc6 in anyway.

pv: d4 f3 d3 Qf2 exf3 Bxf3 h5 Bxc6 bxc6 Qf3 Kb7 b4 h4 b5 hxg3 hxg3
e: d4 resolves the centre on your terms: it shuts the g2 bishop out of the game behind its own pawns, fixes e3 as a backward target, and hands you the d3 square. After f3 d3! the wedge cramps White completely, and exf3 Bxf3 h5 leaves his pieces with no active squares at all.
ep: h5 is a move too slow: cxd5 exd5 opens the long diagonal for the g2 bishop straight at d5 and c6, and your central pawn mass loses its punch. That's the game continuation.

pv: Qe5
e: Qe5 centralises and does two jobs at once: it defends the d4 knight and eyes b2 and g3. The knight on d4 is your best piece, blocking the d-file and hitting e2 and f3, so anchoring it rather than retreating it keeps White completely passive.
ep: Nc6 voluntarily withdraws your strongest piece and invites Rxd8+ Rxd8. In the game a4-a5 then gained queenside space against your king and the knight ended up passively on e5.

pv: Rg1#
e: Rg1 is mate at once. The rook can't be taken because the knight on f3 covers g1, White's own bishop on h3 blocks the king's only flight square, and the rook itself takes h1 and the g-file away. Look for the mate before the material.
ep: Nxd2 wins a rook but removes the very knight that guarded g1, so the mate disappears. White then had Qd8+ and Qd6+ with checks, and simply took the knight back with Qxd2.

pv: Qd3 Qf4 Rc4 Bg6 a5 Bxh5 e3 Qxe3 Qxe3 fxe3 Kb8 Bf7 Rc2+ Kh3 Kc7 h5
e: Qd3 does three jobs in one move: it attacks the f5 bishop (the piece eyeing your c8 rook), defends the e4 pawn, and offers a trade of queens. After Qf4 Rc4 the rook joins the defence, and the e-pawn becomes a real asset with e3 coming.
ep: Qb7 leaves the e4 pawn loose, and Qe5 followed by Qxe4+ takes it with check; the check then makes Bxc8 possible. In the game Qe6 and Be4+ collected the pawn all the same.

pv: Ka7 Qf3
e: The g2 bishop and the queen on e4 sit on the same long diagonal, so the moment the queen steps aside to a8 the bishop defends her there. That means the d8 rook must never leave the eighth rank. Ka7 sidesteps the mating square and keeps the position roughly balanced.

pv: f5 Nfd2 a5 a4 O-O h4 e5 h5 Bf7 gxf5 exd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 cxd4 Rae8 Nxe4
e: f5 anchors your knight on e4 with a pawn, and that knight is the whole point of the position: it screens your g6-bishop from the Bd3 battery and can never be chased away. After Nfd2 a5 a4 O-O you finish development, and ...e5 follows to hit the d4 centre while the bishop sits safely behind the f5/g6 pawn wall.
ep: Ng5 steps off e4 and opens the d3-g6 diagonal: Bxg6 Nxf3+ Qxf3 hxg6 shreds your kingside pawns, removes your best piece and leaves the king still stuck on e8. That is exactly the sequence the game followed.

pv: Rh6 h4 gxh4 Qe3 Kg8 Reg1 R6h7 Nf4 Qg5 f3 Na5 b3 Nc6 Re1 Rh6 Rh2
e: Rh6 doubles the rooks on the open h-file, where h3 is the only target left, and it also guards f6 and g6 along the sixth rank so the h5-knight has no outpost. After h4 gxh4 Qe3 Kg8 Reg1 R6h7 the file stays yours and Nf4 can be met by ...Qg5, keeping the initiative on the kingside.
ep: g6 takes control of f5 but gives up the f6 square: Nf6 hits your rook on h7 and, once it drops back with Rh4, Nxd5 simply collects the d-pawn. The knight jump was the move the pawn push invited.

pv: Qf4+ Kd1 Qxg4+ f3 Qh4 Ne2 Ne7 Nc1 Nf5 Qe2 Qh1+ Kc2 Nh4 Nd3 Nxf3 Kb3
e: Qf4+ is a fork with check: from f4 the queen checks along the f4-c1 diagonal and simultaneously attacks the loose g4-pawn. After Kd1 Qxg4+ you have won a clean pawn with tempo, and f3 Qh4 leaves your queen dominating while the knight comes to e7-f5 to hit the weakened kingside (+3.6).
ep: Kg7 is a useful square but the pawn was hanging only for one move: Ne2 covers f4 and defends g4, and White then turns the tables with Qxd5, restoring material equality.

pv: e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Ne2 Qc6 b3 Qb5 Nc1 f6 Kd2 Qd7 Nd3 Nxg4 Qg3 Nh6 Qb8
e: e5 is the freeing break: after dxe5 Nxe5 your knight lands on a perfect central square where it hits g4 and f3, and the queen swings out with Qc6-b5 to hit the loose queenside while the white knight shuffles on c1/e2. Black's pieces all get jobs at once instead of waiting.

pv: Qc8 Ne2 Qa6 Nc1 e5 dxe5 Qc4 Nd3 d4 Qf3 dxc3 Qf6+ Kg8 bxc3 Qxa2+ Kd1
e: Qc8 keeps the queen active on the light squares: Qa6 next eyes the queenside and the a2/c-pawns, and only then does e5 come. In the line Qc8 Ne2 Qa6 Nc1 e5 dxe5 Qc4 Nd3 d4 the central pawns roll forward with the queen supporting from behind, and dxc3 rips open the white king.
ep: Ne7 buries the knight and hands White the centralising Qe5+, which comes with check and hits both d5 and g5 at once, so you end up defending pawns instead of pushing them.

pv: Qd6 Qe3 Qh2+ Kb3 Nc6 Ka3 b5 Ne5 Nxe5 dxe5 a6 b3 Qh4 Qf4 a5 b4

pv: Qe8 Qh8+ Ng8 Qh7 a6 b3 Qe7 a4 b5 a5 Qe8 Kb2 Qe7 b4 Qe8 Kb1
e: f7 is attacked twice, by the queen on f6 and the knight on e5, and defended only by your king - so it needs another defender. Qe8 does the job: the queen covers f7 from e8, and after Qh8+ Ng8 Qh7 a6 there is no way through and you can start pushing on the queenside instead.
ep: Ng8 leaves f7 with the king as its only guard: Qxf7# is mate on the spot, because the knight on e5 covers the recapture and the queen takes e8 and g8 away.

pv: Rxc3 Be3 Nh6 Bd1 Na5 Bd2 Rxa3 Bb4 Ra2 Bxa5 Rxa5 Rxb7 O-O Nh4 Bxd1 Rxd1

pv: Kf8 Bc6 Rc8 Bd7 Ra8 Nd2 Bf5 Rb4 a3 Bc6 Rc8 Bb7 Rc7 Nb3 g5 Nc5
e: Kf8 keeps the king out of check range on the seventh rank. The a4-pawn is hard to hold, but after Bc6 Rc8 Bd7 Ra8 the rook stays behind it and ...a3 keeps it running — White's pressure never turns concrete and the game stays level.
ep: Ke7 walks onto the rook's rank: Bc6! hits a8, and after ...Rc8 comes Rb7+ — the check drives your king and Bxa4 collects the pawn with tempo, exactly as the game went (Rb7+ Kd8 Bxa4).

pv: Kf8 Ng5 Ne7 Bd7 Rd8 Rcb1 g6 Bxa4 Ra8 f3 Bf5 Rb8+ Kg7 Rxh8 Rxh8 Rb7
e: Kf8 tucks the king out of the tactics. The a4-pawn falls anyway (Bxa4), but after Ng5 Ne7 Bd7 Rd8 and later ...g6, ...Bf5 your pieces coordinate and resistance is real — the key is staying off the d-file, where discovered checks lurk.
ep: Kd8 steps into the d-file: after Bxa4 Ne7, White has Rd7+! Ke8 Rxd5+ — the pawn falls with a discovered check from the a4-bishop (...exd5 is illegal), which is exactly how the game continued.

pv: Ra8 dxe5 h5 Rxe7 Rxa4 Rf7+ Ke8 Rxg7 Ra8 Kg2 h4 f4 Rc8 Rge7+ Kf8 Rxe6
e: Keep the knight on e7 — it blocks the seventh rank and stops the rooks from doubling on f7. Ra8 is the useful move: it hits the a4-bishop, and after dxe5 h5! (luft) Rxe7 Rxa4 you fight on down material instead of being mated.
ep: Nd5 removes the one blocker on the seventh rank: Rf7+ Kg8 Rxg7+ Kf8 Rbf7# — with the knight gone from e7, the b7-rook joins on f7 and it's mate in three. The game ended exactly this way.

pv: Qh4 hxg5 Nxg5 Kg7 Ne2 Na6 Rg1 Rh8 a3 Rb8 Nf4 Nxf4 Qxf4 Rb7 O-O-O

pv: Nxe4 dxe4 Bxe4 Kh8 Ne5 Nd7 Nxc6 Qf6 Na5 Rb8 Rg1 Qd6 Bf3

pv: Qc7 O-O-O
e: With both kings castled long, don't open lines in front of your own: Qc7 tucks the queen safely behind the king, keeps the queenside pawns at home, and leaves White nothing better than O-O-O with a roughly balanced middlegame (+0.3).

pv: Ne8 Nc4

pv: Kd8 a5 Nxa5 Nxa5 bxa5 Raxa5 Rxb5 Rxa7 Rxb2 Rxa8+ Kc7 Ra7+ Rb7 Rxb7+ Kxb7 f4

pv: d4 f4 gxf4 Bd5 Nd7 Kd3 Nxc5+ Kxd4 Nxa4 Bxf7 Nc3 h4 Kc7 Ke5 f3 Kf4

pv: Kc8 Kc5 Kxc7 Kd4 Nc6+ Kd5 Ne7+ Kc5 Ng6 Kb5 Nf4 h4 h5 a7 Kb7 hxg5

pv: Ne5 a7 Kxa7 Kd8 Qd7#
e: Ne5! keeps the knight and closes the net: it guards d7, so Qd7# is already the threat. White's only tries are a7 — met by Kxa7 — and Kd8, when Qd7# arrives anyway with the knight protecting the queen: mate in 3.

pv: Qd4 Kc6 Ka7 Kc7 Kxa6 Kc6 Ka7 Kb5 Kb7 Ka5 Kc6 Ka6 Qb6#
e: Qd4! dominates: the queen seals the fourth rank and d-file, so White's king can never reach the center. Every king move loses ground; your own king strolls over, takes the a6-pawn, and herds White to the edge — Qb6# finishes: mate in 7.

e: Qb7! is the textbook squeeze: it seals the white king on the a-file from a safe distance — no stalemate accidents — while your king marches Ka5, Ka4, Kb3. After Kb1 the long diagonal delivers Qh1#: mate in 5.

pv: Kf6 g5+ Kxg5 Rxe8 Rxe8 Rxc5+ Kh4 Kg2 Be4+ f3 Bd3 f4 Re2+ Kf3 Rh2 f5

pv: Rf8 Kg1 Nd3 c4+ Kxc4 Nc6 Be4 Ne7 Rxf2 Nf5 Kd5 Rxh7 Rg2+ Kf1 Ra2 Kg1
e: Rf8 attacks the one genuinely weak pawn: f2 is defended only by the king. After Kg1 Nd3! the knight joins in, and once White must deal with c4+ your rook simply eats on f2, at which point the extra piece finally counts. Aim the rook at the target that cannot be defended twice.

pv: Ne6 f3 Ke5 Rf7 Nf4+ Kg1 Rc1+ Kf2 Rc2+ Ke1 Bxg6 Re7+ Kd6 Rb7 Bh5 Rb6+
e: Ne6 keeps the e4 square free for your king, which is what makes the position safe: Rf5+ can then always be answered by stepping toward the rook. After f3 Ke5 Nf4+ Kg1 the checks on the c-file (Rc1+, Rc2+) win time and ...Bxg6 picks up the passed pawn, leaving you an extra piece with the pawns gone.

pv: Nf6 Rf8 Rf3+ Kg2 Rf4 Kh3
e: Nf6 is the only blockader: from f6 the knight covers g8 and h7, so the g-pawn can never promote, and the rook stays free to check from f3/f4. After Rf8 Rf3+ Kg2 Rf4 White has no way to make progress and the ending is a draw.

pv: Rc1 Ra6+ Kf7 Ra7+
e: Rc1 gives the rook checking distance from the side, which is the drawing technique here. After Ra6+ Kf7! your king boxes White's king in the corner — g7 and g8 are both covered — so the pawn can never advance with support, and Ra7+ only repeats.

pv: Re1 Kg7 Re7+ Kg8 Rc7 Rb6 Rc8+ Kg7 Rc7+ Kg8
e: Re1 moves the rook far enough away to check with impunity: after Kg7 Re7+! Kg8 Rc7 White's king cannot escape the checks along the rank and file, and Rc8+/Rc7+ repeats. The rook needs distance from the enemy king to survive giving checks.

pv: Qf3 Qa5 O-O-O Nc6 Nge2 cxd4 exd4 b5 Ng3 b4 Nb5 Qxa2 g5 hxg5 hxg5 Rxh1
e: Develop with Qf3!: it pressures d5, connects for O-O-O, and keeps g5 in reserve. That reserve is the point — in the line White castles first and only then plays g5, with the rook still on h1, so hxg5 hxg5 opens the h-file straight at Black's king. Same break, twice the punch.

pv: Bxb7 Qd2 Qxd2 Bxd2 Rd1 Ba5 Kg2 Ke7 Rd5 Bc7 Rhd1 hxg5 hxg5 f6 Bc6 Nb6
e: Bxb7! collects a loose pawn — nothing defends b7 — making it two up with the bishop pair. The freeing try Qd2 is met by Qxd2 Bxd2 and then Rd1!, hitting the d2-bishop with tempo (Ba5), after which White's rooks own the open files and the conversion is routine (+3.5).

pv: e5 Bxe5 Nxe5 Qd4 Nxf3+ gxf3 Bd7 Nc3 Nf6 O-O-O Qb6 Qe5+ Qe6 Bb5
e: e5! wins a piece using the g4-pin: the pawn attacks the f4-bishop, and the f3-knight can't help — Nxe5?? drops the queen to ...Bxd1. So after Bxe5 Nxe5 White is a bishop down for a pawn; the trick Qd4 is answered by ...Nxf3+ gxf3 Bd7, keeping the material (+3.4).

pv: Rc8 Bxf5 Nxf5 O-O Nxg3 hxg3 Qc7 Rad1 g6 e4 Be7 exd5 Nb4 Qa4 Nxd5 Qxa7
e: Rc8 finishes development and puts the rook opposite White's queen on the c-file; after Bxf5 Nxf5 O-O Nxg3 hxg3 Qc7 the minor pieces come off in an orderly way and the position is simply level (+0.4). Nothing more was required — settle the f5-bishop question without dropping anything.
ep: Ne5?? moves the knight to a square attacked twice (Nf3 and the g3-bishop) but defended once: after Nxe5 Bxe5 Bxe5 White's bishop makes the last capture and you are a clean piece down — the exact game continuation (-4.4). Even declining with ...Re8 stays a piece down.

pv: Rh1 Bc6 Rf2 Nf4 Kd2 g5 Rg1 Reg8 Bf1 Kd8 a4 Ke7 b4 Kf6 b5 axb5
e: Your h4-pawn is attacked by the g6-knight and defended by nothing: Rh1! simply holds it while keeping the rook useful, and after Bc6 Rf2 Nf4 Kd2 you cover e2 and stand fine (-0.3). Quiet defence was all the position asked for.

pv: Kd2 Rg8 Ne3 Rg6 Be4 Rf6 Rg1 Rf2+ Kd1 Rf8 Kd2 a5 b3 b5 Nf1 Rg8
e: Kd2! takes the e2- and e1-entry squares away from Black's rook and frees your rook to fight the g-pawn; Ne3 then covers g2 and blockades (line: Kd2 Rg8 Ne3 Rg6 Be4). Still worse (-1.9), but coordinated - every piece holds a defensive job.
ep: Bg2? invites Re2!: the rook hits c2 and the bishop at once, and after Bf3 the pawn itself decides - g2! deflects your rook to g1 and Rf2 renews the attack. The game went exactly that way (Re2 Bf3 g2 Rg1 Rf2) and the position fell apart (-4.8).

e: Kd1! is pure prophylaxis: it covers e2, the one square from which the f4-knight forks king and rook (Ne2+ hitting c1 and g1). With the fork prevented, Be4 and Rg7 give real counterplay (line: Kd1 h5 Be4 h4 Rg7) and White hangs on at -0.9.

pv: Ra7 Ne2+ Kb1 Rd1+ Ka2 a5 Nf7+ Kc8 Nxd6+ Rxd6 Rxa5 Rb6 Ra7 Rc6 c3 Rh6
e: Ra7! holds the draw through activity: the rook hits a6 from the seventh, and your h6-knight has just enough tricks - after Ne2+ Kb1 Rd1+ Ka2 a5, Nf7+! and Nxd6+ forks the rook back (Rxd6 Rxa5), reaching a level rook ending (0.0).

pv: Ng6
e: Ng6 brings the passive e7-knight to life: from g6 it hits the e5-pawn and covers f4 and h4, and it clears the way for ...f6 to break White's big centre and free the f8-bishop. The knight on c6 stays where it is, pressing d4 - both knights get useful work.

pv: Nec6 b4 Bxd6 exd6 f6 O-O Rc8 Rfe1 fxg5 b5 Nxd4 Nxd4 Qxd6 Nf3 Qe7 Qd4
e: Nec6 puts the second knight on a square where it hits d4 and b4 and supports the key idea Bxd6: after b4 Bxd6 exd6 f6 you attack the g5-bishop, open the f-file and the d6-pawn is picked up later by ...Qxd6. That plan untangles you while keeping the material balance.

pv: dxc4 Rc1 cxb3 Nxb3 Rfd8 g3 Qa3 Qe2 a5 Rfd1 Rd5 Rc4 Rb4 Rd2 Rxc4 Qxc4
