ep: Nc6? walks into Bb5!, and the pin turns nasty: ...a6 fails to Nxc6!, when ...bxc6 Bxc6+ forks king and a8-rook, so Black must grovel with ...Qc7 and Nxe7+ nets material. The game's ...Bd7 Nxd7 Qxd7 kept things together, but the free d4-pawn was gone for good (-0.5).

pv: Qxc6 Nc3 Nf6 Qe2 b4 Nb5 e6 a4 Be7 O-O O-O b3 c4 Bf4 Rfc8 h3
e: Take the passer: Qxc6! removes White's one trump and wins a clean pawn, since nothing defends c6. Keeping queens on also favors you - White's whole queenside is still at home - and after Nc3 Nf6 Qe2 b4! the knight is kicked while you consolidate a healthy pawn up (+1.2).
ep: Qxd1+? trades your active queen and does White a favor: Kxd1 centralizes his king for the endgame and the c6-pawn survives. After ...e6 Nc3, Nxb5 wins your b-pawn, and by the time ...Nxc6 finally removes the passer, material is level again (-0.1).

pv: f5 f3 exf3 gxf3 Be7 Nf4 Nxf4 Bxf4 Bf6 c3 bxc3 bxc3 Kf7 a4 Bxc3 Rb1
e: f5! cements your space: it shores up the e4-pawn and frees ...Be7-f6 against the queenside dark squares. If White breaks with f3, then ...exf3 gxf3 wrecks his structure; after ...Be7, Nf4 Nxf4 Bxf4 Bf6 the bishop lands on the long diagonal and ...Bxc3 collects a pawn a few moves later (+1.8).
ep: Rc8 is a tempo too slow: White gets a3!, prying at b4 before you are coordinated, and the queenside opens in his favor - the edge largely evaporates (+0.6). In the game White pushed c7 instead, and after ...Nxc7 you simply won the pawn.

pv: e4 Nc6 Be3 Qa5 a3 Nxe4 Ne2 d5 cxd6 Nxd6 Nd4 Be7 Nxc6 bxc6 Bf4 Nf5
e: e4 treats the c5-pawn as a gambit and takes the centre instead. After Nc6 Be3 Qa5 a3 the pawn may go, but Ne2, Nd4 and cxd6 give you the two big pawns, quick development and pressure down the d-file - far more than the extra pawn is worth this early.
ep: b4 tries to hang on to c5 with pawns, but the chain has no base: ...b6 hits it immediately, and after a3 bxc5 b5 Nc7 - the game continuation - the queenside pawns are loose and black's pieces come to good squares.

pv: Ba5 Qc8 Qxc8 Rdxc8 Ra2 Nd4 Rd1 Nd7 Bc3 g5 Rb2 Bf6 Be4 Rxb2 Bxb2 Rb8
e: Ba5 saves the bishop with tempo: from a5 it attacks the queen on c7. After Qc8 Qxc8 Rdxc8 the queens come off and only then Ra2 goes after the knight on c2, so you emerge with the bishop pair and the pieces coordinated instead of dropping a piece.
ep: Ra2 attacks the knight but forgets that the bishop on d2 was undefended: Rxd2 simply wins it, and after Nc3 Rd6 Nb5 Rxa6 the rook activity leaves black a clean piece up.

pv: Qxc3 Nxc3 Ra1 Bf6 Ra8 Rxa8 Bxa8 g5 Kg2 Kf8 Bb7 Bd4 f4 gxf4 gxf4 Ke7
e: Qxc3 trades off black's dominating queen while you still can. After Nxc3 Ra1 Bf6 Ra8 Rxa8 Bxa8 the rooks come off too, and although you are worse, an endgame with the bishop pair pointed at the queenside is far more defensible than being attacked by a queen on c3.
ep: Qe4 leaves the knight on c4 without a defender, since your queen no longer sees it down the blocked c-file: Rb4 skewers it and after h4 Bf8 h5 Qxc4 the piece drops - your opponent played Rb4 at once.

pv: Nd7 Bc2 a5 Re3 b5 a3 Bb7 Nf1 b4 Ng3 Rac8 Nh5 bxc3 bxc3
e: Nd7! keeps e5 firmly under control and turns to Black's classic plan in this structure: the minority attack — a5, then b5-b4 with Bb7 (the line runs Bc2 a5 Re3 b5 and b4), creating a permanent weakness on c3. The e5 break needs far more preparation than it has.
ep: e5? drops material to the pile-up on e5: dxe5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 Rxe5! Rxe5 and now Nc4! forks queen and rook — and dxc4 runs into Bh7+! Kxh7 Qxd6 winning the queen anyway. In the game White chose the simpler Rxe5 Qxe5 Nf3, gaining decisive tempo against your queen and the weak d5-pawn.

pv: Bxg4 Rxe8+ Nxe8 Qh4 Bxh3 Kh2 Bf1 a4 Ng7 Kg1 Bh3 Bb3 Ne8 a5 h5 f3
e: Bxg4! wins a clean pawn, because hxg4?? loses a rook to Rxe1+ — nothing defends e1. So White must settle for Rxe8+ Nxe8, which conveniently hits the f6-queen, and after Qh4 Bxh3 you have taken a second free pawn while the attack dissolves: two up and winning.
ep: Qe7? lets White off the hook: Qf4! declines the trade, Nf3 holds g4 (hxg4 hxg4), and Bb3 turns against d5 — the loose g4/h3 pawns get consolidated. In the game Qxe7 Rxe7 f4! flipped things: the f4-f5 storm hit your e6-bishop and g6, and a +2.2 position became a difficult defense.

pv: Be4+ Ke3 f5 a3 f4+ Kf2 d4 cxd4+ Kxd4 Ba2 f3 a4 a5 Bf7
e: Be4+! wins by force: it drives the king back (Ke3), and then the pawns roll — f5, f4+ and d4!: after cxd4+ Kxd4 your king invades d4, and f3! creates a decisive passed pawn while the e4-bishop covers everything behind it.
ep: h5? spends the tempo the breakthrough needed: Ke3! and the white king reaches the blockade — with d4 and e4 covered, f4+ no longer comes with the king invasion, and +3.4 faded to +0.6. The game confirmed it: after Bg4 a3 f5 Bc2 f4+ Kf2 White held the fort.

pv: Kb3 Bxb7 a5 a4 Kxb2 Bc6 Kc3 Bb5 Kd4 Bc6 Ke5 Bb5 Kd5 Be8 Kd6 Bb5
e: Kb3! goes straight for the queenside pawns: after Bxb7 a5! puts the a-pawn out of the bishop's reach, and a4 Kxb2 wins the b-pawn — your outside a-pawn plus the active king then give the only genuine winning chances, since the lone bishop cannot hold both wings forever.
ep: b6? gives White time for Bc2!, covering b3 — the king's only entry square to the queenside. With the kingside fixed (h5 against h4) and no way in, it is a dead draw; the game's Bb7 a5 fizzled the same way.

pv: Bxf7 Nxa2+ Kb1 Nc3+ Nxc3 Bf8 Qxf8 h5 Qg8#
e: Bxf7! finishes: the bishop covers g8, so Qg8# is the threat and Black has only spite checks — Nxa2+ Kb1 Nc3+ Nxc3, then Bf8 delays it once, Qxf8 h5 Qg8#. Mate in 5. The e8-queen had done the infiltration; f7 was the one square that needed a helper to deliver mate.
ep: Bxe7 takes a pawn but abandons the mating net — without a defender of g8 there is no Qg8+, and c4! Bxb4 cxb3 axb3 let Black liquidate your attacking pieces. Still completely winning (+4.4), but a forced mate became a long technical game, which is how blitz points get away.

pv: Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 Rc8 Kb1 e6 Nh3 Na5 Ng5 Nc4 Bc1 Bd6 g3 b5 Ne2 b4
e: The f5-bishop points straight at c2, right next to your castled king — challenge it now with Bd3. After Bxd3 Qxd3 the pressure is gone, Kb1 comes next, and the g1-knight can develop via h3 to g5, poking at f7, as in the main line.
ep: Nge2 lets Black pile up on c2: Nb4!, and Bxc2 can't be prevented — Qxc2 would run into Nxc2, winning queen for bishop and knight. After Bg5 Bxc2 Re1 Bh7 the pawn is gone and the bishop is safe. Black played h4 in the game and missed it.

pv: g4 hxg3 Nxg3 Bg6 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 h4 Bd6 Nce2 Bxf4+ Nxf4 Qc7 Qd2 O-O-O
e: g4! asks the f5-bishop the question with tempo, and that tempo is the whole game: after hxg3 Nxg3 the bishop is hit again, and Bg6 Bd3 finally trades off the piece eyeing c2 — Black never gets a free move for Nb4.
ep: g3 attacks nothing, and the free move is Nb4!: c2 collapses — g4 Bxc2 g5 Nh5 a3 Bxd1! and the bishop grabs a whole rook on its way out. In the game Black recaptured hxg3 at once, and you transposed to roughly what g4 would have given.

pv: Nxe6 Nxe5 Qd4 Qd6 Ng7+ Kf8 f4 Bf6 Nf5 gxf5 fxe5 Bxe5 Qxd5 Qxd5 Nxd5 Rc5
e: Take the right pawn: Nxe6! comes with tempo on the d8-queen, and fxe6?? loses to Qxg6+ — Kf8 Qg7+ Ke8 Qxh8+ collects the rook. Black has to decline with Nxe5, and after Qd4 Qd6 Ng7+! Kf8 f4 you keep the extra pawn and the initiative.
ep: Nxg6 counts on the fork of e7 and h8, but Nc5! interrupts with a hit on your queen, and only after Qd4 does Black take fxg6 — a knight for two pawns. In the game it went worse still: Bg5+! f4 Bh6, and after Nxh8 Nxe5! your position fell apart.

pv: Nxf7 Nxf7 Rg8+ Kd7 Nxd5 exd5 Qh3+ Qe6 Qxe6+ Kxe6 Rxc8 Kd7
e: Nxf7! rescues the cornered knight at a profit: after Nxf7 comes Rg8+! Kd7, and now Nxd5! blows up the center — exd5 Qh3+ forces Qe6, and Qxe6+ Kxe6 Rxc8 wins a whole rook. Every move is a check or capture, so Black never gets to consolidate.
ep: Rf1 hands Black a breather: Nc4 hits b2, and after Qg8+ Kd7 Rxf4 Qxf4 Qxf7+ the forced trades leave far less than the rook-winning line. In the game Kd7 Nxf7 Nxf7 followed — the knight escaped, but the advantage kept shrinking.

pv: c3 Qg5 Rxf4 Qg2 Rd1 b5 Rg1 Qxh2 Rxc4 Rxc4 Qe3 Kd6 a3 e5 Qb6+ Rc6
e: Qf6 and the c4-knight both aim at b2: Qxb2, supported by the knight, would be mate. c3! blocks the f6-b2 diagonal first, and only then is the bishop really won — Qg5 Rxf4 Qg2 Rd1 leaves you a clean piece up with the king finally safe.
ep: Rxf4 grabs the bishop and gets mated: Qxb2#, the queen protected by the c4-knight, with a1 and c1 covered and every other square blocked by your own pawns. One diagonal — f6 to b2 — was the only thing that mattered. That is how the game ended.

pv: Nxe4 Qxe4 Qd5 Qe3 Bf5 c3 e6 Nf3 Be7 g3 Nd7 Bg2 Qe4 a4 Qxe3+ Bxe3
e: Trade first: Nxe4 Qxe4 and only then Qd5, hitting the queen and offering an exchange that solves all of black's problems. After Qe3 the bishop comes out with ...Bf5 anyway, but now with the knight on e4 gone it is completely safe, and ...e6, ...Be7, ...Nd7 follow with an equal game.
ep: Bf5 forgets that the knight on f6 is the only thing shielding the new bishop from the queen on d3: Nxf6+ forces exf6 (or gxf6), and then Qxf5 simply wins the bishop. In the game white missed it and played f3.

pv: Qc7 Ne5 Nd7 Nxd7 Qxd7 gxh6 gxh6 Bf4 Bd6 Bd2 Bc7 O-O-O O-O-O Qf3 Qxd4 Bd3
e: Qc7 keeps the h-file shut and finishes development: Ne5 Nd7 Nxd7 Qxd7 trades a pair of pieces, and only then gxh6 gxh6 with a solid, roughly level position. The rule of thumb in these lines is that you should not open the h-file toward your own bishop on h7 and king on e8 while white's rook is aimed at it.
ep: hxg5 opens exactly that h-file: white recaptures hxg5, and after ...Nd7 the g6! break rips open f7 and g6 while your king is still sitting in the centre.

pv: Nd7 Bg2 c5 Qc3 O-O-O d5 exd5 Rxd5 Nb6 Rxd8+ Rxd8 b3 Nd7 h5 Bf6 e5
e: Nd7 brings the last piece out and prepares ...c5 and ...O-O-O, getting the king off the open e-file: Bg2 c5 Qc3 O-O-O and black is fully coordinated. Note that the bishop on g6 depends on the pawn on f7 staying put, so the pieces must come out before the queen goes hunting.
ep: Qg3 puts the queen on a square where Rg1 traps it, and Nxe6! deflects the f7 pawn first: fxe6 Rg1 Qxh4 Rxg6 leaves the bishop hanging. In the game Bd2 chased the queen and it was traded off on d3 instead.

pv: Qd2 a4 Nxe6 fxe6 Rab1 Rb8 h5 h6 Rbe1 Rb5 f4 Nf7 Rb1 Rxb1 Rxb1 Qd6
e: Your queen on d3 is attacked by the c4-pawn — Qd2 deals with that first. Nothing runs away: after a4 Nxe6 fxe6 you make the same capture a move later under clean conditions, keeping the bishop pair, the g4/h4 space and a solid +1.0.
ep: Nxe6? ignores the attack on your queen and allows a zwischenzug: Qb6+! Bf2 Qxf2+! Rxf2 cxd3 and Black wins queen for bishop — Nf4 dxc2 Rxc2 recovers some material, but the edge is gone. In the game Rxe6? missed it and you stayed on top.

pv: e4 Qa5 Bd2 Qxc5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 Be7 Qe2 Ng4 Nb5 O-O h3 Nge5 Nxe5 Nxe5
e: e4 stakes the big center: the c5-pawn cannot be held anyway, so after Qa5 Bd2 Qxc5 Nf3 you convert it into development and tempi against the early queen - a broad center, quick Bd3 and O-O, full value for the pawn you were always giving back.
ep: Bf4 lets Black regain c5 with the natural Bxc5, and after e3 Bb4 the pin plus Nd5! harasses your bishop - Nxf4 exf4 doubles your pawns. In the game Bxc5 came with tempo ideas, and Qb6 with Bxf2! soon snagged a pawn.

pv: Nxf2 Qxf2 Ne4 Qb6 Nd6+ Ke7 Qc3 f6 h3 Nh6 Nxc8+ Rxc8 Qxc8 Nf7 Bxb8 Ne5
e: Nxf2! simply wins material: both invaders are loose, so the knight takes the bishop, and Qxf2 runs into Ne4! hitting the queen again - after Qb6 Nd6+ Ke7 the king is stuck, and Qc3 with Nxc8+ wins heavy material (+4.5). Two Black pieces jumped in unsupported; make them pay.
ep: e3 overlooks that the f2-bishop bites back: Bxe3! forks your queen and the f4-bishop, and after Bxe3 Qxe3 the pressure lands on d2 again - the queens come off and you are a pawn down instead of winning. The game continued exactly that way.

pv: Nf2 h5 Nf4 Ng4 Nxh5 Ne5 Nd3 Nbd7 Nxe5 Nxe5 Re1 Nd7 Rd3 g6 Rg3 a5
e: Nf2! slams the cage shut on the h2-knight: g4 is covered by your new knight, f3 by the g2-pawn and f1 by the d1-rook - it has no square at all. Black's only rescue attempt, h5 and Ng4, runs into Nxh5: you win a pawn and keep the knight boxed in - real compensation for your pawn deficit.
ep: a4 lets the knight walk home: Ng4! and via f6 it rejoined play - exactly the game's course after Rd4 Nf6 - while a4 and b4 achieved nothing. With Black three pawns up for the piece, rounding up the cornered h2-knight was your best practical chance.

pv: Rd4 Nc6 Rh4 h5 Rxh5 Ng4 Ng5 f6 Rdh1 Nh6 Nf4 fxg5 Rxg5 Rxf4 Rxh6
e: Rd4! does two jobs: it hits the loose b4-pawn and lifts toward h4, where it keeps g4 covered so the h2-knight stays in its box - and it starts an attack: Rh4, Rxh5 and Ng5 crash in on the black king. Activity like this is worth more than a queenside pawn.
ep: a5 is a pawn move in a piece battle: Ng4! and the trapped knight escapes toward f6, exactly as in the game (Rd4 Nf6 followed), after which Black's extra pawns simply tell. The lift Rd4-h4 would have kept the knight caged and created threats of your own.

pv: Bd1
e: The d5-pawn is defended by the f6-knight, so leave it alone: Bd1 saves the bishop from its dead end on b3 and reroutes it toward f3, where it hits e4 and d5 with real pressure instead of giving itself up for a pawn.
ep: Bxd5 runs into Nxd5 - the knight both recaptures and hits your b6-rook, so there is no Rxf6 trick, and you are simply a piece down. In the game Black recaptured exd5?, letting Rxf6 restore the material, and the e-pawn race ended in a draw.

pv: Re6+ Kf5 Rxa6 h4 Rh6 h3 gxh3 g3 Rh7 Rg8 Rf7+ Kg5 Rf1 Rb8 a6 Kh4
e: Re6+! is a fork in two steps: after any king move Rxa6 wins the pawn, and Rh6 then rounds up the h-pawn as well (h4 Rh6 h3 gxh3) - with the kingside pawns gone, your a- and b-passers walk in. The check makes everything come with tempo.
ep: Re5 lets the pawns off the hook: h4! and after c4 h3 gxh3 gxh3 your rook gets chained to the h-file while the a6-pawn survives - the win is gone. In the game Rc6 defended a6 laterally and Black held the draw.

pv: Kf2 Kf6 Rh5 h2 Rxh2 Rd2+ Kg3 Rd3+ Kf4 Rd4+ Ke3 Ra4 Rh6+ Ke7
e: Kf2 marches straight at the h-pawn: after Kf6 Rh5! h2 Rxh2 the pawn is gone, and Black's checks (Rd2+, Rd3+, Rd4+) dry up quickly - then Rh6+ cuts the king off and the a/b-pawns decide. King to the pawn, rook stays free: standard technique.
ep: Kf3 allows Rd2!, seizing the second rank: h2 follows and your rook ends up nailed to the h-file (Re1, then Rh1) while Black's rook harasses from behind - exactly the game's course, and the win from +4.6 became a grind that later slipped away.

pv: Kg2 h1=R Kxh1 Kf7 b6 Rd1+ Kg2 Rb1 Kf2 Kf6 Rh5 Rb2+ Ke3
e: Kg2! ends the h-pawn story: the king attacks h2 and covers h1, so even h1=Q+ Kxh1 just removes the pawn - after Kf7 b6 your rook is still active on e5 and the connected passers win trivially (+5.0).
ep: Re1 condemns your rook to passivity: Rd5! wins the b5-pawn while your rook must keep watching h1, and rook against the lone a-pawn with Black's king near is a dead draw - the game's Rd2, Ra2 and later Ra5 held exactly that way.

pv: a6 Ra2 Rh1 Kf6 Rxh2 Rxh2 a7 Ra2 b6 Ke6 b7 Rxa7 b8=Q Rd7 Ke4 Re7
e: a6! wins the race by a tempo: after Ra2 Rh1 Kf6 you can even give rook for the h-pawn (Rxh2 Rxh2), because a7! and b6-b7 cost Black his rook - Rxa7 b8=Q and you emerge a whole queen for rook up. The pawn standing on a6 rather than a5 is the entire difference.
ep: Rh1 is a tempo too slow: Rd5! wins the b5-pawn while you collect h2, and rook plus the lone a-pawn against an active king and rook is a book draw. The game's Ra2, a6, Ra5 defense held the same way - the win needed a6 first.

pv: Rxh2 Rxh2 a7 Ra2 b6 Ra6 b7 Rxa7 b8=Q Rd7 Qf8+ Rf7 Qd8+ Ke6+ Ke4 Rd7
e: Cash in the h-pawn now: after Rxh2 Rxh2 your connected passers beat the rook — a7 Ra2 b6 Ra6 b7 Rxa7 b8=Q and the new queen wins against the rook (+2.5). The rook trade looks scary, but two connected pawns on the 6th, supported by the king, are faster than Black's counterplay.
ep: Kg3 attacks h2 one tempo too late: Ra5! hits b5 first, and after Rxh2 Rxb5 the rook holds your lone a-pawn easily — a book draw. The game's Ke6 came to the same thing: Rxh2 Ra5 and the b-pawn fell (+0.0).

pv: Rh7 Ra3+ Kf4 Ra4+ Kf5 Ra2 a7 Rf2+ Kg4 Rg2+ Kf4 Rf2+ Ke3 Ra2 Rh5+ Kd6
e: Rh7! wins because the rook guards the queening path sideways along the seventh rank: after Ra3+ Kf4 Ra4+ Kf5 Ra2 you play a7 with the rook defending it, and once the checks run out (Rf2+ Kg4 Rg2+ Kf4 Rf2+ Ke3) Rh5+ drives the black king back and the pawn promotes (+5.1).
ep: Rh5+ chases the king exactly where it wants to go: Kc4!, and b5 cannot be held — after Kf3 Kb4 the king and a5-rook gang up on it. With b5 gone the rook just sits behind the a-pawn (Ra2, Ra1) and it's a standard draw, as the game confirmed (+0.2).

pv: a5
e: a5! fixes the queenside and — the real point — takes b6 away from the d5-knight, whose route to c4 ran through it. With the knight contained, White's rooks hold the c-file and the balance survives; without that move the a4-pawn becomes a permanent hook.
ep: Rb2 invites Nb6!, hitting a4: after a5 Nc4 the knight forks the b2-rook and the e3-pawn, and Ra2 c5! breaks through the centre as well. In the game Nb6 forced axb5 cxb5, and Black's knight and king took over the light squares.

pv: Ra1 Kf7 Rb3 Ke6 f3 Kd5 Be1 Rc4 Ba5 Ra4 Rxa4 Nxa4 Kf2 Rc8 h4 Rc2+
e: Ra1! puts a rook behind Black's passed a-pawn — the only arrangement that holds runners like these — while the other rook blockades from b3. Combined with f3, undermining e4, and the Be1-a5 regrouping, White builds a blockade with genuine drawing chances.
ep: Rbc2 offers exactly the rook trade the pawns are begging for: Rxc2 Rxc2 b4! and the b-pawn runs with Rb8 and Nc4-d2 as escorts while your rook sits passively on b2. Fewer pieces means faster pawns; the same trade happened in the game and the queenside decided.

pv: Rc6+ Kd7 Rd6+ Ke7 Rxc8 Nxc8 Rg6 Kf7 Rc6 a5 Rc7+ Ke8 Rb7 a4 Rxb5 a3
e: Rc6+! Kd7 Rd6+ Ke7 Rxc8 Nxc8 trades a pair of rooks with checks and unleashes the survivor: Rg6! hits g7, and after Kf7 Rc6 a5 Rc7+ Ke8 Rb7 the rook wins the b5-pawn from behind — active rook play that defuses the passed pawns before they start.
ep: Be5 leaves the bishop loose: Rxc2 Rxc2 Nc4! forks the e5-bishop and the e3-pawn, and after f4 a5 the passers roll with the knight ideally placed. In the game all the rooks came off instead — a pure minor-piece ending where Black's queenside pawns simply win.

pv: Bxg7 a5 Kf1 b4 Ke2 Nb6 Kd2 Kf7 Bh8 a4 d5 Nxd5 f3 Nf6 fxe4 Nxe4+
e: Just take it — Bxg7 is a free pawn (h6 does not cover g7), and in a pawn race every unit counts. After a5 Kf1 b4 Ke2 Nb6 Kd2 the king arrives in time to fight the queenside pawns, and White's d4-pawn plus kingside majority give real counterchances.
ep: Bc7 wins nothing and loses the race: b4! Ba5 b3 Bc3 and Nd6-c4 comes — once the pawn reaches b2 the bishop has to give itself up for it (Bxb2 Nxb2). In the game Kd5-c4 escorted the pawns to the same conclusion.

pv: Kf1 b4 Ke1 Na7 Kd2 Nb5 Bd8 Kc4 f3 Nc3 h3 h5 Ba5 Kb5 Bd8 exf3
e: Only the king can help: Kf1! starts the run. After b4 Ke1 Na7 Kd2 it arrives just in time, the bishop rechecks the pawns from d8, and f3 creates counterplay against e4 — the defense holds together move by move, something no bishop shuffle can achieve.
ep: Ba5 burns a tempo the defense could not spare: Nd6! and the knight heads for c4 — after Kf1 Nc4 Be1 a5 Ke2 b4 Kd1 Nb2+! it escorts the pawns home with gain of time. In the game Kc4 showed the other escort: the king walked up and shepherded b4 through.

pv: Qg6+ Kh1 Qf7 Re1 Qxb3 axb3 Kf7 Be3 Bf6 Ra4 Nc6 d5 Ne5 Raa1
e: With an extra piece for two pawns, the plan is to trade queens and kill White's activity. Qg6+ forces Kh1, and then Qf7 hits the b3-queen along the f7-b3 diagonal: after Re1 Qxb3 axb3 Kf7 the queens are off, your king is safe on f7, and the extra knight decides the endgame.
ep: Qxf3 grabs a pawn but leaves your king on e8: Re1 pins the e7-bishop against it, and with your queen off on f3 you had to spend moves on Rf8 and checks just to untangle — most of the piece-up advantage evaporated. You still converted in the game.

pv: Nc6 Be3 Rf6 Qd1 O-O-O Rb1 Rd7 Rb2 a6 Rg1 Qe4+ Rg2 Rg6 Qf1
e: Nc6 develops with tempo on the d4-pawn and blocks the a4-e8 diagonal, defusing White's checks. After Be3 Rf6 you follow with O-O-O — the king finally leaves the center — and the extra piece takes over.
ep: Qd7 puts the queen on the fatal diagonal: Rxe7+! Kxe7 Ba3+ Ke8 Re1+ Ne6 Rxe6+ Kd8 Rd6 and the pinned queen is lost. Your opponent missed it with Qb4 and you went on to win.

pv: Bxf3 gxf3 Bxd4 Qxd4 Nxd4 Bxd7 Nxf3+ Kg2 Nxg5 Rfb1 Ng6 a4 Rfd8 Rxb7 Nxe5 Bb5
e: Bxf3! gxf3 unlocks Bxd4: after Qxd4 Nxd4 Bxd7, the zwischenzug Nxf3+! forks king and g5-bishop — Kg2 Nxg5 and you emerge two pawns up with White's kingside wrecked. The d4-pawn only looked defended: every recapture sequence runs into that knight check on f3.
ep: h6 asks no question and gives White time to fix everything: g4 shuts your h5-bishop out via Bg6, and once Be3 or Bf4 covers d4 the whole combination is gone. In the game Be3 came at once and the chance never returned.

pv: Qxd6 Bxc6 bxc6 f3 Bc2 Qd2 Ra4 Be3 Bh7 Rfc1 Rc8 Qb2 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Bxc5
e: Your queen is attacked by the e5-knight and the d6-passer is the long-term danger — Qxd6! solves both at once. After Bxc6 bxc6 the passer is gone, both your bishops stay active, and White's whole bind dissolves (+1.6). When a retreat and a capture both save the piece, compare what each leaves on the board.
ep: Qd8 leaves the passer alive and it runs: Nxc6 bxc6 Bxc6! hits the a8-rook, and after Ra7 d7 the pawn reaches the seventh with Bc7 coming to escort it — your pieces end up chained to the promotion square. In the game the pawn duly arrived on d7.

pv: Bd3 Qg4 Bxf1 Nh5 Bf8 Rxf1 Ne7 Rc1 Nf5 Rc3 Kh8 Kh2 Qf1 Qf3 Qb1 g4
e: Bd3! invades on a square your b5-queen protects — Qxd3?? Qxd3 wins queen for bishop — while attacking the f1-rook. White's best is to give the exchange: Qg4 Bxf1 Nh5 (threatening g7) Bf8 Rxf1, and you emerge up rook for bishop with the attack blunted (+2.1).
ep: Bg6 retreats into the path of white's pawns: f4-f5 came in the game, burying the bishop on h7, and after fxe6 fxe6 Qh5 the attack arrived for free. The one-move chance to invade on d3 under the queen's protection was gone (+0.3).

pv: Qxa1 Qg4 Qxe5 Qxb4 Rb8 Qd2 Qd6 Qd4 Rc7 Re3 Bg6 Qg4 e5 Nc3 Rc6
e: The a1-rook is simply loose — your d4-queen sees it down the long diagonal and nothing defends it. Qxa1! wins a whole rook, and after Qg4 Qxe5 you collect the e5-pawn too, killing the attack: white has nothing for the material (+4.4).
ep: g6 hits the queen but hands back the crucial tempo: white saves the rook with gain of time — Rd1! hitting your queen, or Raf1 after Qg4 Qxe5 as in the game. The rook hung for exactly one move, and with it went the whole advantage (-0.2).

pv: Qxa1 Qxb4 Qxe5 Qh4 Qg7 Qg4 Re7 Nc5 g5 Nxe6 Qe5 Nc5 Rd8 Nd3 Bxd3 Rxd3
e: The a1-rook is still hanging: Qxa1! takes it, and even after Qxb4 you have Qxe5 — netting the exchange and a pawn once the dust settles, with white's checks running out quickly (+2.5).
ep: Qxe5 collects one pawn where a whole rook was on offer, and it gives white time for Nb6!, hitting the a8-rook — you must find Bc5 to keep an edge (+1.1). In the game Raf1 finally tucked the rook away.

pv: Bd6 Kg1 Rc7 h4 Re8 Kh1 Kh8 b4 Rc4 Qh3 Qd4 b5 Qxh4 b6 Qxh3+ gxh3
e: Your b4-bishop stands on the same rank as white's queen and needs attention. Bd6! steps out of the hit and joins the e5-queen on the b8-h2 diagonal aiming at g3, keeping you a sound pawn up with the safer king (+3.0).
ep: Rf8 leaves the bishop hanging: Qxb4! wins it, and the try Rxf3 fails to Rxf3, when Qf8+ Bg8 Qxh6+ turns into a mating attack on your own king (-4.8). In the game white's Rxf8+ let the bishop slip back to f8 — the punishment went begging.

pv: Bc5 Qf3 Rc7 Na8 Rc8 Qf7+ Kh8 Qb7 Rb8 Qc6 Qd6 Qa4 h5 Qa1+ d4 b4
e: Bc5! attacks the stray b6-knight and starts hunting it: after Qf3 Rc7 the knight's only square is a8, and Rc8 keeps it locked in the corner — effectively a piece out of play while you stay materially fine and solid (+3.3).
ep: Rf7 invites Rxf7 Kxf7 Nd7! — the knight forks your e5-queen and f8-bishop. After Qd6 Qf3+ Kg8 Nxf8 Qxf8 white has traded off the stranded knight and reached full equality (+0.0), exactly as the game went.

pv: Qd6 Qf3+ Kg8 Nxf8 Qxf8 Qc3 Qd6 b4 h5 Kg1 d4 Qc8+ Kg7 Ne4 Qe5 Qb7+
e: The d7-knight forks your queen and the f8-bishop, and Qd6! is the only move doing both jobs: it steps off the attack while still defending f8 along the d6-f8 diagonal, so Nxf8 Qxf8 just liquidates and the position stays balanced (+0.0).
ep: Defending the queen with Bd6 does not work — Nxe5+ wins queen for knight anyway, since the recapture Bxe5 cannot undo a nine-for-three trade and the check rules out any in-between move (-5.3). The game ended just so: Nxe5+ Bxe5 Qf3+.

pv: O-O Nc5 a4 Nxd3 Qxd3 Bd7 Qd2 h6 Rae1 Rae8 b3 Rf7 h3 d3 Qxd3 e5
e: Castle before the center opens: after O-O, Black's ...Nc5 raid is met by a4 and the trade Nxd3 Qxd3, and the cramping d4-pawn is eventually rounded up (the line ends with Qxd3 collecting it after ...d3) - a level middlegame (0.0) with your king safe.
ep: g3? hands Black the tempo for ...e5!, when ...e4 next forks your d3-bishop and f3-knight with your king still in the middle - the complications (c4 e4 cxd5 Nc5!) all end badly (-3.7). In the game the panic sacrifice Bxh7+? Kxh7 Ng5+ just lost a piece.

pv: f3 Nf6 h4 h6 g4 Nbd7 Nge2 Nb6 Ng3 Nh7 Be2 e5 g5 Qe7 f4 hxg5
e: f3! puts the question to the g4-knight immediately: it must retreat to f6 (e3 and e5 are covered), and with opposite-side castling White's attack then plays itself — h4, g4 and g5 roll at the king, e.g. h4 h6 g4 Nbd7 Nge2-g3 and the storm breaks through (+2.4).
ep: Be2? blocks your own queen's defence of f2 — Qd2 was guarding it along the rank. Now Nxf2! wins the pawn and hits the h1-rook, and only the messy Bb5 bail-out limits the damage. In the game it came a move later anyway: Nxf2 and Nxh1 won the exchange (+0.7).

pv: h4 h6 f3 Nf6 g4 Rh8 Bc4 exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Qe3 Be6
e: h4! keeps building the storm: h5 will pry at g6, and after h6 f3 Nf6 g4 the knight is pushed back with gain of time; Bc4 and Qxd4 then collect the center — e.g. exd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Qe3 with a strong attack still in the bank (+1.9).
ep: h3? pokes the knight toward its best square: Nxf2!, grabbing a pawn and hitting the h1-rook — and since Be2 still blocks your queen's defence of f2, there's no clean way to win it back (best is the murky Bb5 c6 Qxf2 cxb5). The game's Nf3? made it worse: Nxh1 won the exchange (+0.6).

pv: Bb5 c6 Qxf2 cxb5 Nd5 Qd8 Ne2 Nc6 dxe5 dxe5 g4 Be6 h4 h6 Rhg1 b4
e: The f2-knight forks your rooks, so deflect before it cashes in: Bb5! attacks the e8-queen, and with the bishop off e2 the queen's path opens — after c6, Qxf2! scoops the knight; then cxb5 Nd5! (eyeing c7) and Ne2 untangles, keeping a small plus (+0.5).
ep: Nf3? does nothing about the fork: Nxh1!, and after Rxh1 Black has won rook and pawn for the knight (-2.5). The f2-knight had to be met tactically — Bb5!, clearing e2 so the queen could recapture on f2 — not by developing around it.

pv: Ne4+ Kf5 Bxf3 Nxd5 Qg5+ Ke6 Bg4+ Rf5 Bxf5#
e: Ne4+! forces Kf5 (g5 is covered by your queen), and the quiet Bxf3! closes the net — the bishop is headed for g4. Even Nxd5, grabbing a piece, allows Qg5+ Ke6 Bg4+ Rf5 Bxf5#: mate in 5, with every white piece trained on the stranded king.
ep: Nh5+? lets the king reach f5 with the knight offside: the follow-up Ng7+ just repeats after Kf6, and the forced mate is gone (+5.4). The game stayed winning with Bd3+ and Qf4+, but the king escaped the net that Ne4+ would have closed.

pv: Qg3+ Kf5 gxf3 Qxh5 Rxh5+ Kf6 Qg5+ Kf7 Rxh7+ Ke8 Qxe7#
e: Qg3+! drives the king forward: after Kf5 the calm gxf3! renews the mating threats around g4, and Black's best is already to give up the queen with Qxh5 — then Rxh5+ Kf6 Qg5+ Kf7 Rxh7+ Ke8 Qxe7# forces mate in 6 regardless.
ep: Bxe4+? looks crushing but Nf5! blocks everything — the knight covers g7 and g3 — and with all the material White has invested, Qxf3 leaves the attack spent and the game dead level (+0.0). You were rescued by Bf5??, when Qg4+ Kf7 Qg7# mated after all.

pv: Bh6 e5 Bxg7 Kxg7 Be2 Nf4 dxe5 dxe5 g3 Nxe2+ Ngxe2 Rh8 Qh6+ Kg8 Rd6
e: Bh6! trades the fianchetto bishop first: after Bxg7 Kxg7 the h5-knight becomes the question — Be2! attacks it, and after Nf4 g3! it must give itself up; the best line flows into Qh6+ and Rd6 with White's initiative in full swing (+0.9). The capture on h5 would still be there if it were ever good.
ep: Rxh5 gxh5 gives rook for knight with no second wave: after Bh6 e5! (the game) and Qf6, Black's dark squares held and nothing came through — you stayed the exchange down for nothing (-0.8). A sacrifice on h5 needs another attacker ready to land.

pv: f4 Ng4 Rh1 Nf6 Bxh5 Nxh5 Rxh5 f6 f5 Qe7 Nf3 Bd7 g4 d5 e5 fxe5
e: f4! pushes the e5-knight back and goes after the weak h5-pawn: after Ng4 Rh1 Nf6, Bxh5! Nxh5 Rxh5 regains it with the rook actively placed, and f5 gains space next (best line, -0.6 — your best practical chance in a slightly worse position).
ep: Nf5 jumps into a defended square: Bxf5! exf5 removes your good knight and splits your pawns, and d5! (punish line and game) fixes the structure with Black's e5-knight dominating the e2-bishop. The game's Bxh5 won a pawn back but Nc4! and b5 seized the initiative (-2.4).

pv: Ng3 Rg8 Bxf7 Rxg3 fxg3 Qe4 Qxe4 dxe4 Bxc4 bxc4 Re1 c3 Rxe4 Rf8 Re6 cxb2+
e: Ng3! guards e4, so the queen trade can only happen on your terms, and meets Rg8 with Bxf7!: after Rxg3 fxg3 Qe4 Qxe4 dxe4 Bxc4 bxc4 Re1 the smoke clears into a winning rook endgame — the f6-pawn and extra pawns decide (+2.4).
ep: Rg1 hits the queen but allows Qe4! — now the trade comes in Black's version, leaving him the exchange up (+0.2 at best). In the game you avoided it with Qh6 and the back rank bit: Rg8! Bxf7 Rxg1+ Nxg1 Qe1# — mate. e1 was the square nobody was watching.

pv: Rg7 Qh1+ Ng1 Qxg1+ Rxg1 Rxg1+ Bd1 Re8 b3 Ne5 Kb2 a5 Bh5 a4 Qd2 a3+
e: Rg7!! is the only move: it steps off g1 — killing the Rxg1+ trick — while counterattacking the g8-rook. Black's best is the forcing Qh1+ Ng1 Qxg1+! Rxg1 Rxg1+ Bd1, giving his queen for rook and knight: a level endgame (+0.0) instead of mate. Back-rank problems get solved with maximum tempo.
ep: Bxf7 attacks the g8-rook one move too late: Rxg1+! Nxg1 Qe1# — the game ended exactly this way. With the king boxed in by b2 and c2 and only the e2-knight covering g1, the back rank had to be dealt with before anything else.

pv: Bd3
e: Bd3 finishes development and keeps your king's future open. With black's pawns already on b5 and c6 and his queenside ready to roll, you want to see where he commits before choosing a side — the bishop on d3 is useful in every version.
ep: O-O-O castles straight into the pawn storm: b4! hits the c3 knight, and after Bxf6 bxc3 Qxd7+ Qxd7 Rxd7 cxb2+ the pawn wedge on b2 leaves your king permanently draughty for at most a pawn.

pv: f4 Bb4 Nf3 Nxe4 Qe3 Nxg5 fxg5 O-O Ne4 Qc7 Bd3 Qa7 Qxa7 Rxa7 c3 Be7
e: f4 strikes at e5 while black is still uncastled and opens the f-file toward his king. Keeping the bishop on g5 matters: it ties the f6 knight down, and after Bb4 Nf3 the black pieces have no time to consolidate around the centre.
ep: Bxf6 trades your active bishop for a developed knight and hands black the bishop pair; worse, Qxf6 puts his queen on the best square in the position, hitting f4, f2 and the long diagonal. You had to play the f-pawn forward anyway a move later.

pv: Ke1 Rxd1+ Kxd1 Kf6 Kd2 Kg5 Kc3 g6 fxg6 hxg6 Nd2 f5 exf5 gxf5 b3 Kg4
e: Ke1 steps off the a6-f1 diagonal before anything else. Then the rook trade Rxd1+ Kxd1 costs black no tempo, the king comes to d2 and c3 in front of the a5/c4 pawns, and the knight gets back into the game via d2.
ep: Ke2 walks onto the a6 bishop's diagonal, so c3+ arrives as a discovered check: Ke1 Rxd1+ Kxd1 cxb2 leaves the pawn one square from queening and Bc4xa2 cleans up the rest. That is exactly what happened.

pv: Qd4 Bd7 Bd3 Qa5 Bc4 Be8 Rhg1 Rd8 e4 c6 Kb1 h5 Bd2 h4 Ne2 Qc5
e: Sidestep the trade: Qd4! keeps queens on against a king stuck on f8 with the h8-rook buried — after Bd7 Bd3 Qa5 Bc4 you keep probing f7 and the queenside while Black's rook never enters the game. Your +2.5 is made of attacking chances; the queen trade is exactly what the defense is praying for.
ep: Bd3 walks into Qxe4 Bxe4, and with queens off the exposed f8-king stops mattering: Black's structure holds everything, and in the game the kingside pawns rolled for free — g5, h5, h4 — turning +2.5 into a +0.8 grind. The advantage was dynamic, and it did not survive the simplification.

pv: Bc5 Ne7 Rhg1 Kf7 Bxe7 f5 Bd3 Kxe7 Rg7+ Kf8 Rc7 Be6 Rxb7 Rg8 Rh7 Rd8
e: Bc5! keeps the g8-knight in its box — e7 is its only square, and after Ne7 Rhg1 Kf7 Bxe7 the replacement is removed too; Kxe7 Rg7+ Kf8 Rc7 then puts the rook on the seventh to harvest b7. With +4.5 the recipe is domination: the knight stays buried while the rooks feast.
ep: Bc7 leaves the key diagonal and unblocks e7: Ne7! finally develops the knight (in the game Ke7 and Nh6 did the same job), and your bishop bites on air on c7. The win shrank from +4.5 to a +2.3 grind — a dominated piece must be kept dominated; every escape tempo costs.

pv: Qxc4 Ka5 Qc6 b3 Kd4 Kb4 Qc5+ Ka4 Kc4 b2 Qb4#
e: Qxc4! takes the pawn and mates in 6: Ka5 Qc6! boxes the king on the edge, then b3 Kd4! brings your king in — Kb4 Qc5+ Ka4 Kc4, and the pawn's spite push changes nothing: b2 Qb4#. In queen versus pawns, capture so the enemy king stays confined; your own king is the second mating piece.
ep: Kd2?? misses that your queen on c3 stands on the b4-pawn's capture square: bxc3+! removes her with check, and after Kxc3 it is a dead draw — you round up the c-pawn but nothing more. From mate in 6 to a half point in one move, and in the game the ending even slipped into a loss.

pv: Qc4 bxc6 Qxd4 Rh7 b4 Qc7 Qe3+ Ne6 O-O-O Re7 Bxe7 Qxe7 Ng3 Qf6 Ne4 Qf4
e: First save the queen - the c5-knight attacks it - and do it with tempo: Qc4! keeps hitting c5, and after bxc6 it centralises with Qxd4!, a double attack on the c5-knight and the h8-rook (line: Qc4 bxc6 Qxd4 Rh7). +3.9 with total board control.
ep: cxb7 ignores the hanging queen: the cool Bxb7! forces you to move it anyway, with the c-passer gone (+2.2). In the game Black grabbed Nxb3? instead, allowing bxa8=Q, and you won - but Bxb7 was the refutation.

pv: dxc5
e: dxc5! bxc5 — and the disappearance of the b6-pawn decides the game: when Black locks up with ...c4, your king now has an entry route, Kd4–c5–d6, winning e6 and d5 while the black king is stuck munching f4. After c3 and a5 the invasion is unstoppable and you promote first (+2.4).
ep: c3? allows ...c4!, sealing the queenside while b6 still covers c5 — with no entry square anywhere your king can only shuffle while Black's takes f4: a dead draw (+0.0). You were let off in the game: Black played ...a5 instead, and dxc5 was still available a move later.

pv: h6 Ra2 Qb4 Qxb4 Nxb4 Ra3 Bc2 Be3 Rc8 Bb3 Nbd5 Bxd5 Nxd5 Rc1 Nxe3 fxe3
e: You are two pawns up with the queen deep on b2 - the job is to consolidate, not to move pieces to loose squares. h6 gives the king air and takes all back-rank ideas out of the position; then Ra2 Qb4 Qxb4 Nxb4 trades the queens off and leaves a comfortable, safe endgame with the extra material.
ep: The knight was fine on c6; Na5 puts it on the e1-a5 diagonal where the queen simply takes it, Qxa5, and a winning position becomes level. In the game white played Ba2 instead and you got away with it.

pv: Ne2 d5 a3 Bxc3+ Nxc3 Nbc6 e5 Qd7 Bb5 a6 Ba4 b5 Bb3 f6 exf6 gxf6
e: Ne2 deals with the pin on c3: the knight stands ready to recapture, so after d5 a3 Bxc3+ Nxc3 the e4/d4 center stays intact and black's bishop pair means little. Keeping c3 covered while holding the big center is the whole battle in this structure (+0.4).
ep: Bc4 puts the bishop on the one square d5 hits with tempo: after exd5 Nxd5 the knight attacks your f4-bishop, and with c3 pinned by Bb4 the trades Nxf4 and Bxc3+ leave black slightly for choice (-0.7). In the game black took on c3 at once and let you regroup.

pv: h4 exd5
e: h4! comes with the concrete threat of h5, hitting the g6-knight before black gets settled. It keeps your g3-bishop doing its job and forces black to spend time on the knight's future — you meet exd5 on your own terms (+0.9).
ep: Nf4 offers a trade that solves black's problems: Nxf4 Bxf4 Qf6! hits the f4-bishop, and after Qd2 exd5 black simply pockets the d5-pawn (-2.0). In the game Qg5 was just as awkward, hitting f4 immediately.

pv: h5 d4 e6 Nc3 c5 Bg5 f6 Bf4 cxd4 Qxd4 Nc6 Bb5 Kf7 Bxc6 bxc6 Qd2
e: h5! stops h4-h5 dead and keeps the g6-bishop breathing. Yes, it concedes g5, but that bishop is the whole point of this Caro line — after d4 e6 Nc3 c5 Bg5 f6 Black has a normal game with the good bishop outside the pawn chain (+1.0).
ep: h6 ignores the threat. h5! shoves the bishop to h7, where it stares at its own e6/d5 pawns, and after d4 c5 c3 Nc6 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 Black has traded his good bishop for White's and stands slightly worse. +1.0 to -0.3. When White plays h4 at your g6-bishop, h5 is almost always the answer.

pv: e5 Qh4 Bc5+ Ke1 Nhf6 Nd2 Rhe8 b4 Bf8 Nb3 d4 Bd2 dxc3 Nxc3
e: e5! grabs the centre with tempo — the d4-queen must run to h4, and then Bc5+ comes with check, after which Nhf6 and Rhe8 pour in against the king stranded on f2. b4 Bf8 Nb3 d4 and Black's pawns roll (+3.3).
ep: Qb6 offers to trade Black's best attacking piece. Qxb6 axb6 and with queens off the exposed white king on f2 is perfectly safe, while b4 and Ng3-f5 give him a plan. +3.3 down to +1.8. With the enemy king stuck in the middle, keep queens on and open the centre.

pv: Re2 Rb1 Kc4 Rd1 Kd3 a5 c4 Kg3 c3 Rb1 Kc4
e: Re2! The rook defends d2 from the side and cuts the white king off the e-file, so the black king can march up: Rb1 Kc4 Rd1 Kd3 and the pawn is escorted home. +7.3, completely winning. Escort the passer with the king before advancing anything else.
ep: c4 pushes the wrong pawn and leaves d2 unsupported. Ke3! and White's king walks straight in: c3 Kd3 Kxc3 and both black queenside pawns eventually drop while Black grabs f3 in return. Still winning at +4.3, but a rook ending instead of a forced promotion.

pv: Ke5 Kxc3 Kf4 Kc2 Kxf3 Rf1+ Rf2 Rh1 Rg2 Rh3+ Kxg4 Rh1 Kf3
e: Ke5! Let c3 go and win the race on the other wing: Kxc3 Kf4 Kc2 Kxf3 and Black's king eats f3 and then g4, while the h2-rook holds the d2-pawn on its own. Two connected passers against nothing, +4.7.
ep: Rf2 ties the rook to a passive defensive job and loses the race outright: Kxc3 and after Rxf3+ Kxd2 White has picked off both black pawns for nothing. +4.7 down to +0.9 — a drawish rook ending instead of a win. In races, activity beats material every time.

pv: Ke6 Ke4 b6 Kf4 Kf6 Kf3 Kg5 Kg3 Kf6
e: Ke6! Keep the king in contact with the kingside pawns — the b5-pawn is not running anywhere. After Ke4 b6 Kf4 Kf6 Kf3 Kg5 Black's king holds the key squares in front of g4/h5 and it's a dead draw (0.00).
ep: Kc5 goes pawn-hunting on the wrong wing and loses the race: Kf5! Kxb5 Kg6 Kc5 Kxg7 and the kingside pawns queen first. -1.4. In a pure king-and-pawn ending, count the race to the last square before you chase anything.

pv: gxh6 Kf5 b5 Kg6 b4 Kxh6 b3 Kg7 b2 h6 b1=Q h7 Qb2+ Kg8 Qb3+ Kf8
e: gxh6! Take the pawn while you still can — it is the one that is closest to promoting. After Kf5 b5 Kg6 b4 Kxh6 b3 Kg7 b2 h6 b1=Q h7 both sides queen and Black has the checks; the engine calls it level (0.00).
ep: b5 leaves the h6-pawn alive, and it is decisive: hxg7! Now the g-pawn queens with the h-pawn right behind it — Kb6 h6 Kc5 g8=Q h7 and it is mate in eight. The b-pawn was several tempi too slow. Deal with the enemy passer nearest the queening square first, always.

pv: Kf5 Kh5 Qxh7#
e: Kf5 is mate in two. The king takes g4, g5 and g6 away, so White's only legal move is Kh5 (Kg7 runs into the h8-queen), and Qxh7# finishes: the queen covers the h-file while the king on f5 seals every flight square. Walk the king to the square that removes escape squares, then deliver mate.
ep: Kf6 still wins easily, but it leaves g4 free, so after Kh5 Qxh7+ Kg4 the white king escapes and Black has to spend another dozen moves driving it to the edge. A queen against a bare pawn should be mate in two here — the difference between f5 and f6 is exactly the g4-square.

pv: a6 Bf4 Be7 Be2 Nd7 a3 g5 Be3 Bg6 Qd2 h6 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 O-O h4
e: a6! deals with the one real threat — Bb5 pinning the c6-knight — before doing anything else. With b5 covered, White's c5-pawn stays a long-term weakness: best line a6 Bf4 Be7 Be2 Nd7, and b6 comes later under good conditions; you are at worst level (-0.4).
ep: b6 lets the pin land first: Bb5! Rc8 Ne5! piles onto c6 faster than you can defend it — after a6 Nxc6 Qc7 Bxa6, White has won material by force (-4.2). The game's Be3 missed it and you went on to win, but the tactic was sitting there the whole time.

pv: a6 Qa4 b5 Qd1 g6 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 b4 Na4 Nd7 O-O Qb8 a3 Bg7 axb4
e: Again a6! — until b5 is covered, every exchange favors White. After a6 Qa4 b5! Qd1 g6 you keep the extra pawn, trade light-squared bishops with Bxd3, and stand solid (-0.6). Prophylaxis first, pawn-grabbing second.
ep: bxc5 opens lines while c6 is still pinnable: Bb5! Rc8 Ne5 Nd7 Nxc6! Rxc6 Bxc6 wins the exchange and more (punish line, -4.0). In the game White recaptured dxc5 and the moment passed — you even won — but the same pin motif kept hanging over the position.

pv: Rb8 Qa4 Qd7 Bb5 Rxb5 Nxb5 e5 Rc1 d4 Nd6+ Bxd6 cxd6 Nd8 Qxd7+ Bxd7 Bg5
e: Rb8! steps off the c-file and hits b2, creating counterplay before White consolidates the c5 bind. The best line even includes an exchange sacrifice — Qa4 Qd7 Bb5 Rxb5! Nxb5 e5 — to get the central pawns rolling; at -2.5 you are worse but active, the only way to live in this structure.
ep: Qa5 leaves the c-file loaded: Bb5! (the game) renews the pin and Nd4! piles on — after Bxc5 comes Nxc6!, hitting your queen, and the forcing Bxc5 Qxc5 Qd4 trades queens with White material up (-4.5). Activity that runs into a pin isn't activity.

pv: Ne4 Nd4 Nxc3 bxc3 Qxc3+ Kf1 Bxc5 Rc1 Bxd4 Rxc3 Bxc3 Bc5 Kd8 Qa4 Na5 Bd6
e: Ne4! creates counterplay at the last moment: it hits c3, and Nxc3 bxc3 Qxc3+ followed by Bxc5! grabs two pawns and breaks the bind. The forced liquidation (Rc1 Bxd4 Rxc3 Bxc3) gives rook, knight and pawns for the queen — still worse at -2.0, but fighting.
ep: Nd7 releases the pressure at the worst time: Bxc6! Rxc6 b4! hits your queen with tempo, and Nd4 forks the c6-rook next — the punish line wins the exchange (-3.7). In the game b4, Qa4 and Bf4 kept you tied up for a long stretch before you broke free and won.

pv: Bxc5 Nb5 Bd3 Ndc7 a6 bxc5 axb5 Na6 Rhd8 Rad1 e4 f3 f5 fxe4 Bxe4 Rxd8
e: Bxc5! solves the attacked e7-bishop by grabbing a pawn and hitting the d4-knight in one move. The tactical point: bxc5 is met by Rxc5!, regaining the pawn while attacking the d5-knight — everything holds. Best line Bxc5 Nb5 Bd3! keeps harassing, and the position stays balanced (+0.1).
ep: Rhd8 allows Nxe7! Kxe7 anyway — the trade White wants, since afterwards Rad1 and f4 leave his knights and extra queenside pawn ruling the board (-3.5). Bxc5 conceded the same trade but got a pawn and active pieces for it. In the game you clung on and eventually won.

pv: Rc6 Ra8+ Kf7 c8=R Rxc8 Rxc8 Be4 Rc7+ Kg6 g4 Bd5 Rd7 Bc6 Rd6 Be4 f3
e: The c7-pawn must be attacked, not just watched: Rc6! hits it, and after Ra8+ Kf7 the promotion c8=Q (or =R) is met by Rxc8 Rxc8, trading your rook for the new queen. You emerge with rook and bishop against two rooks, all pawns on one wing — a comfortable hold (-0.1).
ep: Bf5 guards c8 only passively: Rc1! (instead of promoting at once) supports the pawn, and after Rbd4 c8=R+! Bxc8 Rxc8+ Rd8 Rcc7 it trades itself for your bishop with both white rooks on the seventh (-1.3). In the game c8=Q Bxc8 Rxc8 let your rooks activate — and you went on to win.

pv: Kd2 Kg5 Rd5+ Kf4 e1=Q Rxe1 Kxe1 Ke4 Rd1 g5 Ra1 Kd5 Ra4 Kc6
e: Kd2! escorts the pawn home: with the king covering e1, promotion is unstoppable — Kg5 is met by Rd5+!, and after e1=Q Rxe1 Kxe1 you are a full rook up with the g- and h-pawns still on the board (+7.7). Promote first; the kingside pawns weren't going anywhere.
ep: hxg4 trades exactly the pawns White is desperate to remove: Kxg4 Kd2 h5! gxh5 Kxh5 and only the e-pawn remains. Still winning after e1=Q Rxe1 Kxe1 (+4.6, and you did win), but you handed White every practical drawing chance — Kd2 kept all the material and all the clarity.

pv: Rc8 Ne4 Bb4+ Bd2 Ke7 Nxa7 Bxd2+ Kxd2 Rd8+ Kc3 f5 Ng5
e: Rc8 supports the extra c4 pawn and takes the file the white knight wants to use. Only then is Bb4+ worth playing: after Ne4 Bb4+ Bd2 Ke7 even Nxa7 costs white time, since Bxd2+ Kxd2 Rd8+ Kc3 chases the king and you keep the pawn.
ep: Bb4 first hands white the free tempo a3, so the trade happens on his terms; with the c-file unguarded, Nd6+ Kd7 Nxc4 won the extra pawn straight back, exactly as in the game.

pv: Rd3 Nd6+

pv: Qh4 Re3 Bb6 Bc2 Bxd4 cxd4 f5 exf6 Nxf6 Qe1 Bd7 Bd2 Rac8 Bg6 Ne4 Bxe4
e: Qh4! swings to the kingside with tempo: it attacks h3, forcing Re3 to defend, and - the key point - it controls g4, killing White's Bxh6 trick (gxh6 could then recapture safely with no Qg4+ to follow). Next Bb6 piles on d4 (line: Re3 Bb6 Bc2 Bxd4 cxd4 f5) and your game frees itself (-1.2).
ep: Qb6 heads the wrong way and leaves h6 loose: Bxh6! wins a pawn, since gxh6? invites Qg4+ and a crash on the h-file, and declining (punish: f5 Be3) leaves you a pawn down under pressure. White missed it for one move but landed Bxh6 shortly after anyway.

pv: f6 Qd3 f5 Qg3 Kh7 Be3 a5 a3 a4 Rab1 Nb8 b4 axb3 Rxb3 Qc7 Nb5
e: You're worse, so fight the e5-wedge: f6! opens the f-file for your rook, gives the king air, and after Qd3 f5! the queen-and-bishop battery aimed at h7 is shut down for good (line: f6 Qd3 f5 Qg3 Kh7). Damage control at -1.2 instead of collapse.
ep: Nb8? undevelops and again ignores h6: Bxh6! wins a pawn and keeps the attack alive - f5 exf6! Rxf6 Bg5 hits the rook and White breaks through (the punish line ends Qh7+). In the game White inserted Qd3 first but collected h6 the very next move.

pv: dxe4

pv: Bc6+ Kh2 e5 Re1 exf4 gxf4 Rf6 f5 Kf7 c4 Rxf5 cxb5 Rf2+ Kg3 axb5 Re5

ep: Bd6? lines both bishops up on the d-file: Rd1! and after Bxf4 Rxd7 White wins the d7-bishop straight back, Bxg3 netting only a pawn (+3.6). In the game White missed it with Kg2, keeping you fully winning.

pv: Bc6+ Kh2 e5 Rd1 Rf6 Nd3 e4 Nf4 e3 Re1 Bc5 h4 Bb6 Kh3 Bd7+ Kh2

ep: Bxf4 swaps your monster dark-squared bishop for the cornered knight, and after Rxf4 you can't even take back (Rxf4?? gxf4) - a simplification that halves the advantage, +4.6 to +2.1. In the game you took anyway and White missed gxf4, returning the favour.

pv: e4 Qa5 Bd3 Bxc5 Nf3 Bb4 Bd2 e5 Nb5 Bxd2+ Qxd2 Qxd2+ Nxd2 Ke7 Nc4 d5
e: The c5-pawn was never keepable, so take the centre instead: e4! After ...Qa5 Bd3 Bxc5 Black regains it, but Nf3 and quick development leave you ahead with the strong e4-pawn — a healthy edge instead of contortions to hold a pawn.
ep: Nb5 dreams of Nc7+ but walks into ...Qa5+!: the check attacks the knight at the same time, and after Nc3 Bxc5 Black regains the pawn with easy play. In the game ...e5 came first, and after Bg3 Qa5+ c3?? Qxb5 the knight was lost outright.

pv: Bg5
e: If the bishop must move, Bg5 is the square: it leans on the f6-knight, so after ...Qa5+ Nc3 you always have Bxf6 to damage Black's kingside, and the bishop stays active instead of becoming a target for ...h5–h4.
ep: On g3 the bishop turns into a hook: ...Qa5+ Nc3 h5! and ...h4 comes with tempo against it while Black rounds up c5. In the game the check was blocked the wrong way — c3?? — and ...Qxb5 took the knight; it had to come back via c3.

pv: Nc3 h5 h4 Bxc5 e3 Ne4 Ne2 Bb4 f3 Nxg3 Nxg3 d5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 Qxc3+
e: The b5-knight hangs to the queen, so block the check with it: Nc3 parries and saves the piece in one move. You're still somewhat worse after ...h5 and ...Bxc5, but material stays level — every other block or king move loses the knight.
ep: c3 blocks the check but abandons the knight — ...Qxb5 just takes it. The counter-trick b4 doesn't help: ...Nxb4! cxb4 Qxb4+ and ...Bxc5 next, converting the piece into a winning haul. The game was decided right here.

pv: Rg1 f8=Q Rxf8 Kxf8 Rxg6 b4 c5 bxc5 bxc5 Ke8 Rg8#
e: Rg1 takes the g-file, so promoting doesn't help: f8=Q Rxf8 Kxf8 Rxg6 leaves the white king sealed on the back rank with no escape squares. Once his pawn moves run out (c5 bxc5 bxc5 Ke8) Rg8 is mate in 6. The rook on g1 is doing two jobs at once, attacking g6 and cutting the king off.

pv: Qg5+ Kh8 Qh6+ Kg8 h4 Ne4 Rh3 f5 Nxe4 fxe4 Rg3+ Bg5 Rxg5+ Qxg5 Qxg5+ Kh8

pv: Rd4 Ne4 Nxe4 dxe4 Rxd8 Rxd8 Nh3 Rd5 Nf4 Bg5 Qh5 Rf5 Kb1 Bxf4

pv: Ne5
